metadata.author: Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program

metadata.title: Pax8  - A Cloud Distributor that MSPs Actually Use
metadata.author: Cloud Software Association
metadata.shortDescription:
Join the Cloud Software Association to meet with the speakers directly. http://launchpass.com/cloudassoc/members



In this episode of SaaS Connect by Cloud Software Association, Ryan Walsh, Channel Chief and Chief Product Officer of Pax8—with its 3,000 partners, 200 employees, 20 vendors, and 900 supported products—shares how the company grew when it added the channel, and how you can, too.

Some of the points that are discussed in this profitable presentation include:

* Why do you need a channel? There are a few reasons, the primary one being scale and reach, and other reasons such as the shift to the cloud which is being driven by customers. IDC (the global market intelligence firm) found that MSPs with greater than 50% revenue from cloud offerings outperform those with less. 


* Channel cloud opportunities and where they’re coming from.


* The definition of a channel (essentially, this is a route to market for IT products or services).


* Five lessons from tapping into the channel, and what you can learn from them:
   1. Commit long-term to the IT channel, i.e. 18 months. Don’t walk away because it’s not profitable immediately. That’s not to say you won’t make money during that time, but things start happening at the 18-month mark. For instance, they noticed that they were helping channel partners sell their products to their customers. 18 months is the amount of time that lets the channel community know you're in, you're committed, and you're staying positive.
   2. Build a partner management console.
   3. Support a monthly billing term. Stay away from anniversary billing. Make it simple.
   4. Provide APIs for provisioning and billing.
   5. Partner with channel experts, such as channel communities, cloud marketplaces, integration partners, and new distribution partners.



*Q&A
 - What made Pax8 successful while others struggled?

metadata.title: Microsoft Cloud Solution Provider (CSP) - Simply Explained
metadata.author: m365 Show | M365, Azure Cloud, Power Platform & AI
metadata.shortDescription:
Most businesses buying Microsoft 365 or Azure through a partner are already using CSP without knowing how it works. This episode explains the Cloud Solution Provider program for IT buyers and Microsoft partners: direct versus indirect resellers, how partners earn money, what the new commerce experience changed, and when CSP beats an Enterprise Agreement.

In this episode

  •  00:00 – What CSP is: partners as wholesalers
  •  01:40 – Direct bill versus indirect reseller
  •  03:09 – How partners add value
  •  04:36 – The new commerce experience and term commitments
  •  06:43 – Why customers choose a CSP partner
  •  08:43 – CSP versus Enterprise Agreement
  •  10:24 – Partner requirements and support
  •  12:20 – The big picture
Key takeaways

  •  The Cloud Solution Provider program lets partners resell Microsoft cloud services and own billing, support and provisioning for their customers.
  •  Under the new commerce experience, monthly, annual and triennial terms carry different prices, and seats can be added but not reduced after the short cancellation window.
  •  CSP is a service delivery program rather than a discount program: it suits small and mid-sized businesses, while large, stable organizations should compare it with an Enterprise Agreement.
Worth quoting

“When you buy through a CSP partner, Microsoft is not your billing contact. The partner handles billing, support, and provisioning.” – Mirko Peters (00:57)

“The partner earns the margin on the service layer, not the software. That's the model. The license gets you in the door. The services keep you there.” – Mirko Peters (04:24)

By the end of this episode, you'll know exactly what CSP is, how the money actually flows, and whether it matters for your company. Let's start with the simplest version. What is CSP? The core model, partners as wholesalers. CSP is Microsoft's program that lets partners resell cloud services. That means Microsoft 365, Azure, Dynamics 365, and Enterprise Mobility and Security. Think of it like a wholesale club. Microsoft is the manufacturer. They sell their cloud services at bulk prices to partners. Those partners buy at wholesale, add their own services on top, and sell the whole package to customers. You have three players in the system. Microsoft builds the cloud services. The CSP partner buys them and manages the relationship. And the end customer just wants their email, files, and meetings to work. Here's the thing most people miss. When you buy through a CSP partner, Microsoft is not your billing contact. The partner handles billing, support, and provisioning. 20 years ago, if your email server went down, you called Microsoft or fixed it yourself. Today, you call your partner. They own the relationship. Let me give you an example. Say you run a 50-person company. You buy Microsoft 365 through a local IT partner. That partner manages your licenses, sends you one invoice every month, and provides support when someone can't log in. You never talk to Microsoft directly. You talk to your partner. What does this mean for you? If you're buying Microsoft cloud services through someone right now, you're likely already using CSP. You just didn't know it had a name. Now, not all CSP partners are the same. There are two different flavors, and the one you pick matters. Direct versus indirect reseller. So, there are two paths for partners in the CSP program, direct bill and indirect reseller. They sound similar, but they're actually very different. Direct bill partners buy directly from Microsoft and handle everything themselves, billing, support, infrastructure. It's the hard path. The requirements are steep. You need at least $1 million in trailing 12-month revenue, 12 months of prior experience as an indirect reseller, a solutions partner designation, and a paid Microsoft support plan. In the entire United States, only about 30 partners are direct bill. The other path is indirect reseller, and that's the most common way to become a CSP partner. Instead of buying directly from Microsoft, you work through a distributor, companies like Ingram Micro, Pax8, or Rhipe. The distributor handles the Microsoft relationship, the billing platform, and tier two support, while the reseller focuses on the customer. Picture it like a car dealership. Microsoft is the manufacturer, the distributor is the regional warehouse that stocks the parts, and the reseller is the dealership you walk into when you want to buy a car. You don't talk to the factory, you talk to the dealer, and the dealer gets their inventory from the warehouse. More than 90% of CSP partners are indirect resellers. That's the vast majority. And there's a reason for that. The indirect model has low barriers to entry, no revenue minimum, no support plan required. The distributor provides the backstop. This makes it easy for small IT shops to start reselling Microsoft services without a huge upfront investment. So, what does this mean for you? If you're a small partner wanting to resell Microsoft, indirect is the path. That's how almost everyone starts. You focus on your customers, and the distributor handles the rest. How partners add value. Now you know the two paths a partner can take, but here's the real question. How do these partners actually make money? And what do they bring to the table that you can't get by buying direct from Microsoft? The short answer is that partners don't just resell licenses, they bundle services on top. Think of it like buying a phone. You can buy the phone itself for a certain price, or you can buy the phone with a case, a screen protector, and a warranty. The phone is the license, everything else is the value add. Typical partner offerings include onboarding help, migration from your old system, training for your team, around-the-clock support, and security monitoring. Some partners will even manage your entire IT environment. They become your IT department. Now, here's the thing about the money. The margin on the license itself is small. We're talking about 8 to 15% depending on incentives and volume. That's not nothing, but it's not where the real profit lives. The real profit is in the managed services wrapped around that license. Let me give you a concrete example. Say a partner sells Microsoft 365 Business Premium for $22 per user per month. You can buy that same license directly from Microsoft for $22. Same price. But the partner adds identity setup, device management, and a help desk for an extra $8 per user per month. Now, the customer is paying $30 total, and they get one bill, one support number, and someone who actually knows their business. The partner earns the margin on the service layer, not the software. That's the model. The license gets you in the door. The services keep you there. Now, here's where CSP gets a little tricky. The New Commerce Experience changed the rules. The New Commerce Experience term commitments. In 2022, Microsoft launched something they called the New Commerce Experience or NCE for short, and it completely changed how CSP subscriptions work. Before NCE, the process was straightforward. You bought monthly subscriptions, canceled whenever you wanted, and adjusted seats freely. Hire five people, add five licenses, let two go, remove two without penalties or commitments. It was flexible, almost too flexible. After NCE, everything shifted. Now, you have term commitments. You pick between a one-month, one-year, or three-year term, and each choice carries a different price tag. The monthly term gives you the most flexibility since you can cancel at the end of any month, but you pay a 20% premium over the annual list price. So, if the annual price is $100 per user per month, the monthly price hits 120. That's the cost of flexibility. The annual term is the standard choice. You can pay monthly with a 5% premium, or pay upfront at list price. Most businesses go with the annual term paid monthly because it sits right between cost and flexibility. Then there's the triennial term, which locks in your price for 3 years, and saves you about 12 to 18% compared to renewing annually. But you are locked in. No changes for 3 years. Here's the part that catches people off guard. After you place an order, you have a 7-day cancellation window. Just 7 days to change your mind or adjust quantities. After that, the commitment is binding and seat reductions are not allowed mid-term. You can only add seats, never remove them. Microsoft did this for predictable revenue. They wanted to see their recurring revenue laid out months and years ahead. Partners hated because customers change their minds. A company might plan for 100 seats in January and then need 80 by March, but under NCE, they are still paying for those 20 unused seats until the term ends. The practical impact is simple. Plan your headcount carefully before buying. If you are unsure, it is safer to overbuy slightly than to underbuy. You can always add seats, but you cannot remove them. One more thing. The old grace period, which ended in May 2026, has been replaced by something called the extended term. If your subscription expires and you do not act, it automatically moves to the extended term, billed at the monthly rate plus an additional 3% uplift. It is designed as a short-term bridge, not a long-term solution. Let it sit too long and your costs climb fast. Why customers choose a CSP partner? So, what does all this mean for a business buying Microsoft services? Let's look at it from the customer side. The biggest reason customers choose a CSP partner is consolidated billing. One invoice covers all your Microsoft services plus anything the partner adds on top. You don't have to log into Microsoft's portal, figure out which subscription is which, or reconcile multiple invoices because it all comes from one place. Your partner. Next, support is included. When you buy through a CSP partner, that partner becomes your first line of support. So, you don't need a separate unified support contract from Microsoft. Your partner handles day-to-day issues. Meaning, if something breaks, you call them instead of Microsoft. For a small business without a dedicated IT team, that is a huge deal. Then there's flexibility. Yes, the monthly term costs a 20% premium, but for some businesses that premium is worth it. Think about a landscaping company with 80 employees in the summer and 30 in the winter. Under the old rules, they could scale down easily. Under NCE, they cannot reduce seats mid-term, but they can choose the monthly term and pay the premium for the right to adjust. For seasonal workforces, that trade-off makes sense. Beyond licenses, many partners offer value-add services. They set up security baselines to lock down your tenant, back up your data, provide training when your team moves to new tools, and help with adoption so you actually use what you are paying for. Here is a rule of thumb. If you are under 500 employees, CSP is probably the right path. If you are larger, an enterprise agreement might be cheaper. EA pricing typically comes in 20 to 35% lower per seat for organizations with 500 or more users because Microsoft negotiates volume discounts directly with large customers. But those discounts come with a catch. You are committing to a multi-year term, so you cannot walk away. One more thing to keep in mind, CSP does not include software assurance, which is Microsoft's program for on-premises upgrade rights. If you have a hybrid setup where some stuff is in the cloud and some is on your own servers, software assurance matters. In that case, an enterprise agreement might serve you better. The trade-off is simple. CSP for flexibility and support, EA for the lowest price at scale. CSP versus enterprise agreement, when to use which? So that leads to the big question. When should you go with CSP instead of an enterprise agreement? Enterprise agreements are meant for organizations with 500 or more users, especially when your head count is predictable and you're willing to commit to a multi-year deal. You get volume discounts, software assurance, and a direct relationship with Microsoft. But you also get complexity, true up cycles, enrollment periods, and plenty of fine print. CSP is built for a different kind of customer. Small and medium businesses spending under a million dollars a year on Microsoft services, companies with fluctuating head count, or organizations that want a partner to lead the way instead of figuring it out themselves. Here's something that makes this decision easier. Microsoft has been shutting down older licensing programs. The Microsoft products and services agreement, or MPSA, closed to new business in mid-2025, and new enterprise agreement enrollment stopped in October 2024. You can still renew an existing EA, but you can't start a new one. For most businesses, the choice is already made. CSP under the new commerce experience is the default. Now, I want to be clear about something. CSP is not a discount program. It's a service delivery program. The discount doesn't come from Microsoft. It comes from the partner service. A good partner saves you money by reducing your IT headache, not by selling you a cheaper license. Think of it like buying a car. You can buy direct from the factory and save a few thousand dollars, but the dealership offers test drives, helps with financing, and fixes it when something breaks. You're paying for convenience and support, not just the metal and rubber. What this means for you is pretty straightforward. Under 300 seats, CSP is almost certainly your best bet. Over 500, run the numbers on an enterprise agreement before you decide. If you're in between, it depends on how stable your head count is and how much you value having a partner in your corner. The partner reality, requirements and support. So, being a CSP partner sounds great so far, but it's not free. Microsoft has been raising the bar, especially for direct bill partners, and the requirements are real. Let's start with direct bill. If you want to buy directly from Microsoft and manage everything yourself, you need to meet some serious thresholds. $1 million in trailing 12-month revenue, at least 12 months of experience as an indirect reseller first, at least one solutions partner designation, and you have to purchase a paid Microsoft support plan. Advanced support for partners runs about $15,000 a year, and that's the minimum. Now, compare that to the indirect reseller path. No revenue minimum, no support plan required, the distributor provides the backstop. You sign up, partner with a distributor, and you're in business. That's why the vast majority of partners choose this route. Here's something that surprises a lot of people. All CSP partners are required to provide first-line support to their customers. You cannot escalate most issues to Microsoft. If a customer calls with a problem, you own it, you diagnose it, you fix it or find someone who can. The customer's first call is always to you, not to Microsoft. The support landscape is shifting, too. Microsoft's legacy support plans for partners are being retired. Advanced support for partners, or ASFP, ends in January 2027, and premier support for partners follows shortly after. The replacement is called Unified for Partners, or UFP for short, and it's expected to launch in Microsoft's fiscal year 2027. Here's the opportunity in that change. Partners who earn the support services designation can get up to 50% off on Unified for Partners. That's a significant discount. Microsoft is essentially saying, "Show us you're serious about support, and we'll make it affordable for you." There are also security requirements. All CSP partners must meet the Partner Center Security Score, which means multi-factor authentication, secure application model, and basic security hygiene. Microsoft checks this, and if you fall short, you can lose your ability to transact. The message from Microsoft is clear. Being a CSP partner is about delivering value, not just passing through licenses. The days of buying a block of seats and marking them up are fading. If you're not providing real service, you're not really a CSP partner. The big picture, why CSP matters. So, let's zoom out for a second. CSP delivers most Microsoft cloud transactions for small and medium businesses. It's not a discount program. It's a partnership model. Microsoft hands the customer relationship to partners, and that trust is what makes the whole thing work. Three layers to think about. Microsoft builds the services. Partners wrap those services with support and expertise. Customers get one bill and one point of contact, one person to hold accountable when something breaks. But, here's where the real power lives. Connection. The partner who sets up your Microsoft 365 tenant can also deploy Intune to manage devices. They can configure Defender to block threats. They can help your team actually use Teams instead of just installing it and forgetting about it. You end up with a cohesive set up instead of random tools that don't talk to each other. Think of it like an office building. Microsoft built the building, the walls, the wiring, the plumbing. The CSP partner runs the front desk. They handle the maintenance. They manage the IT closet. Everything works together, so you can just show up and do your job. For customers, here's the good news. You don't need to be a licensing expert. You don't have to know the difference between E3 and E5, or what software assurance covers, or how true up cycles work. Your partner handles that complexity. You just tell them what you need. For partners, the benefits are real. Recurring revenue that smooths out the business cycle, deeper relationships that make you essential. Growing demand from businesses who'd rather not manage IT themselves. The bottom line is this, CSP is how most businesses will consume Microsoft Cloud going forward. The old programs are closing. New ones have arrived and the partner sits right at the center. Here's what I want you to remember. CSP is Microsoft's way of letting partners handle the messy parts, billing, support, and service so customers can focus on running their business. If you're buying Microsoft services today, check who your partner of record is. If you don't have one, now you know why that matters. Microsoft just laid out its FY27 vision at MCAPS Start for Partners and it's a big one. In this episode of TECHnically Unraveled, Kristen Fehrenbach, VP of Global Microsoft Alliance at Pax8, sits down with Dana Abrams Cohen, Director of Global Partner Marketing at Microsoft, to unpack what the latest MCAPS announcements really mean for partners. 

🔑 Key Topics Covered
 ✅ What Frontier Transformation actually means and why Microsoft has built FY27 around it
 ✅ Microsoft's vision for people and AI agents working together
 ✅ The $1.3 trillion partner opportunity and the $625 billion SMB segment
 ✅ Understanding Microsoft IQ, Agent 365, and agentic workflows
 ✅ The new Agentic Partner Capability Score and why partners should care
 ✅ Frontier Partner specialization and new agentic specialization paths
 ✅ Partner skilling, certifications, and Agent P opportunities
 ✅ The new $0 Microsoft 365 Copilot trial for up to 25 users and how partners can leverage it
 ✅ Why security, governance, and trust are critical in an AI-first world

metadata.title: How MSPs Are Becoming Managed Intelligence Providers | Pax8 Beyond EMEA 2026 Partner Panel
metadata.author: Pax8
metadata.shortDescription:
How do MSPs turn AI into real revenue? Three MSP owners share how they went from an MSP to MIP (managed intelligence provider), and what they would avoid.

AI is changing what small and mid-sized businesses expect from their technology provider. In this Pax8 Beyond partner panel moderated by Pax8 EMEA CEO, Harald Nuij, three managed service providers share how they moved toward becoming managed intelligence providers. They cover the wins, the mistakes and the one thing they'd tell any MSP owner to do on Monday.

Meet the panel: 
• Markus Gratopp, Owner, Gratopp.IT (Siegen, Germany) 
• Ian Groves, Managing Director, StartTech (West Midlands, UK) 
• Gert-Jan Slot, Co-founder, Fit Secure

What you'll learn: 
✅ Why handing customers Copilot licenses alone doesn't drive AI adoption 
✅ How an AI transformation assessment opens CEO-level business conversations 
✅ How to get your team on board, and why your techs may become business consultants 
✅ Building AI agents vs. brokering tools: when each makes sense 
✅ How MSPs are pricing AI services, from one-time projects to MRR 
✅ "Assess, secure, build, adapt": how assessments buy you time while AI moves fast

Chapters 📚
0:00 - Introduction by Harald Nuij on why AI is changing what SMBs expect from MSPs 
0:58 - Meet the panelists 
2:29 - The first proof point: MSP to MIP 
5:22 - What had to change: team, process and skills 
8:51 - How customer conversations changed 
10:46 - The Transformation Discovery Assessment (TDA) 
12:14 - Roadmaps and capacity planning 
13:27 - Why the assessment changed everything 
16:48 - What didn't work: lessons and pivots 
18:38 - Builder or broker? 
22:04 - Marketing and branding an AI offering 
25:05 - Monetizing AI: projects, pricing and MRR 
28:40 - Buying time: assess, secure, build, adapt 
29:45 - Harald's final question: one thing to do on Monday

👉 Subscribe for more insights on AI adoption and the future of managed services.

There must be something worse that you did. >> Oh, where should I start? Yeah, when you try much things there is room for error. So yeah, we had that quite often but it it all been narrowed down to compare we're all like technical companies, right? And most of our clients are not. Yeah I know that. >> And I well most of the people know this joke. I want to make it Gert is like technical in Janis sales. So that that's what happened there. >> So you're not a builder? We've been through focusing on cyber, we've been through telephony, we've been through cloud. And I think you've got to be confident that if you're not going to lean into this and try and do something in your MSP, then you've got to brace yourself to potentially be left behind. So you've got to be comfortable that you've you've picked the right path on that. >> Yeah. And John, your golden tip? >> Yeah. Um I think I I'm I already said it a little bit. Um stop worrying about the tech so much. It's important. It's a tool set. Because what we will do is all the assessments and I will ask my clients, can I use them to convince other clients to do this assessment as well? And that really goes very fast. And also with with partners we work together with on AI, we help them with doing the assessments. So it it goes really fast. So go out there, maybe Thursday, not Monday, and and talk about the business part and less about the tech. That's what I would say. >> Good stuff. Um we've come up to the end of this session, but I know for a fact that these three gentlemen are more than happy to answer any questions. So if you meet them at the expo or on the hallway, just give them a gentle gentle nudge. Please save your questions, bottle them up and and send them over to these guys. Big round of applause for our panelists today. >> Well done, mate. >> Thank you guys. >> Thank you. Thank you.

segments.text: - [Instructor] VIP Marketplace is a platform
that enables resellers like you
to offer Adobe licenses directly on your online marketplaces
and making it easy for your small business
or large organization to manage the process
from purchasing, to provisioning and billing.
In the VIP Program,
there are a few things you should know,
and in this video we will cover
the roles within the program,
who can sell and key benefits for resellers,
like customizing software proposals
for your customer's unique needs,
and simplify selling and managing Adobe licenses
so you can get the best customer retention.
Okay, more about the roles.
Direct Partners or Adobe Partner Connection, or APC,
reseller partners who contract with Adobe.
Typically, they're platinum resellers or distributors.
They manage and distribute Adobe VIP Marketplace licenses
through their technology platforms or marketplaces,
integrated directly with Adobe through APIs.
They also provide support to their resellers.
Resellers can either be Direct Partners,
selling directly to end customers,
or distributor authorized resellers.
They resell VIP Marketplace licenses
through Direct Partners marketplaces.
Resellers manage their customers through these marketplaces.
VIP Marketplace members or customers
manage their licenses through the Adobe Admin Console,
which works seamlessly
with the Direct Partner's marketplaces.
It's important to note that the customer experience
remains nearly identical for those migrating
from VIP to VIP Marketplace.
You might be wondering who can sell
through the VIP Marketplace?
Direct Partners can purchase directly from Adobe
and manage the distribution of VIP Marketplace licenses.
While resellers, including distributor authorized resellers,
can offer VIP Marketplace licenses to customers
through Direct Partner's platforms.
Whatever the role, our goal is to make everything
from purchasing to managing Adobe software licenses
easy for everyone.
To do this, there are two web-based tools
used to administer VIP Marketplace,
one for customers and one for Direct Partners or resellers.
The Admin Console is a centralized management tool
that customer administrators use
to easily add and administer licenses,
assign and unassign users,
inform users about software deployment and monitor storage.
With VIP Marketplace,

It may even be the only move but it's also a confession. Adobe is no longer sure people will come to it, so it's going to them. And look at who the conference was really for. Adobe MAX has always been the show for individual creative professionals. This year, one respected industry publication noted the focus shifted to artificial intelligence workflows for large companies. The incoming chief executive took the stage. Talk was about content at scale, brand systems, and marketing teams. That's where the money is, but it raises a hard question for anyone who learned Photoshop in a bedroom. Is Adobe still building tools for you or for the corporation that hires you? There was one more thing missing from the keynotes, a price. Adobe announced a wave of agents, models, and shortcuts, but didn't say what most of them would cost, and some of the headline tools are still in private testing. For subscribers who already pay $70 a month and then spend generative credits on the newest features, that silence lands badly. Every new agent raises the same thought in a designer's head. Is this included or is it another toll? Adobe needs artificial intelligence to justify its price. If it starts to feel like a second bill stacked on top of the first, it won't keep customers in. It will push them toward the door. The case against panic. Now, it would be easy to write Adobe's obituary. Plenty of people already have, but that would be lazy, and the numbers won't let us. Walk into almost any advertising agency, newsroom, or post-production house today, and you'll still find Adobe on nearly every screen. Clients still ask for the layered file. Printers still expect the familiar formats. Teams still share projects across Photoshop, Illustrator, and Premiere every single day. Habits that took 30 years to build don't disappear in one bad year on the stock market. Adobe generated a record $2.52 billion in operating cash in its third quarter and spent 2.23 billion of it buying back about nine and a half million of its own shares. In April, its board approved a new buyback program worth up to 25 billion dollars. Its artificial intelligence first products now bring in more than 650 million dollars a year, growing more than 150 percent. Free versions of its creative apps have pulled in more than 100 million users, up more than 70 percent. Its interim finance chief says the goal is long-term durable growth. And some experts argue the threats are really opportunities in disguise. One technology research firm argued that Google's image model could actually help Adobe users, letting them brainstorm quickly and then move into Creative Cloud for detailed refinement and final production. Analysts note that Adobe's earnings estimates are still rising every year. Its adjusted operating margin sits around 44 percent, the kind of profitability most software companies only dream about. At around nine times forward earnings, the stock is priced as if the business is shrinking. It isn't. One film industry publication put the situation in a useful frame. Adobe faces a Kodak-style question, it argued, but not a Kodak-style collapse. Kodak had the technology and still failed to change its business model in time. Adobe has the technology, the customers, and the cash. What it doesn't yet have is proof that it can charge for the new world the way it charged for the old one. But here's the problem with the bull case. 650 million dollars sounds enormous until you set it against 27 and a half billion dollars in total recurring revenue. The new business is real. It's just tiny next to the old one it's supposed to protect. And that old business still rests on one assumption, that professionals will keep paying 70 dollars a month because they have nowhere else to go. In 2026, for the first time, they have plenty of places to go. What happens next? The next few weeks will matter more than anything Adobe has faced in years. On December 1, Anil Chakravarthy becomes chief executive and Narayen moves to executive chair. Then, in mid-December, Adobe reports its fourth quarter. Every analyst on Wall Street will be checking one thing first. Did new recurring revenue really double the way Adobe needs it to? If it did, the bears look early. If it didn't, a new chief executive gets the perfect excuse to reset expectations lower and start the clock fresh. And beyond the numbers, the new chief executive inherits three questions that no earnings call can answer. Can artificial intelligence make Photoshop, Illustrator, and Premiere more valuable or does it simply make them easier to replace? Can a company built on keeping customers locked in learn to win them over instead? And can a leader from the corporate marketing side of the business protect the tools that made Adobe a household name? But the real verdict won't come from one earnings call. It will come from people you'll never read about in an analyst note. Imagine a young designer finishing art school this year. Every teacher trained her on Photoshop and Illustrator. Every job listing still asks for them. Then she sends her first freelance invoice and does the math on $70 a month. She downloads Affinity for nothing. She cuts her reel in Resolve for nothing. She asks a chatbot to fix a photo and it does. She doesn't hate Adobe. She isn't making a statement. She just never becomes a paying customer. Now multiply her by a million. That's the future Wall Street is trying to price. It isn't a sudden collapse. It's a slow, silent shrinking of the next generation. That's what's really at stake for Photoshop, Illustrator, and Premiere. The question isn't whether they're good. They're still extraordinary. The question is whether anyone will need to learn them. For 30 years, Adobe won because the whole creative world had to come through its doors. This month in Miami Beach, Adobe opened those doors and invited the machines to walk in and do the work. Adobe built the tools that taught the world how to create. Now it's teaching the machines to use them and hoping the world still remembers who made them. If you want more stories like this, subscribe and like the video. There's a lot more coming.

It started in a basement in Ann Arbor, Michigan. In 1987, a doctoral student named Thomas Knoll wrote a little program to display and change digital images on his Mac. His brother John, who worked in visual effects, saw what it could become. Adobe licensed it in 1988 and on February 19th, 1990, it shipped the very first version of Photoshop for the Macintosh only. Back then, basic retouching on a dedicated high-end system could cost around $300 an hour. Photoshop put that power on a desk. To understand why the 2026 decision matters, you have to remember how Photoshop used to be sold. For most of its life, it came in a box. You paid once, you installed it from a disk, and it was yours for as long as your computer could run it. A full Creative Suite 6 Design Standard bundle listed at $1,299. Painful, yes, but you owned it. Then came May 2013. Adobe announced that Creative Suite 6 would be the last of its kind. From then on, Photoshop and its sister apps would be rented month by month through something called Creative Cloud. The reaction was instant. A and college student from Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, named Derek Schoffstall, started a petition asking Adobe to keep selling perpetual licenses. It collected 4,400 signatures in 4 days. By the middle of August, it had passed 38,000. The people signing it had done the math. At $50 a month, a subscription overtook the price of that design standard box after just 26 months. After that, every month was money you'd never have spent before, and you'd never stop spending it. Here's the part the petitioners didn't want to hear. It worked anyway. By mid June 2013, Adobe had 700,000 subscribers and was on track for 1 and 1/4 million by the end of the year. An Adobe executive had already set a goal of 4 million by 2015. The anger was loud. Photoshop stopped being a product you bought and became a bill you paid, like electricity, like rent. And once something becomes a bill, the company sending it starts to believe it can always send a slightly bigger one. That's exactly what happened. videos.full_text: Adobe is giving things away for free. Photoshop inside ChatGPT for free. Firefly, Express and Acrobat, paywalls pulled back. Two free months for the same customers it used to charge just for leaving and a price increase worth half a billion dollars quietly put on hold. For 13 years Adobe never had to ask nicely. Now it's practically begging. And here's the strange part. It's working. Adobe just passed 1 billion monthly users and posted the best quarter in its 44 year history. Wall Street is selling anyway. So why is the most powerful company in creative software suddenly crawling back to its customers? And why isn't anybody buying it? To understand why this is such a big deal, you have to remember how Adobe used to treat the people who paid it. For most of its life, Adobe sold software the old way. You paid once, you owned it, and you could keep using that copy of Photoshop for as long as your computer would run it. Then in 2013 Adobe made a decision that changed the entire industry. No more ownership. From now on you would rent Photoshop every month forever. They called it Creative Cloud and for Adobe it was a masterpiece. A one time sale is lumpy. A subscription is a toll booth. Every month the same customers drive through the same gate and drop the same coins in the bucket. Investors will pay almost anything for that kind of predictability. And Adobe didn't just have a toll booth. It had the toll booth on the only road in town. If you worked in design, photography, video or advertising, Adobe wasn't really a choice. It was the standard. Agencies traded Photoshop files. Printers expected InDesign. Editors were trained on Premiere. You could hate Adobe all you wanted, but leaving meant leaving the language everyone in your field was speaking. So Adobe learned something very early. Its customers would complain and then they would pay. And Adobe built its pricing around that lesson. The plan most people ended up on was called annual paid monthly. It looked like a monthly subscription. It was priced like a monthly subscription. It was billed like a monthly subscription. But it wasn't one. It was a one-year contract chopped into 12 installments. And if you tried to leave early, there was a catch. Adobe charged an early termination fee worth half of every payment left on your contract. So if you signed up for a three-month freelance job in January and tried to cancel in April, Adobe would tell you that before you could go, you owed it half of the next eight or nine months for something you weren't going to use. According to the federal government, a lot of people didn't know that fee existed until the moment they tried to leave. The government said the details were buried in fine print or hidden behind tiny icons you had to hover over to find. And when people did try to cancel, they ran into page after page of warnings, offers, and extra steps online or were passed between representatives on the phone. That wasn't a bug in the system. For years, it was the system, and it worked beautifully. Subscriptions now make up about 97% of Adobe's revenue. In fiscal 2025, Adobe brought in $23.8 billion. It generated $9.85 billion in free cash flow that year, nearly five times what it produced a decade earlier. And over the last four quarters, it kept almost 36 cents of every dollar it sold as operating profit. The typical company in the S&P 500 keeps about 19. So for a long time, there was simply no reason for Adobe to be nice. And it wasn't. In 2025, Adobe renamed its flagship bundle. Creative Cloud All Apps became Creative Cloud Pro. The new name came with new generative tools, a pile of monthly credits for creating images and video and a new price. In North America, the annual plan billed monthly went from $59.99 a month to $69.99. And Adobe didn't ask existing customers whether they wanted the upgrade. In June 2025, it moved them over automatically. If you did nothing, you just saw the higher price on your next bill. Then the smaller plans started moving too. By 2026, the Lightroom plan with a terabyte of storage had gone from $11.99 a month to $14.99 on the annual plan billed monthly. Paying for the whole year upfront went from $119.88 to $119. Existing subscribers would see the new price at renewal. And if you were a business, you got your own version. Adobe raised the price of Acrobat Standard for its teams and enterprise customers starting April 1st, 2026. At the same time, it offered those customers a discount to move up to a more expensive product called Acrobat Studio. So the deal was simple. Pay more for what you have or pay a little more than that for something bigger. Even the way Adobe raised prices around the world was creative. In August 2026, it started adjusting Creative Cloud and Acrobat prices in a list of countries including Argentina, Brazil, Egypt, India, Indonesia, Korea, Kuwait, the Philippines, and Turkey. The official reason was currency fluctuations. The practical result was a bigger bill. So you can imagine how Adobe's customers felt about all this. Actually, you don't have to imagine. They wrote it down. On Adobe's own community forum, one customer in Europe described logging into their account in October 2026 and finding two choices. Renew for another year at €144 or pay an early termination fee of almost €100 to leave. They asked, quite reasonably, how Adobe could justify charging nearly 100 euros just because someone wanted to cancel. Another forum user had a sharper idea about Adobe's retention tactics. When you try to cancel, Adobe often offers you a discount or a few free months to stay. This person's suggestion was simple. Instead of offering me free months I don't want, why not just refund me for the time I'm not using? Someone else wrote that after signing up for Adobe Express, the only way they could finally stop the charges was to go to their bank. Their verdict, never again. On Reddit, one user explained they'd tried to cancel an After Effects subscription they weren't using and wanted to avoid a $100 cancellation fee. metadata.title: Understanding Agentic AI in CX- An Executive Interview with Zoom
metadata.author: Telarus
metadata.shortDescription: In an interview with Chris Morrissey of Zoom, the conversation delves into the transformative potential of agentic AI in customer experience (CX). This advanced AI technology can autonomously make decisions and take actions, significantly impacting the CX market, especially in contact centers with the use of voice bots. While AI enhances efficiency by providing 24/7 support, it is acknowledged that human agents are still essential for fostering connections. Zoom is expanding its offerings to include innovative CX solutions, experiencing notable growth with over 1500 customers. The discussion emphasizes the importance of leveraging AI to create new opportunities in the evolving market.

metadata.title: Gartner UCaaS Magic Quadrant 2026 EXPLAINED (Cisco, Microsoft, RingCentral, Zoom)
metadata.author: CX without the BS
metadata.shortDescription:
Gartner named Cisco, Microsoft, RingCentral, and Zoom Leaders in the 2026 UCaaS Magic Quadrant. So why does RingCentral sit at 1.8 stars on Trustpilot across nearly 2,000 reviews?

That gap is the whole episode. On G2 and Capterra, RingEX sits at 4.2 out of 5. Go to Trustpilot, where the people who actually live with the phones and the billing leave reviews, and it drops to 1.8. The BBB is worse - roughly 1.06 out of 5, with 596 complaints filed in the last three years and 206 in the last twelve months alone. Sixteen phone calls to cancel. Four months to close an account. Overbilling that took an FCC complaint to move. One reviewer could hear motorbikes and chickens in the background of the support call.

And it isn't only RingCentral. Gartner flagged Cisco for capping financial remedies on Webex Calling outages at 5% of the monthly fee. Microsoft's Copilot still sits outside standard UCaaS licensing with its own price tag. Zoom got called out for inconsistent AI experiences and licensing bundling that leaves renewing customers facing higher costs and shifting entitlements. Then Gartner quietly walked back its own forecast - 90% of organizations running calling through their office suite by 2028, revised down to 70%. A twenty point retreat on a prediction barely a year old.

Second half is NICE and RingCentral finally going bidirectional. NICE resells RingEX, RingCentral keeps selling CXone, and on paper both sides get the one pane of glass everybody's been asking for. But when the tightly integrated system breaks at 9PM on a Friday, whose queue does that ticket land in? Does the customer get one company owning one outcome, or two companies pointing at each other while the advisor holds the angry phone call?

Leader badges and partnership announcements are not the product. Support that shows up and pricing that doesn't surprise you on the first invoice - that's what you're actually selling. Telarus Partner Summit is August 11-13 in Grapevine, Texas. Find me at booth 801.

Been a RingCentral, NICE, Cisco, or Zoom customer? Drop your experience in the comments. That's the data the Magic Quadrant doesn't capture.

1:25 RingCentral: 4.2 Stars on G2, 1.8 on Trustpilot

3:05 Cisco's 5% Outage Cap, Copilot Pricing, Zoom's Bundling
3:50 Gartner Walks Back Its Own Forecast 20 Points
4:20 Real Support vs. Fake Support
4:45 NICE and RingCentral Go Bidirectional
5:45 Who Owns the Ticket at 9PM on a Friday?
6:25 What Buyers Should Demand as Proof
7:00 Telarus Partner Summit 2026, Booth 801
8:05 Level365, VoiceIQ, and Selling the Way Buyers Buy

metadata.title: 6 Steps to Win Every Software Negotiation
metadata.author: Tropic
metadata.shortDescription:
Most teams either over prepare for weeks and still wonder if they got a good deal, or wing it and face a 20% price increase they never saw coming. The result is lost leverage, missed savings, and vendors who know you're unprepared.

Here's how to fix it with a streamlined 6-step playbook that turns software renewals from reactive fire drills into strategic wins.

Courtney Meagher. a procurement expert at Tropic, breaks down exactly how to prepare for renewals 60-90 days in advance, run discovery calls that uncover vendor leverage points, and negotiate terms that go far beyond just price. You'll learn why starting early isn't over preparing but essential for multiple negotiation rounds, how to use timing as leverage when reps have commitment dates, and the specific research that takes just 15 minutes but creates powerful negotiation angles.

The episode covers how to align internal stakeholders before talking to your rep, what baseline data to gather from your current contract, and how to run discovery calls strategically by understanding their position before revealing yours. You'll discover why keeping decision makers out of early discussions gives you natural negotiation buffers and how to request quotes for different scenarios based on your team's actual needs.

For the negotiation itself, learn how to anchor lower than where you want to land, protect pricing while improving terms, and handle new AI features that vendors try to bundle at inflated prices. The final step reveals how to layer on strategic value beyond price once commercial terms are settled, including uplift caps, free months, and flexible payment terms.

Key topics covered:
[00:00] Intro
[00:15] Why most renewal negotiations fail
[00:35] Strategic negotiation beats reactive fire drills
[00:56] Start 60 to 90 days early
[01:17] Research vendor pricing and alternatives
[01:37] Align stakeholders before vendor calls
[01:57] Gather contract baseline data first
[02:32] Run discovery calls strategically
[03:21] Quote different growth scenarios
[03:53] Negotiate with full leverage picture
[04:24] Push steep discounts on AI features
[04:48] Layer strategic value beyond price
[05:14] Cap future price increases
[05:31] Complete renewal preparation checklist

Subscribe for more SaaS buying and renewal strategies that save time and money.

Learn more about Tropic:  https://www.tropicapp.io/
Join The Spend Table newsletter here: https://www.tropicapp.io/newsletter

Unlock the secrets of SaaS renewals 🚀 Dive deep into the challenges companies face in managing software subscriptions and renewals. From the ease of an employee swiping a credit card leading to uncontrolled sprawl, to the lack of visibility and policies, discover why it's a constant struggle. Hear insights from procurement pro and SaaS negotiator Dylan Margonari, on the impact of limited bandwidth within organizations, often leaving department managers negotiating and monitoring agreements on top of their busy schedules. Explore the dynamic nature of the market and how it influences negotiation tactics. Join us as we break down the three critical factors that make SaaS renewals a daily management challenge. #SaaS #Renewals #TechManagement #procurement

want to talk about today. My name is

issues that we see when we're

clients that have not done enough

time do you really need to negotiate one

depends. It depends on the size of the
agreement. It depends on the risk
profile of the particular technology. It
depends on, you know, the vendor that
you're dealing with. And it depends on
how much money you're spending. But, you
know, at a minimum, I think you'd
probably want 60 days to negotiate one
of these agreements. If it's going to be
a large enterprise deal, you're going to
want much more time. Um, it just depends
on the deal. But you don't want to rush
this process. You want to take a
reasoned review and analysis of these
agreements. You want to discuss them
with counsel. You want to have a
strategy for dealing with the software
vendor. You want to distill down what
the concessions are that you're going to
ask for. You want to have backup
positions. And ideally, you'd want to be
negotiating with more than one vendor at
a time. There's a whole process
associated with this. And it's not
something that you can just jump into. I
think you know the mistake that many of
our clients make and it's not really
their fault. It's really the
unreasonable expectations that are put
on them by the vendor is that these are
simple contracts. They'll put in front
of you, you know, a onepage docu sign or
a two-page document. But the reality is
as you look at that agreement, it often
times will reference via URLs other
agreements that are more substantive.
I've had a document recently that looked
like a simple two-page order form that
uh incorporated by reference um and not
in a very clear way about a 15-page
contract that required massive
substantive review that was incredibly
one-sided, unreasonable, and ownorous.
And that really is what you're getting
yourself into. Um you know, it's not
going to be as simple as you think it's
going to be. The next gotcha is really
clients that don't understand what their
business requirements are. They don't
have an understanding of what their
current state is. They don't have an
understanding of what their future state
is going to be. And the problem with
that is that they don't have an
understanding of what types of
functionality gaps are going to be
present in that software. And where that
comes out in the software negotiation
process is really in a couple places.
You want to have a robust user
acceptance testing process. You want to
understand what the deliverable the
deliverables are going to be. You want
to make sure that the software is
identified in the contract accurately,
that you know what you're licensing,
that it is consistent with what you
think you're buying and what you think
you're getting. So, all of that needs to
be done on the front end. In connection
with the negotiation of these SAS
agreements, you really have to make an
effort to understand the vendor's
pricing model. I think that should go
without saying, but it's not always
intuitive. It doesn't always uh present
itself in a clear way. And I think what
goes handinhand with understanding how
much money you're going to spend is
having an understanding of, you know,
what the renewal rate is going to be
when you have to renew that contract.
Typically, these SAS agreements are
going to have a limited term, an initial
term. It could be anywhere from two to
seven years on the front end. And
ideally, you will have capped the
vendor's ability to increase uh the cost
of that software on a year-over-year
basis or maybe it will be capped for the
duration of that initial term. But when
there is a subsequent term, that vendor
is going to want to increase the price
and capture additional revenue. And
ideally, what you want to do is
incorporate into your agreement a
restriction on that vendor's ability to
increase the uh price of the software
for subsequent terms. I think you've got
to be aware as you're negotiating those
that they're going to want to have
certain carveouts. They're going to
exclude certain pricing models. They're
going to exclude certain types of
products from that cap. And that can all
be reasonable, but it's going to be a
nuance negotiation and you need to know
what you're getting yourself into. As
far as the key provisions in these
agreements that you want to look at, I
think, you know, in today's day and age,
really data security comes to the
forefront. You want to have an
understanding of what they're going to
do with your data, how they're going to
treat that data, what their obligations
are with respect to that data. And then
you're going to want to be able to hold
their feet to the fire. you're going to
want to have want to have contractual
obligations with the way that they
process that data, with the way that
they store that data. And if something
goes wrong, if there's a data incident,
if there's some sort of confidentiality
issue, if there's a breach, you want to
be able to have substantive remedies.
And typically, you know, what remedies
you're going to have, whatever remedies
you're going to be able to negotiate
with respect to a data incident, you're
going to want to either have those
damages subject to a super cap or be
carved out from any kind of cap on the
liability. Um because I think you know
th those can be substantive damages and
it often does not make sense depending
on the size of the deal to cap those
damages at you know the 12 the the the
amount of money that you spent in the 12
months preceding the issue giving rise
to the claim. You want to think about
scalability. You want to think about
your future expansion. Again, you want
to have all the flexibility built into
that contract that you can so that
you're not giving that vendor the
ability to extract additional fees from
you as you go ahead and and utilize that
software in your business. You want to
make sure that you've got the ability to
add users at defined prices. You want to
be able to swap out users um or whatever
other metric is applicable. Again, it's
all about flexibility and scalability
and being able to think proactively on
the front end so that you minimize the
likelihood that you're going to be um
you know paying exorbitant fees to that
vendor for using the software or the way
you that you need to use that software
in your business. You want to focus on
exit and termination clauses. You don't
want to enter into any kind of a
contract that you're unable to get out
of. And I think that should go without
saying, but in the SAS SAS context, you
know, vendors are very wary of giving
you the ability to terminate for
convenience. And the reason for that
really is that they are going to provide
you with some sort of discount off the
list price of that software. And it's
going to be based off of the length of
your utilization of the software for the
duration of that term. And you know,
they're not going to want you just to
walk away uh from that obligation. and
then there they will then be, you know,
out all the revenue that they expected
to generate from you. And often times
what you will see is some sort of a
provision that will allow you to get out
of that contract, but there's an
acceleration clause and all the fees
that would have been due and owing for
the remainder of that term are
automatically you you're automatically
obligated to pay those to the vendor. I
think you you've got to understand that
you've got to figure out ways to
mitigate that and negotiate something
that's reasonable and works for you. You
want to pay particularly close attention
to the SLAs, the service level
agreement. And really what this is is
there should be some sort of uptime
guarantees associated with your
utilization of that software product. Uh
you know, typically it would be a 99.99
percentage uptime guarantee with some
sort of real remedy if the vendor
doesn't meet that obligation. And that
remedy can be, you know, credits, it
could be a refund, it could be a
termination right, depends on what it
is. We would typically give a vendor,
you know, three bytes at the apple,
letting them uh, you know, deviate from
that uptime guarantee for a certain
amount of time. You know, maybe three
times in a six-month period or three
times in a year. And if it happens a
fourth time, then you've got a real
remedy. You have the ability to walk
away from that contract without further
obligation or you've get some sort of a
refund or whatever whatever it is. And
then the last thing I think you really
want to think about is, you know, in
connection with the termination of that
initial term or the expiration of that
initial term, what kind of renewal
rights do you have? Um, you know, what
is the notification period? How do you
notify the vendor that you either do not
want to renew or you do want to renew?
You want that process to be easy. You
want to be in control of that process
and you don't want to be in a situation
where you are inadvertently signed up
for, you know, another seven-year term
when you have no intention of continuing
to use that software. I think that is
going to be fundamentally problematic
for you. One of the other things that
you want to think about in the context
of termination really is how are you
going to get your data out of that cloud
system? You know, that that that vendor
has your data. It's on a server
somewhere. It's your data. you want to
be able to get it out, extract it, be
able to utilize it in connection with a
new product if you're deciding not to to
continue with that product. So, these
are some of the things that I think you
really need to focus on as you're
negotiating these SAS agreements.
Certainly not a definitive list, but
something to uh really think about and
get you pointed in the right direction.
I hope you find this information useful.
To the extent you have any questions
about any of the issues uh I spoke about
in this video, please feel free to reach
out to me at tafflaw.com. I'd love to
talk to you. Thank you.

metadata.title: What Most People Miss in Software and AI Contracts That Costs Them Thousands
metadata.author: Tropic
metadata.shortDescription:
You negotiated great SaaS and AI pricing but missed the contract terms that matter most. Mandy McGovern, a leader on Tropic's procurement services team, breaks down the critical clauses beyond pricing that protect you from surprise costs, auto renewals, and steep price increases at renewal time.

Most buyers focus only on upfront pricing and miss the terms that determine long-term costs. This episode covers billing terms, auto renewal clauses, price caps, rollover provisions, and co-marketing language that can save or cost your company thousands.

Key topics covered:
[00:00] Intro
[00:25] Great pricing without favorable terms fails
[00:40] Billing terms suppliers sneak past buyers
[01:06] Auto renewal clauses hide in agreements
[01:25] Opt out periods vary wildly
[01:54] Price caps prevent renewal shock
[02:27] Pricing model changes bypass price caps
[02:50] Language that protects against repackaging
[03:13] 90 day notice requirements for changes
[03:31] Rollover clauses save unused volume
[03:53] Overage billing methods impact costs
[04:23] Rate tables enable scalable growth
[04:45] Co marketing terms require brand protection

Learn how to negotiate protective contract language, avoid common renewal traps, and set up automated alerts to track critical dates. Mandy shares specific language templates and strategies used by procurement professionals to maintain favorable terms throughout the contract lifecycle.

Whether you're buying new SaaS tools or preparing for renewals, these contract negotiation tactics will help you avoid costly surprises and maintain the pricing you worked hard to achieve.

This video is about " what is a group purchasing organization or GPO?"

In the United States, a group purchasing organization is an entity or platform that allows any business to join a group of other buyers who are interested in the same products and services. By joining a GPO, you’re able to leverage the collective buying power of a group of businesses to get discounts from vendors, meaning you can take advantage of those larger discounts without actually purchasing more.

metadata.title: Hospital Group Purchasing Organizations (GPOs) Explained
metadata.author: AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained
metadata.shortDescription:
Hospital Group Purchasing Organizations (GPOs) Are Collective Buyers for a Hospital's Supplies.  Those Supplies Include Medications, Hospital Beds, Linens, Operating Room Supplies... Even Cleaning Supplies.

Hospital Supplies Make Up About 33% of a Hospital's Budget and They Are the Second Largest Budgetary Item After Payroll.  US Hospitals Spend About $240B Per Year on Supplies.

Examples of the Largest GPOs are Premier, which has $1.3B Per Year in Revenue and Vizient, which has $714M Per Year in Revenue.

GPOs Make Money By Charging the Manufactures an 'Administrative Fee' of 1.5% to 3% of Total Sales to a Hospital.  Even Though the GPO is Negotiating Discounts for the Hospital, They Are Still Being Paid a Commission by the Manufacturer.

GPOs Have a 'Safe Harbor' Exemption from the Federal Anti-Kickback Statute.  In the 1980s when Medicare Moved to Prospective Payment with Set Prices, GPOs Were No Longer Seen as a Possible Source of Escalating Medicare Costs and So Were Granted Their 'Safe Harbor' Status.

Some Complaints Against GPOs Include:
1) That They Are Anti-Competitive Against Smaller and Newer Supply Manufacturers in Favor of Large Manufacturers That Give Them Larger Unit Discounts.

2) They Have a Conflict-of-Interest Against Lowering Costs for Their Hospital Clients Since They are Paid a Commission by the Supply Manufacturers.

Hospitals That Run Health Insurance Plans Such at UPMC and Intermountain Healthcare Might Be Particularly Focused on Their Supply Costs Since They Collect Premium and Are At Risk for the Cost of a Patient's Medical Care... and in fact, these two hospital systems do work with their GPO in a unique fashion.

Sources: https://www.supplychainassociation.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/GPO-Kusserow-Assessment-2013.pdf; http://www.singerpubs.com/ethikos/html/premier.html; https://intermountainhealthcare.org/news/2015/05/intermountain-reaches-agreement-in-principle-to-acquire-ari-ownership-in-amerinet/; https://www.modernhealthcare.com/article/20160707/NEWS/160709971/upmc-launches-supply-chain-venture-with-ibm-s-watson; https://www.owler.com/company/vizientinc; https://www.statnews.com/2019/11/19/hospital-supply-chain-overspending-too-many-choices/; https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20190618005619/en/Premier-Inc.-Partners-with-Pensiamo-Inc.-and-UPMC-to-Launch-AI-Powered-Pharmaceutical-Supply-Chain-Solution

In this edition of The PBM Insider, I discuss an often overlooked yet significant revenue source for the corporations that own major PBMs, Group Purchasing Organizations (aka, GPOs). Never heard of them? You're not alone. BUT, GPOs are a critical link in the movement of drugs from the pharmaceutical manufacturer to the patient and they are collecting BILLIONS of dollars along the way and, rather than adding value, seem to be significantly adding to the cost of prescription drugs in the US. Take a listen...

#PBM #ThePBMInsider #PrescriptionNetwork #letustakecareofyou #PBMdoneright

metadata.title: What is a Group Purchasing Organization or GPO?
metadata.author: OMNIA Partners
metadata.shortDescription:
A group purchasing organization (GPO) combines the purchasing power of a collective of businesses for better pricing, service levels and account representation from suppliers. The group purchasing model is quickly gaining adoption within leading procurement teams. By partnering with a group purchasing organization, businesses of all sizes can gain more spend under management and transform their supply chain. 

How a Group Purchasing Organization Works:
Buying groups create and manage GPO contracts for indirect and direct services or commodities – and they also create and manage relationships between three parties: the GPO itself, its members and its suppliers. To show exactly what this looks like, we'll examine the basic details of how GPOs that focus on indirect spend in the enterprise space work. Indirect spend describes any company expenditures that are required for running a business – such as office supplies, temporary labor and industrial supplies – but aren't directly related to a company's products or services.

Learn the basics of group purchasing organizations (GPO), why the GPO model is crucial to the success of procurement teams and businesses across the nation, and why OMNIA partners is the RIGHT group purchasing organization to fulfill any purchasing needs, not matter how unique.

-----------------------------------------------

As your ally in the purchasing process, OMNIA Partners is dedicated to optimizing procurement for your organization. Your free membership provides full access to our portfolio of value-driven contracts, spend visibility, analytics, and subject matter experts. Join thousands of members who are discovering a better way to buy.   

Visit www.omniapartners.com

metadata.title: Demystifying GPO Contracts: How Healthcare Supply Chain Unlocks Savings and Strategy
metadata.author: Healthcare Supply Chain Hub: Angelique W. Beslic
metadata.shortDescription:
Demystifying GPO Contracts: How to Maximize Savings, Leverage, and Strategy in Healthcare Supply Chain

GPO contracts can feel like alphabet soup, LOC, LOP, commitment %, tiers, carve-outs — but once you understand how they work, you unlock one of the biggest strategic levers in healthcare supply chain. This session breaks down the fundamentals and the advanced strategies that separate reactive contracting from true system-level performance.

Whether you’re new to sourcing or looking to sharpen your strategic edge, this video gives you a practical framework to use GPOs smarter, protect leverage, and drive better financial and clinical outcomes.

You’ll learn:
• What GPOs actually do (beyond pricing) and how they create leverage at scale
• The difference between LOC vs LOP and when each one makes strategic sense
• How to use carve-outs responsibly without destroying contract leverage
• How to apply commitment % as a strategic tool, not a restriction
• Why compliance tracking, documentation, and reporting protect rebates and trust
• How to shift from transactional “sign and forget” contracting to true strategic sourcing

Who this video is for:
Supply chain leaders, analysts, contracting teams, value analysis professionals, suppliers, and anyone navigating GPO strategy in healthcare.

Why this matters:
When you understand the mechanics, commitment %, compliance, rebate flow, carve-out logic, contracting terms, you stop leaving money on the table and start shaping contracts that support resilience, alignment, and long-term value.

metadata.title: Who is Intalere and What is a GPO?
metadata.author: Intalere
metadata.shortDescription: Intalere is a group purchasing organization, or GPO. A GPO is a company that saves you money on the things you need to buy for your healthcare organization. We do that by using the buying power of thousands of providers of all types and sizes to negotiate better prices from suppliers, manufacturers and distributors, allowing our members to obtain the right products at the very best price for virtually everything they buy. GPOs do not buy or sell products. We simply work with your current suppliers to get you the lowest possible prices on the items you already purchase. Learn more at www.intalere.com.

metadata.shortDescription: Group purchasing organizations, or GPOs, are vital for obtaining the best prices for certain business supplies and equipment. GPOs span a large variety of business sectors. They are becoming an increasingly popular option for companies looking to utilize the power of group negotiating and purchasing to keep down prices for the essential indirect things they need. If you're curious about what GPOs are, how they run, and how they might be able to help your company, you're in the right place. In this video, we go over everything you need to know about GPOs, including what they are, what business types they are great for, and their fee structures. We talk about several ways GPOs can help your company save time and money and potentially act as a networking vehicle for company growth.

Learn how GPOs actually operate, why being on one won't guarantee hospital approval, and what you should do instead to save time and money while closing deals.

05:49 - The Fallacy: Why being on a GPO doesn't mean hospital approval

06:56 - What to do instead: How to handle GPO questions from buyers and supply chain

08:24 - Case Studies & Closing Remarks

metadata.title: Microsoft Partner Center - Simply Explained
metadata.author: m365 Show | M365, Azure Cloud, Power Platform & AI
metadata.shortDescription:
Many partners think Partner Center is only a portal for big resellers and leave benefits, credits and incentives unused. This episode explains Microsoft Partner Center for consultants, managed service providers and software companies: who it is for, what the Launch, Core and Expanded tiers include, how to set it up safely and which upcoming API and MFA changes to prepare for.

In this episode

  •  00:00 – Why Partner Center matters
  •  00:44 – What Partner Center actually is
  •  02:09 – The old way versus the new way
  •  03:39 – Who Partner Center is for
  •  05:28 – The FY26 benefit tiers and what you get
  •  09:25 – How to get started
  •  11:28 – Common pitfalls and how to avoid them
  •  13:49 – The future of Partner Center
Key takeaways

  •  Microsoft Partner Center is the single hub where any Microsoft partner, from a one-person consultancy to a large reseller, manages benefits, incentives, customers and certifications.
  •  The FY26 benefits refresh groups partners into Launch, Core and Expanded tiers, with internal-use licenses, Azure credits, security tools and, through designations, Microsoft 365 Copilot (https://www.m365.fm/entity/copilot/?utm_source=podcast&utm_medium=shownotes&utm_campaign=microsoft-partner-center-simply-explained)  licenses.
  •  Avoid common pitfalls by setting up under your primary Entra ID (https://www.m365.fm/entity/entra-id/?utm_source=podcast&utm_medium=shownotes&utm_campaign=microsoft-partner-center-simply-explained)  tenant, using role-based access and a break-glass account, checking earnings reports and making API automation MFA-ready.
Worth quoting

“Partner Center isn't just a reseller portal. It's the central hub for your entire Microsoft partnership.” – Mirko Peters (15:49)

“Use the role-based access control to give each person exactly what they need and nothing more. That prevents security headaches down the road.” – Mirko Peters (10:33)

Explore more on M365.FM

  •  Episode page (https://www.m365.fm/show/episodes/microsoft-partner-center-simply-explained/?utm_source=podcast&utm_medium=shownotes&utm_campaign=microsoft-partner-center-simply-explained) : the full episode with chapters, key quotes and an FAQ on Partner Center
  •  Microsoft 365 Copilot (https://www.m365.fm/entity/copilot/?utm_source=podcast&utm_medium=shownotes&utm_campaign=microsoft-partner-center-simply-explained)  – internal-use Microsoft 365 Copilot licenses come with the Expanded tier and specific designations
  •  Microsoft Entra ID (https://www.m365.fm/entity/entra-id/?utm_source=podcast&utm_medium=shownotes&utm_campaign=microsoft-partner-center-simply-explained)  – set up Partner Center under your primary Entra ID tenant and keep a break-glass account
  •  Multifactor authentication (MFA) (https://www.m365.fm/entity/mfa/?utm_source=podcast&utm_medium=shownotes&utm_campaign=microsoft-partner-center-simply-explained)  – by April 2026 every app plus user Partner Center API call needs an MFA token
  •  Related episode: ENTRA PIM EXPLAINED: Securing Privileged Access with Mark Orr [MVP] (https://www.m365.fm/show/episodes/entra-pim-explained-securing-privileged-access-with-mark-orr-mvp/?utm_source=podcast&utm_medium=shownotes&utm_campaign=microsoft-partner-center-simply-explained) 
Follow and rate M365.FM in your podcast app, and join the free M365 community at m365con.net.

Become a supporter of this podcast: https://www.spreaker.com/podcast/m365-fm-microsoft-365-azure-cloud-power-platform-ai--6704921/support (https://www.spreaker.com/podcast/m365-fm-microsoft-365-azure-cloud-power-platform-ai--6704921/support?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=rss) .

metadata.title: Microsoft Cloud Solution Provider CSP   Simply Explained
metadata.author: m365 Show | M365, Azure Cloud, Power Platform & AI
metadata.shortDescription:
Are you confused about the best way to purchase Microsoft cloud services for your organization? Understanding the Microsoft Cloud Solution Provider program is the key to unlocking better support, consolidated billing, and expert guidance for your digital transformation.

In this video, we dive deep into the world of CSP to explain how the relationship between Microsoft, partners, and customers actually works. We break down the wholesale model where partners act as the bridge, providing not just licenses but essential managed services like security monitoring, data migration, and technical support.

Key Topics Covered

👋 The wholesale relationship between Microsoft and partners
👋 The difference between Direct Bill and Indirect Resellers
👋 How the New Commerce Experience NCE changed term commitments
👋 Choosing between CSP and Enterprise Agreements
👋 Why support and security requirements matter for partners

You will learn why over 90 percent of partners choose the indirect path and how the NCE cancellation window impacts your seat management. We also explore why businesses under 500 users typically find the most value in the CSP model compared to traditional volume licensing. Whether you are an IT professional or a business leader, this guide explains the financial flow and the strategic benefits of the Microsoft partner ecosystem.

Chapters
0:00 M365Con and Future of Work
1:18 Understanding the CSP Model
3:00 Direct vs Indirect Resellers
4:45 How Partners Add Value
6:18 The New Commerce Experience NCE
9:02 Benefits for Customers
10:43 CSP vs Enterprise Agreements
12:12 Partner Requirements and Support
13:40 The Big Picture of CSP

Ready to take your Microsoft environment to the next level? Head over to m365con.net to secure your spot for our 10 day event this January and join the global community. Don't forget to subscribe for more expert IT strategy content.

metadata.title: How Ingram Micro and Cisco help partners grow together
metadata.author: Ingram Micro USA
metadata.shortDescription:
Discover how the Ingram Micro and Cisco partnership combines Xvantage™'s AI-powered platform with dedicated expertise to simplify complexity across cybersecurity, networking, cloud and hybrid work. From customized enablement to hands-on training at the Business Transformation Center, learn how partners gain the tools and support needed to scale faster and win in today's market.

#IngramMicro #Cisco #Xvantage #Partnership #TechDistribution

Stay up to date with the latest in B2B Tech, IT Solutions and all things Channel:
Visit Xvantage: https://bit.ly/2J4DnaQ
Subscribe to Ingram Micro USA on YouTube: https://bit.ly/2J4DnaQ

Connect with us on social media:
Facebook: https://bit.ly/3zCd7hZ
X: https://bit.ly/3GozbQW
Instagram: https://bit.ly/3UeAxDC
LinkedIn: https://bit.ly/2Io0NJn

Ingram Micro makes B2B easy. We bring together partners, technology and customers around the globe to help organizations solve their toughest challenges. We’ve also perfected the art of blending humanity with the most modern, transformative technology available. Our digital experience platform, Ingram Micro Xvantage™️, is the first in the industry to automate deals, analyze data and make recommendations that both simplify and accelerate buying decisions. It connects thousands of technologists and vendors with our associates spanning six continents to learn, transact and partner to run their businesses better and grow faster.

metadata.title: VoxFlo | CRM Integration for UCaaS & CCaaS Resellers #wearevoxflo
metadata.author: WeAreVoxFlo
metadata.shortDescription:
You sell the UCaaS or CCaaS solution. VoxFlo makes sure the call data reaches the CRM.

CRM integration comes up early in every sale. Without it, deals stall, go to a competitor with native integration, or need a costly bespoke build. And with existing customers, calls happen but the detail never reaches the CRM, so records go stale and accounts are put at risk.

VoxFlo is the integration layer between the phone system you sell and the CRM your customer already uses. It connects to 300+ CRMs, with no bespoke build and no upfront cost. On every call, VoxFlo adds the call details and transcription to the right CRM record, plus summaries, actions and sentiment where the phone system provides them.

Live today with 8x8, Dialpad, Microsoft Teams Meetings, RingCentral and Zoom Phone.

For partners, that means:
✔ More new business, including deals lost to native integration
✔ Bigger deals, with an extra revenue line on every sale
✔ Stickier customers and a new reason to revisit your base
✔ Simple to deliver: VoxFlo handles the build
✔ Sell it under your own brand, or bundle it with your licensing

Start with a free 14-day trial for five users. No integration project required.
