metadata.title: Zoom Multicast: The Next UC Channel Opportunity
metadata.author: UC Today News
metadata.shortDescription:
Multicast is the new buzz in Unified Communications — and Zoom is leading the charge. In this UC Partner Trends session, David Dungay speaks with Mark Jenkins, Head of Global Channel at Zoom, about what multicast means for UCaaS, CCaaS, and the channel.

From digital transformation and AI innovation to security, agility, and scalability, Mark explains why Zoom’s single-platform strategy is changing the way partners deliver value to customers.

�� What’s driving the rise of multicast in UCaaS and CCaaS
�� The strategic benefits for enterprises and SMBs
�� How Zoom is addressing security and compliance challenges
�� Where partners can create differentiation and new revenue streams
�� Why training, enablement, and alliances are key to multicast success

0:00 – Introduction & guest
1:30 – Industry trends driving multicast adoption
4:50 – Strategic benefits of multicast beyond cost
7:10 – Security challenges and partner opportunities
9:50 – The $200bn UC market and Zoom partner growth
14:05 – Skills, enablement, and Zoom’s partner training
17:10 – The channel outlook for multicast in the next 12 months

Subscribe to UC Today’s weekly newsletter: https://uctoday.com/sign-up/

Join the UC community on LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/groups/1951190/

Multicast isn’t just another acronym — it’s a major opportunity for the UC channel. Partners who embrace Zoom’s unified approach can unlock innovation, scalability, and long-term growth.

segments.text: Zoom surveys.
Survey and polling tools aren't
especially common in business phone
systems, but Zoom includes several
built-in options for gathering feedback
before, during, and after meetings.

of time or launch them during live
meetings to collect participant
responses in real time.

use poll responses to help assign
participants to breakout rooms, which
can simplify workshop sessions and
training events.
Hosts can also share polling results
during meetings or download reports
afterward for additional analysis.
This information can provide valuable
survey data for businesses looking to
better understand their audiences.
Zoom also supports post-meeting surveys
and connections to third-party tools
like Google Forms and SurveyMonkey.
During testing, we found the polling
features easy to launch, and it didn't
take long to build different question
types, including multiple choice, short
answer, and rating-based responses.
Keep in mind that polling requires a
licensed host on an eligible paid Zoom
Workplace AI.

now include AI-powered meeting tools,
but Zoom's AI felt more deeply
integrated in day-to-day collaboration
than most competitors we tested.
Previously known as AI Companion, Zoom's
built-in AI features help users manage
their work across meetings, team chat,
canvas, mail, calendar, and other parts
of the Zoom Workplace platform.
The company retired the AI Companion
name in June 2026.
We particularly liked how Zoom AI
handles follow-up tasks and meeting
organization.
It can summarize meetings, pull out
action items, prioritize voicemails, and
help teams keep track of conversations
without relying on separate note-taking
or endless manual recaps.

meetings held on other platforms,
including Microsoft Teams and Google
Meet, which is a nice touch for

partners using different systems.
Some of Zoom's newer AI capabilities are
especially impressive.
Features like my notes, AI generated
task recommendations, and the ability to
search across past meetings and chats
make Zoom feel more like a connected
productivity workspace than a standalone
video conferencing app.
Zoom Mate, a newer AI add on, can also
search for information and automate
tasks across connected business
applications like Salesforce, Jira,
Slack, and Service Now.
For example, sales teams can use Zoom
Mate to retrieve customer information
before a call and update Salesforce
records afterward without switching
applications.
Overall, we liked how Zoom's AI tools
made it easier to manage everyday tasks
without adding more work to employees'
plates.
Remember that core AI features are
included with eligible paid Zoom
workplace plans, but more advanced tools
like Zoom Mate require additional
licensing.
Zoom Mate offers ready to use AI
workflows that help businesses automate
meeting follow ups, share information,
and manage tasks across connected
applications.
Zoom Clips.
While productivity killing meetings are
a common workplace frustration, Zoom
Clips gives teams a quicker way to share
updates, walkthroughs, and training
videos asynchronously.
We found it especially useful for
onboarding videos, internal demos, and
quick project updates that didn't really
need a live meeting.
During testing, we were able to
personalize clips with company logos and
brand colors, organize videos into
playlists, and share recordings across
teams without much setup.
Users can access Zoom Clips through the
portal or Zoom's desktop and mobile apps
to record, edit, and share short-form
videos.
Keep in mind that custom branding
requires Clips Plus,
is included with eligible paid Zoom
Workplace plans.
Zoom Clips lets employees share recorded
updates and track viewer engagement with
statistics on views, reactions, and
completion rates.
Source Zoom.
Team Chat and Collaboration.
Zoom and its competitors offer standard
unified communications features like
messaging and file sharing.
During testing, we liked how Zoom
connects chat, meetings, and AI tools in
one workspace instead of treating them
like separate apps.
Team Chat made it easier to continue
conversations after meetings ended,
catch up on busy threads with
AI-generated summaries, and quickly find
action items and shared files.
We also appreciated how Zoom keeps
meeting notes and conversations
organized.
With My Notes, users can save notes and
meeting transcripts in one place, keep
track of follow-up details, and choose
whether to keep notes private or share
them with the team.
This can be especially helpful for
employees juggling multiple projects or
trying to catch up on discussions they
missed. Video conferencing remains
Zoom's biggest strength.
As a video-first platform, Zoom makes it
easy for employees to move between phone
calls, team chat, whiteboards, and
productive online meetings without
constantly switching applications.
During testing, we especially liked how
naturally meetings connected with other
collaboration tools across the Zoom
Workplace platform, including chat,
whiteboards, and AI-powered features.
Zoom Workplace's free basic plan

participants and a 40-minute time limit.
Businesses that upgrade to Zoom
Workplace Business can host meetings
lasting up to 30 hours with as many as
300 participants.
For larger gatherings, Zoom also offers
a large meeting add-on that can
accommodate up to 5,000 participants
depending on the license.
That flexibility makes Zoom a practical
option for businesses that regularly
host training sessions, employee
onboarding meetings, or large virtual
presentations.
We also appreciated some of Zoom's
collaboration-focused features,
including one-click meeting launches
from whiteboards and AI-generated
meeting summaries.
While competitors like Dialpad, RingEX,
and Nextiva for video conferencing
tools, Zoom still feels more polished
and meeting-centric overall, especially
for businesses that spend much of the
workday collaborating virtually.
Video conferencing remains Zoom's
biggest strength.
As a video first platform ranks highly
for businesses that rely on virtual
meetings.
The platform combines VoIP calling with
Zoom's familiar user-friendly video
conferencing tools, so employees can
move between phone calls, meetings,
messaging, and team collaboration
features without constantly bouncing
between separate apps.
Zoom impressively integrates AI-powered
productivity features into its
communication tools.
Meeting and call summaries, voicemail
prioritization, and AI-generated tasks
can help employees stay organized and
keep track of important follow-ups
without spending as much time taking
notes or reviewing messages.
At the same time, Zoom remains
approachable for less technical users
while still offering advanced
functionality for larger teams and
frequent presenters.
Another advantage is Zoom's flexible
pricing.
Businesses can mix and match plans to
give employees the calling, video
conferencing, and collaboration tools
they actually use without paying for
features they don't need.
Some AI and collaboration tools require
separate Zoom workplace licenses or
higher tier subscriptions, but we still
found Zoom Phone competitively priced
compared to similar business phone
systems.
Overall, Zoom Phone offers much more
than basic business calling.
Its combination of video conferencing,
collaboration tools, and AI assisted
workflows makes it an excellent fit for
organizations that want to manage their
business communications in one place.
Zoom's all-in-one communications
platform is easy to navigate, especially
for businesses already familiar with
Zoom meetings.
During testing, we found the platform's
VoIP calling, messaging, and video tools
straightforward enough for most
employees to start using quickly without
much guidance.
Employees can place and receive calls
through the mobile app, desktop client,
web app, compatible VoIP phones, or
supported analog devices.
Basic tasks felt intuitive.
Even less technical team members should
have little trouble making calls,
joining meetings, or using features like
call transfers, recordings, and hold
controls.
We also like that Zoom offers
functionality through both its desktop
applications and browser-based tools,
giving employees more flexibility
depending on how and where they work.
The administrative side took more time
to get comfortable with.
Businesses moving from traditional
landlines to a VoIP system may find the
number of configuration options a bit
overwhelming at first, particularly when
setting up call routing, reports, and
AI-related settings.
Some competitors, including Ooma and
Nextiva, offer fewer collaboration and
meeting features, but may be easier for
smaller teams with limited IT support to
deploy and manage. Integrations.
Zoom's app marketplace includes
thousands of integrations for CRM,
collaboration, productivity, and
customer support platforms.
We like that many of those
are available across Zoom's business
plans instead of being locked behind
only the highest tier subscriptions.
During testing, we found it easy to
connect workplace tools directly inside
Zoom.
Users can schedule meetings, access
cloud files, and work with apps like
Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, and
Salesforce without constantly switching
between platforms.
Zoom also integrates with many of the
best CRM software platforms, including
Salesforce and Microsoft Dynamics 365,
as well as customer support tools like
Zendesk.
For example, the Zoom phone integration
for Zendesk lets support teams manage
help desk tickets while handling calls
inside the Zendesk interface.
We also appreciated Zoom's team chat
integrations, which help employees
incorporate tools like Jira, Asana, and
Salesforce into their everyday
collaboration workflows.
Zoom phone integrates with Salesforce to
help employees manage business calls
while working with customer records.
Source, Zoom.
FYI,
Zoom phone integrates with some of the
best call center software platforms,
including 59 and Genesis Cloud, helping
businesses connect their phone systems
with their contact center operations.

Zoom phone includes a strong set of call
management and routing features for
businesses handling higher call volumes
or more complex workflows.
The platform is especially flexible for
teams that need shared phone lines,
delegated calling, and customizable
routing rules across departments or
locations.
During testing, we found it easy to set
up business hours routing and shared
calling features without needing
additional software.
We especially like that Zoom phone
offers plenty of options for growing
small businesses while also
accommodating the more complicated
calling needs of larger organizations.

virtual receptionists and IVR menus,
call queues and shared line groups,
call delegation,
business hours and holiday routing,
call monitoring, whisper, barge and
takeover,
call hold, park and transfer,
implementation and onboarding.
Zoom's biggest onboarding advantage is

Since many employees already use Zoom
for meetings, the interface tends to
feel intuitive right away, which can
shorten the learning curve during setup.
New users typically receive an email
invitation to activate Zoom Phone, then
select their country, area code, time

From there, they can customize their
voicemail greetings, confirm their
emergency address and set business
hours.
Once setup is complete, users can start
making and receiving calls through
Zoom's desktop or mobile apps.
Zoom also provides a guided setup
process for administrators.
Account owners can log in through the
web portal to configure the company's
main phone number and extensions, then
assign calling plans and phone numbers
to employees.
Administrators can also set up call
queues, auto receptionists and routing
rules, as well as manage when employees
receive access to Zoom Phone.
Overall, we found standard Zoom Phone
deployments relatively straightforward
to configure, especially for
administrators with prior VoIP
experience.
Most users should also have little
trouble learning the platform's call
calling, messaging and video features.
However, businesses with more advanced
call routing, multiple office locations
or complex permission structures should
expect implementation to take longer
than it would for a smaller team.
Customer Support
Zoom's support setup is a bit more
layered than what we saw from some
competing VoIP providers, particularly
for smaller businesses.
The company offers several support
channels, but the level of access you
get depends on your account type,
subscription tier, and support plan.
Here's what you need to know.
Live support access depends on your
subscription level. Zoom offers phone,
chat, and ticket-based support along
with a large online help center,
but some support options are reserved
for higher spending accounts.

live chat support is available to
accounts with subscriptions over $10 per
month, while live phone support requires
subscriptions over $200 per month.
Businesses that want faster response
times or more hands-on help can also
purchase premier support plans.
The self-service ecosystem is extensive.
We liked Zoom's searchable knowledge
base, community forum, virtual support
agent, and free training resources.
The Zoom learning center includes short
videos, onboarding guides, and
self-paced courses that can help admins
and employees learn the platform more
quickly.
Some support resources may be
challenging for less experienced admins.
Zoom has extensive support
documentation, but we found that many
setup articles rely heavily on text and
technical explanations without as many
screenshots or step-by-step walkthroughs
as competitors like Nextiva provide.
Administrators who aren't as familiar
with VoIP systems may need more time to
figure out advanced call routing,
permissions, and configurations for
multiple locations.
Tip.
Businesses that prefer more hands on
onboarding and easier access to live
support representatives may appreciate
Nextiva's approach, which we discuss in
our Nextiva review.
Limitations.
While Zoom phone offers strong calling,
video, and collaboration features, we
identified a few limitations that may
matter for smaller businesses.
The pricing ecosystem can feel
complicated. Zoom offers separate plans
for its phone and collaboration services
along with additional AI and
productivity tools that may cost extra.
Businesses should look carefully at
what's included in each plan,
particularly when comparing bundles that
combine Zoom Phone and Zoom Workplace.
Live support access is more limited for
smaller accounts. Zoom offers a strong
self-service support ecosystem, but live
chat support requires subscriptions over
$10 per month, while live phone support
is reserved for accounts spending more
than $200 per month.
Smaller businesses that want easier
access to live assistance or more
hands-on onboarding may prefer providers
like Nextiva or Ooma.
See our Ooma Office review for more
information.
International calling options aren't as
broad as some competitors. Zoom supports
international calling and global plans,
but competitors like GoTo Connect offer
unlimited calling to a wider range of
countries.
Businesses with frequent international
calling needs should compare supported
destinations and calling rates before
choosing a provider.
Read our GoTo Connect review to learn
more.
Advanced configurations may take longer
to manage. While basic Zoom Phone
deployments are fairly straightforward,
businesses with multiple locations,
advanced call routing, or complex admin
permissions may face a steeper setup and
management process than they would with
simple SMB-focused systems.
Methodology.
We researched and analyzed dozens of the
best business phone systems to identify
the top VoIP and video conferencing
solutions for different business needs.
We evaluated pricing, calling features,
video meeting capabilities,
collaboration tools, integrations,
usability, scalability, AI features,
onboarding, administrative controls, and
customer support.
When identifying the best business phone

prioritized meeting quality,
collaboration features, ease of use, and
the ability to unify video, messaging,

Zoom stood out for its familiar

conferencing and business
communications.

Organizations that want business

SMBS looking for flexible workplace and

We don't recommend Zoom Phone for

Administrators setting up complex call

Users can access Zoom Clips through the portal or Zoom's desktop and mobile apps to record, edit, and share short-form videos. Keep in mind that custom branding requires Clips Plus, is included with eligible paid Zoom Workplace plans. Zoom Clips lets employees share recorded updates and track viewer engagement with statistics on views, reactions, and completion rates. Source Zoom. Team Chat and Collaboration. Zoom and its competitors offer standard unified communications features like messaging and file sharing. During testing, we liked how Zoom connects chat, meetings, and AI tools in one workspace instead of treating them like separate apps. Team Chat made it easier to continue conversations after meetings ended, catch up on busy threads with AI-generated summaries, and quickly find action items and shared files. We also appreciated how Zoom keeps meeting notes and conversations organized. With My Notes, users can save notes and meeting transcripts in one place, keep track of follow-up details, and choose whether to keep notes private or share them with the team. This can be especially helpful for employees juggling multiple projects or trying to catch up on discussions they missed. Video conferencing remains Zoom's biggest strength. As a video-first platform, Zoom makes it easy for employees to move between phone calls, team chat, whiteboards, and productive online meetings without constantly switching applications. During testing, we especially liked how naturally meetings connected with other collaboration tools across the Zoom Workplace platform, including chat, whiteboards, and AI-powered features. Zoom Workplace's free basic plan supports video meetings with up to 100 participants and a 40-minute time limit. Businesses that upgrade to Zoom Workplace Business can host meetings lasting up to 30 hours with as many as 300 participants. For larger gatherings, Zoom also offers a large meeting add-on that can accommodate up to 5,000 participants depending on the license. That flexibility makes Zoom a practical option for businesses that regularly host training sessions, employee onboarding meetings, or large virtual presentations. We also appreciated some of Zoom's collaboration-focused features, including one-click meeting launches from whiteboards and AI-generated meeting summaries. While competitors like Dialpad, RingEX, and Nextiva for video conferencing tools, Zoom still feels more polished and meeting-centric overall, especially for businesses that spend much of the workday collaborating virtually. Video conferencing remains Zoom's biggest strength. As a video first platform ranks highly for businesses that rely on virtual meetings. The platform combines VoIP calling with Zoom's familiar user-friendly video conferencing tools, so employees can move between phone calls, meetings, messaging, and team collaboration features without constantly bouncing between separate apps. Zoom impressively integrates AI-powered productivity features into its communication tools. Meeting and call summaries, voicemail prioritization, and AI-generated tasks can help employees stay organized and keep track of important follow-ups without spending as much time taking notes or reviewing messages. At the same time, Zoom remains approachable for less technical users while still offering advanced functionality for larger teams and frequent presenters. Another advantage is Zoom's flexible pricing. Businesses can mix and match plans to give employees the calling, video conferencing, and collaboration tools they actually use without paying for features they don't need. Some AI and collaboration tools require separate Zoom workplace licenses or higher tier subscriptions, but we still found Zoom Phone competitively priced compared to similar business phone systems. Overall, Zoom Phone offers much more than basic business calling. Its combination of video conferencing, collaboration tools, and AI assisted workflows makes it an excellent fit for organizations that want to manage their business communications in one place. Zoom's all-in-one communications platform is easy to navigate, especially for businesses already familiar with Zoom meetings. During testing, we found the platform's VoIP calling, messaging, and video tools straightforward enough for most employees to start using quickly without much guidance. Employees can place and receive calls through the mobile app, desktop client, web app, compatible VoIP phones, or supported analog devices. Basic tasks felt intuitive. Even less technical team members should have little trouble making calls, joining meetings, or using features like call transfers, recordings, and hold controls. We also like that Zoom offers functionality through both its desktop applications and browser-based tools, giving employees more flexibility depending on how and where they work. The administrative side took more time to get comfortable with. Businesses moving from traditional landlines to a VoIP system may find the number of configuration options a bit overwhelming at first, particularly when setting up call routing, reports, and AI-related settings. Some competitors, including Ooma and Nextiva, offer fewer collaboration and meeting features, but may be easier for smaller teams with limited IT support to deploy and manage. Integrations. Zoom's app marketplace includes thousands of integrations for CRM, collaboration, productivity, and customer support platforms. We like that many of those are available across Zoom's business plans instead of being locked behind only the highest tier subscriptions. During testing, we found it easy to connect workplace tools directly inside Zoom. Users can schedule meetings, access cloud files, and work with apps like Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, and Salesforce without constantly switching between platforms. Zoom also integrates with many of the best CRM software platforms, including Salesforce and Microsoft Dynamics 365, as well as customer support tools like Zendesk. For example, the Zoom phone integration for Zendesk lets support teams manage help desk tickets while handling calls inside the Zendesk interface. We also appreciated Zoom's team chat integrations, which help employees incorporate tools like Jira, Asana, and Salesforce into their everyday collaboration workflows. Zoom phone integrates with Salesforce to help employees manage business calls while working with customer records. Source, Zoom. FYI, Zoom phone integrates with some of the best call center software platforms, including 59 and Genesis Cloud, helping businesses connect their phone systems with their contact center operations. Call management. Zoom phone includes a strong set of call management and routing features for businesses handling higher call volumes or more complex workflows. The platform is especially flexible for teams that need shared phone lines, delegated calling, and customizable routing rules across departments or locations. During testing, we found it easy to set up business hours routing and shared calling features without needing additional software. We especially like that Zoom phone offers plenty of options for growing small businesses while also accommodating the more complicated calling needs of larger organizations. Features include virtual receptionists and IVR menus, call queues and shared line groups, call delegation, business hours and holiday routing, call monitoring, whisper, barge and takeover, call hold, park and transfer, implementation and onboarding. Zoom's biggest onboarding advantage is familiarity. Since many employees already use Zoom for meetings, the interface tends to feel intuitive right away, which can shorten the learning curve during setup. New users typically receive an email invitation to activate Zoom Phone, then select their country, area code, time zone and voicemail PIN. From there, they can customize their voicemail greetings, confirm their emergency address and set business hours. Once setup is complete, users can start making and receiving calls through Zoom's desktop or mobile apps. Zoom also provides a guided setup process for administrators. Account owners can log in through the web portal to configure the company's main phone number and extensions, then assign calling plans and phone numbers to employees. Administrators can also set up call queues, auto receptionists and routing rules, as well as manage when employees receive access to Zoom Phone. Overall, we found standard Zoom Phone deployments relatively straightforward to configure, especially for administrators with prior VoIP experience. Most users should also have little trouble learning the platform's call calling, messaging and video features. However, businesses with more advanced call routing, multiple office locations or complex permission structures should expect implementation to take longer than it would for a smaller team. Customer Support Zoom's support setup is a bit more layered than what we saw from some competing VoIP providers, particularly for smaller businesses. The company offers several support channels, but the level of access you get depends on your account type, subscription tier, and support plan. Here's what you need to know. Live support access depends on your subscription level. Zoom offers phone, chat, and ticket-based support along with a large online help center, but some support options are reserved for higher spending accounts. According to Zoom's pricing comparison, live chat support is available to accounts with subscriptions over $10 per month, while live phone support requires subscriptions over $200 per month. Businesses that want faster response times or more hands-on help can also purchase premier support plans. The self-service ecosystem is extensive. We liked Zoom's searchable knowledge base, community forum, virtual support agent, and free training resources. The Zoom learning center includes short videos, onboarding guides, and self-paced courses that can help admins and employees learn the platform more quickly. Some support resources may be challenging for less experienced admins. Zoom has extensive support documentation, but we found that many setup articles rely heavily on text and technical explanations without as many screenshots or step-by-step walkthroughs as competitors like Nextiva provide. Administrators who aren't as familiar with VoIP systems may need more time to figure out advanced call routing, permissions, and configurations for multiple locations. Tip. Businesses that prefer more hands on onboarding and easier access to live support representatives may appreciate Nextiva's approach, which we discuss in our Nextiva review. Limitations. While Zoom phone offers strong calling, video, and collaboration features, we identified a few limitations that may matter for smaller businesses. The pricing ecosystem can feel complicated. Zoom offers separate plans for its phone and collaboration services along with additional AI and productivity tools that may cost extra. Businesses should look carefully at what's included in each plan, particularly when comparing bundles that combine Zoom Phone and Zoom Workplace. Live support access is more limited for smaller accounts. Zoom offers a strong self-service support ecosystem, but live chat support requires subscriptions over $10 per month, while live phone support is reserved for accounts spending more than $200 per month. Smaller businesses that want easier access to live assistance or more hands-on onboarding may prefer providers like Nextiva or Ooma. See our Ooma Office review for more information. International calling options aren't as broad as some competitors. Zoom supports international calling and global plans, but competitors like GoTo Connect offer unlimited calling to a wider range of countries. Businesses with frequent international calling needs should compare supported destinations and calling rates before choosing a provider. Read our GoTo Connect review to learn more. Advanced configurations may take longer to manage. While basic Zoom Phone deployments are fairly straightforward, businesses with multiple locations, advanced call routing, or complex admin permissions may face a steeper setup and management process than they would with simple SMB-focused systems. Methodology. We researched and analyzed dozens of the best business phone systems to identify the top VoIP and video conferencing solutions for different business needs. We evaluated pricing, calling features, video meeting capabilities, collaboration tools, integrations, usability, scalability, AI features, onboarding, administrative controls, and customer support. When identifying the best business phone system for video conferencing, we prioritized meeting quality, collaboration features, ease of use, and the ability to unify video, messaging, and business calling in one platform. Zoom stood out for its familiar interface, strong meeting tools, and seamless connection between video conferencing and business communications. Bottom line, we recommend Zoom Phone for businesses that rely heavily on video conferencing and team collaboration. Organizations that want business calling, meetings, and messaging in one platform. SMBS looking for flexible workplace and phone plan combinations with AI-powered productivity and scheduling features. We don't recommend Zoom Phone for businesses that want simple pricing and support structures. Administrators setting up complex call routing systems for the first time. Companies that make frequent international calls and need broader unlimited global calling options.

metadata.title: AI Disruption in UC: Copilot, Zoom & Webex Face Off
metadata.author: UC Today News
metadata.shortDescription:
AI is no longer just a buzzword — it’s the great disruptor shaping the future of Unified Communications. In this UC Today session, Kieran Devon speaks with Cade Herbert, Marketing Manager at CallTower, and Madison D, Partner Marketing Strategist, to explore how AI is transforming UCaaS, CCaaS, and the wider collaboration landscape.

The conversation dives into where AI stands in 2024: moving past hype into practical, ROI-driven solutions. From Microsoft Copilot’s deep integration with Microsoft 365, to Zoom and Webex’s meeting-centric AI tools, and emerging AI-powered contact center platforms, the debate cuts through the noise and focuses on what actually delivers value.

�� Key takeaways:

The state of AI in 2024 across UCaaS and CCaaS

Microsoft Copilot vs Zoom AI vs Webex AI – the real differences

How AI is reshaping customer service and collaboration

Contact center innovation with Teams-native and AI-driven solutions

Future UC trends: seamless, efficient, human-centred communication

0:00 Intro
0:41 Guest introductions
1:32 The state of AI in 2024
3:30 AI in UCaaS and CCaaS
5:22 Microsoft Copilot vs Zoom vs Webex
7:06 How CallTower supports customers
9:00 AI in contact centers
11:00 Future of AI in UCaaS and CCaaS
12:26 Closing thoughts

Subscribe for more insights into how AI and innovation are redefining Unified Communications.

👉 Sign up for UC Today’s weekly newsletter: https://uctoday.com/sign-up/

👉 Join the UC community on LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/groups/1951190/

metadata.title: The Latest Big News on ALE Doubling Down on UCaaS, Enterprise ChatGPT & Zoom's AI Companion
metadata.author: UC Today News
metadata.shortDescription:
In this episode of The Latest Big UC News, hosts David Dungay & Rob Scott welcome some of the industry’s top analysts to talk about the latest news in the UC space.

The panellists discuss a variety of hot topics in the UCaaS space, including:

- ALE launching its own UCaaS platform
- ChatGPT launches an enterprise product
- What Zoom's new AI Companion means for the market

Our panel features the following UC experts:

- Craig Durr, Senior Analyst, Futurum Group
- Zeus Kerravala, Principal Analyst, ZK Research 
- Blair Pleasant, President, COMMFusion

Produced by UC Today News - Unified Communications & Collaboration Tech News #UCNews #UComS #UCaaS

Thanks for watching, if you'd like more like this, don't forget to SUBSCRIBE to our channel. You can also join in the conversation on our Twitter and LinkedIn pages.

For more Unified Communications & Collaboration Tech News visit https://www.uctoday.com/

1) Why do you think Zoom has been so successful? 

2) What is UCaaS expense management and why does it matter to enterprises? (Also known as TEM, telecoms expense management)

3) What benefits does Calero-MDS offer Zoom customers?

4) What analytics and insights provide the greatest value for enterprises?

If you're looking for more information on this topic visit https://www.caleromdsl.com/

Hosted by Rob Scott at UC Today News - Unified Communications & Collaboration Tech News #UCaaS #Zoom #ExpenseManagement

Thanks for watching, if you'd like more like this, don't forget to SUBSCRIBE to our channel. You can also join in the conversation on our Twitter, LinkedIn and Facebook pages.

For more Unified Communications & Collaboration Tech News visit https://www.uctoday.com

metadata.title: The SaaS Licence Audit: You are Paying for More Than You Think.
metadata.author: SaaS Procurement Insider
metadata.shortDescription:
The SaaS Licence Audit: You are Paying for More Than You Think.
Find Every Tool, Cut What You Don't Need, Negotiate the Rest

Most companies are paying for SaaS they don't use, can't see, and have forgotten they bought. This episode shows you how to fix that.
I'll walk you through the complete SaaS licence audit framework used in enterprise procurement: how to find every tool across three data sources (including the shadow IT your finance team doesn't know exists), how to measure actual usage with three metrics that expose waste, and how to categorise your entire portfolio into Eliminate, Rightsize, and Negotiate.
What's covered:
The three data sources for a complete SaaS inventory (ERP/invoices, SSO directory, shadow IT)
Why 15–30% of SaaS spend is invisible to finance — and how to surface it
The only three usage metrics that matter: Last Login, Login Frequency, and Average Session Duration
The SSO Enterprise Tier Trap — and how to use it as a negotiating lever
How to match your licence data against HRIS to find ghost licences and role-changers
The Eliminate / Rightsize / Negotiate framework — with clear usage thresholds for each
Duplicate detection: why you have two whiteboarding tools and how to turn that into a 15–20% consolidation discount
When to run the audit — and why 90 days before renewal is your most important window
Whether you're doing this manually with a spreadsheet or using a dedicated SaaS Management Platform, the framework is the same.
📥 FREE DOWNLOADS — mentioned in this video:
📘 CFO SaaS Playbook (PDF) → [https://payhip.com/b/YbFch]
✅ Renewal Checklist (PDF) → [https://payhip.com/b/6f2SX]
📊 Vendor Scorecard + TCO Calculator (Excel) → [https://payhip.com/b/ikvcO]

metadata.title: Shadow IT & SaaS Sprawl: Controlling the Hidden Software Costs Draining Your Budget
metadata.author: MetrixData 360
metadata.shortDescription:
While you're negotiating Microsoft renewals or rolling out enterprise-wide solutions, SaaS sprawl is quietly draining your budget. From unauthorized tools to duplicate subscriptions and unused licenses, Shadow IT is now one of the biggest hidden sources of waste in enterprise environments.

In this session, MetrixData 360 CEO Mike Austin breaks down the real-world financial impact of SaaS chaos, and what decision-makers can do to regain control.

Key outcomes:
- Uncover what IT doesn't see: identify Shadow IT and SaaS sprawl that traditional tools miss
- Quantify the cost: learn how companies are losing millions on untracked, redundant software
- Control the chaos: a practical framework to regain governance across Microsoft, Zoom, Adobe, and other high-spend platforms
- Align to your goals: tie visibility back to contract negotiation leverage, cost savings, and risk mitigation

Designed for CIOs, IT Procurement leaders, Vendor Managers, and SAM teams responsible for optimizing software spend.

Watch more on-demand sessions: https://metrixdata360.com/webinars/
Talk to our team: https://metrixdata360.com/contact-us/

segments.text: How to Build Recurring SaaS Review Cycles
SaaS adoption is accelerating across every client environment.
While decentralized purchasing increases agility,
it also introduces subscription sprawl, shadow IT,
compliance gaps, and unnecessary spend.
In this video, we'll show you a structured, repeatable
SaaS review framework you can standardize across clients.
Before we begin,
be sure to subscribe to NinjaOne's IT video hub
or our YouTube channel for more tech content like this.
How to Build a Recurring SaaS Review Cycle in 6 Steps
Step 1: Define a Review Cadence
Choose a cadence aligned with client complexity:
Quarterly reviews for high-change environments,
ideally aligned with QBRs.
Semi-annual reviews for stable clients with limited SaaS churn.
Annual baseline reviews before renewals,
after mergers, layoffs, or compliance audits.
Reviews should occur 60–90 days before
major renewals to allow time for optimization.
Step 2: Establish SaaS Visibility
Start by integrating your SaaS management platform
with Microsoft Entra ID or Okta.
This allows you to inventory applications accessed with corporate credentials.
Your reporting should focus on four core metrics:
Full application inventory by department,
Active versus dormant users,
License allocation versus actual utilization,
Security posture (MFA, SSO, and access controls).
This data becomes the foundation for renewal decisions and risk assessments.
Step 3: Standardize Your Review Framework
Each SaaS review should consistently evaluate four categories:
Usage and adoption:
dormant accounts represent both waste and security risks.
Cost and licensing: eliminate redundant platforms
performing overlapping functions.
Security and compliance:
identify unsanctioned shadow IT applications that may introduce audit exposure.
Business value: if an application's ROI is unclear,
evaluate consolidation or retirement.
Step 4: Automate Data Collection Between Reviews
For ad-hoc checks or smaller environments,
you can standardize reporting using PowerShell.
This is an optional step, but one that's highly recommended.
Export login data from Microsoft Entra ID into a CSV file, such as sso_logs.csv,
then run:
For the full automation workflow, including export configuration
and scheduled reporting, refer to the complete script in the blog.
Step 5: Conduct Structured Review Sessions
Start each session with a dashboard summarizing:
app inventory, usage trends, license waste, renewal timelines, security gaps.
Go through these findings with your client.
Then decide whether to retain, consolidate,
replace, retire, or renew an application.
Step 6: Document Decisions and Automate Reminders
Maintain a centralized SaaS decision log that captures
application name, decision, justification, and follow-up actions.
This creates an audit trail for renewals and compliance reviews.
To prevent missed renewals,
automate reminders in your PSA or RMM.
For lightweight automation,
configure reminder workflows using your preferred notification platform.
For the complete sample script and step-by-step implementation guide,
check out our blog linked below.
By implementing a recurring SaaS review cycle,
you create structured visibility into application usage,
license efficiency, renewal exposure, and security posture.
Proactive lifecycle control is key to strengthening client trust.
For more information, check out our official blog post on
how to build recurring SaaS review cycles to optimize spending,
curb shadow IT, and ensure compliance,
linked in the description below.

metadata.title: Vendor Risk Management: Auditing Your SaaS Vendors for Cyber Liability
metadata.author: The Tech Compliance Blueprint
metadata.shortDescription: In this video, we break down how to build an actionable, legally enforceable Vendor Risk Audit framework to eliminate third-party cyber liabilities.

segments.text: Over 60% of enterprise data breaches do
not originate within the target
company's primary infrastructure.
They occur through third-party SaaS
vendors, service providers, and cloud
integrations.
When a software vendor connected to your
network suffers a security failure or
misconfigures an API, your enterprise
remains legally accountable to your
customers and regulators.
Yet most companies treat vendor risk
management as a passive annual checkbox
exercise relying on unverified
questionnaires.
In this video, we break down how to
build an actionable, legally enforceable
vendor risk audit framework to eliminate
third-party cyber liabilities.
Effective vendor risk management begins
with risk classification.
Not all software vendors pose equal risk
to your organization.
Divide your vendor network into three
distinct tiers. Tier one, high
criticality.
Vendors that store, process, or transmit
sensitive customer data, financial
records, or code repos.
Tier two, moderate impact.
Vendors with operational access but
limited data ingestion.
Tier three, low impact.
Off-the-shelf software with no access to
internal networks or personal data.
Your legal and security audit resources
must focus heavily on tier one vendors,
requiring mandatory security
certifications like SOC 2 Type II, ISO
and comprehensive penetration test
summaries.
A security questionnaire is legally
unenforceable unless reinforced by
strict contractual terms.
Every vendor agreement must include four
non-negotiable clauses. First, the right
to audit.
Your contract must grant your team or
third-party assessors the right to
review annual security certifications
and independent audit reports.
Second, minimum security warranties.
Require vendors to maintain multi-factor
authentication, end-to-end encryption in
transit and rest, and continuous
vulnerability patching.
Third, mandatory incident reporting.
Specify that vendors must notify your
security team within 24 to 48 hours of
any security event impacting your data.
Fourth, cyber insurance requirements.
Require tier one vendors to hold
standalone cyber liability insurance
with minimum coverage caps appropriate
for your data risk profile.
Legal agreements must be paired with
technical controls.
Implement the principle of least
privilege across all third-party
integrations.
Regularly audit API permissions, enforce
single sign-on access, and immediately
revoke vendor access credentials upon
contract termination or project
completion.
By converting vendor risk management
from a passive administrative task into
a structured legal and technical
protocol, you protect your company from
supply chain compromises.
Like this video, subscribe to the Tech
Compliance Blueprint, and leave your
questions in the comments.

metadata.title: Shadow IT and SaaS Sprawl: Managing Hidden Cyber Risks
metadata.author: IronEdge Group
metadata.shortDescription:
🔒 Uncontrolled software usage — from personal Dropbox accounts to unapproved SaaS tools — is one of the fastest-growing cybersecurity risks for small and midsize businesses. Known as Shadow IT, these hidden apps create blind spots for IT teams, expose sensitive data, and increase the risk of compliance violations.

In this live panel discussion, our team of cybersecurity and IT experts will unpack the realities of Shadow IT and SaaS sprawl, explain why human error and misconfiguration remain top threats, and share practical strategies SMBs can use to regain visibility and control.

Whether you’re a business leader, compliance officer, or IT manager, this session will give you the insights needed to strengthen your defenses without slowing productivity.

🎙 Meet the Experts
• Robert Foit — Director of Security, IronEdge Group
• David Groot — Security Advisor, Galactic Advisors
• Dan Mallard — Director of Client Success, IronEdge Group
• Jackson Stephens, Esq. — Galactic Advisors

Learning Objectives
Attendees will leave this session with a clear understanding of:
1. What Shadow IT really means — how unauthorized SaaS usage develops inside organizations, and why it’s more common than you think.
2. The risks of SaaS sprawl — from data leaks and cyberattacks to compliance gaps and wasted budget.
3. How attackers exploit hidden apps — and why traditional perimeter defenses no longer provide enough protection.
4. Governance and monitoring best practices — including policies, tools, and cultural changes that help curb Shadow IT.
5. Action steps for SMBs — practical ways to start reducing risk and creating a more secure, productive IT environment.

How many SaaS subscriptions does your company pay for?

In this episode of Insight in Minutes, we walk through a SaaS audit step by step, from building the inventory and reading usage data to cutting idle tools and heading into renewals prepared.

Apps get bought on expense reports and team cards, so the full bill rarely lands in one place. An audit ties every app to an owner, a license count, and a renewal date, which turns each renewal into a decision you can back with usage data.

metadata.title: **The Hidden IT Tax: 5 Surprising Ways Your SaaS Stack Is Wasting Money**
metadata.author: Provision Networks
metadata.shortDescription:
Your organization may be paying for hundreds of software licenses that nobody uses, subscriptions that renew without anyone noticing, and applications that duplicate capabilities you already own.


But here’s the surprising part: Cutting unused software isn’t always the smartest way to reduce IT costs.


In this episode of Connectivity Without Chaos, Provision Networks explores five often-overlooked truths about SaaS spending, software utilization, and the hidden inefficiencies buried inside modern enterprise technology stacks.


We’ll examine how automatic renewals quietly drain IT budgets, why low software adoption sometimes signals a training problem rather than a bad investment, and how reclaiming unused licenses can generate savings without disrupting operations.


We’ll also explore why a proper technology audit should measure more than subscription costs. The real question isn’t simply how much you’re spending—it’s whether your technology is making employees more productive, improving business performance, and delivering the value you expected.


In this episode, you’ll discover:


* The auto-renewal trap: How forgotten subscriptions and departmental purchases create recurring expenses that escape scrutiny.


* The adoption paradox: Why low software usage may indicate an opportunity for better employee training rather than cancellation.


* The ghost-license problem: How dormant accounts and unused seats quietly inflate software spending.


* The productivity disconnect: Why evaluating software based solely on price can lead to the wrong decisions.


* The governance gap: How usage intelligence, vendor negotiations, automation, and employee accountability work together to control SaaS costs.


We’ll also discuss how software usage tracking, license reclamation, and proactive contract management can help organizations identify unnecessary spending, reduce shadow IT, and make better technology investment decisions.


The bottom line: SaaS optimization isn’t about buying less technology. It’s about getting more value from the technology you’ve already purchased.


Before approving another software renewal, ask yourself: How much of your technology budget is supporting actual business outcomes—and how much is simply running on autopilot?


Discover how Provision Networks helps organizations uncover the Hidden IT Tax and bring greater visibility, accountability, and financial discipline to enterprise technology spending.
 

This is a public episode. If you would like to discuss this with other subscribers or get access to bonus episodes, visit techgeek207.substack.com (https://techgeek207.substack.com?utm_medium=podcast&utm_campaign=CTA_1)

So if we keep using the example I used before, With a VP of customer support, let's say they're working on reducing cost to serve. What I want to leverage here is what's called authority bias. And this can work in good and bad ways, but it's essentially our natural inclination to trust people. In positions of authority, that's why we trust doctors, because the doctor is in a position of authority when it comes to the subject matter of our health. So in sales, the way that we can use this to our advantage is by sounding like we know what the heck we're talking about, by talking about what other people like them are focused on. Okay, it makes us more of an authority figure on the subject matter. So instead of asking a question that's really open ended that provides very little context, like, So what are you doing to reduce support costs right now? That doesn't really show the prospect that I know their world. What I want to do instead is front load the question with context. And this gets the prospect thinking about the question in a particular way while also demonstrating that you talk to a lot of people like them. And that's gonna sound something like this. Well, hey, I'm curious because I was on your website earlier and saw the chat bot and one of the things that we're seeing other customers do is point people to FAQ pages, and one of the challenges they often have is that Those FAQ pages don't end up answering the customer's question, and they just call into the contact center anyways. How does that compare to your experience? Or another question could be, you know, how do you prevent customers from going to FAQ pages and not getting their questions answered, and then calling into the contact center anyways? And hopefully what I've done here is painted a picture, of what the common problem is that I'm asking the prospect about and seeing if they deal with something very similar. So I can get them talking about it, and people are often way more receptive to talking about their problems If they know that their peers are having similar problems. Your goal in this section is to craft two or three really great questions that you can use going into a cold call. Ones where the questions are front loaded with common problems and then ask the prospect how they've dealt with it. Now for the close. So this is where we say goodbye. The goal of this part of the call is to secure the meeting and just get the heck out of the prospect's hair. And we're going to do this in a couple different ways. The ultimate power move is for you to be the one to cut the call short and say goodbye and not let the call drag on for too long. So once you've asked the prospect a few questions, and you feel good about the conversation, we're simply going to summarize what we heard. And that might sound something like this. Hey David, so what I heard today is that reducing cost to serve is a really big focus for you guys right now. You've tried FAQ pages, and you don't really have a system that you feel like is good enough. To help you determine where people might get stuck and where it causes them to hop into the contact center queue. Is there anything that I missed? I'm summarizing what I heard and inviting the prospect to correct me. And usually what you'll get here is a, yeah, you got it, or they'll correct you. Anything they share here is good. Now we're gonna schedule the meeting. And I'm gonna ask, hey, you mind if I make a quick suggestion? And usually you'll get a funny response like, yeah, yeah, sure, what's up? And you're gonna respond with something like this, hey, I know I promised I'd be brief today, This is the exact thing that we've been helping other companies like A, B, and C with. How about we unpack that a little bit more when I'm not cold calling you in the middle of your day? Do you have your calendar handy? And that line I love using, it's money. Do you have your calendar handy? And we're just going to go straight into scheduling the meeting. The goal here is to schedule the meeting as close as possible to the time that you made the call. So if today's Wednesday, I want to try to set up that meeting for later today or tomorrow at the latest. I don't want to let it drag on for too long. Time kills all deals as they say. And in the case of cold calling, time kills conversion rates when getting people to show up to meetings. Lastly, I'm going to do what I call a triple confirmation. And this is the. Power move once you figure out a time with a prospect. It's got three parts. Part one. I'm going to confirm that they received the invite on the call. And I'm going to ask, Hey, so I sent that invite over to you for Thursday at 10 a. m. Pacific. Would you mind opening up your email real quick and hitting accept? I want to make sure it didn't go to spam. Part two. Confirm the agenda. So again, we're going to be talking about what you're looking to accomplish in reducing costs to serve in your contact center. We've talked about the state of cold calling today and the top performer gap, and one thing I want you to think about is that cold call contact rates are so low, you know, the average pickup rate's about 5 percent right now. metadata.shortDescription:
Cost Reduction Consultants - Contingency Based - Check out http://www.expenseconsulting.com. Please subscribe to our channel for new and exciting videos.

Over the years you’ve worked hard to get your organization off the ground. You adjust for inflation, raise expectations, and stay on top of the winds of change. As a result, your organization experiences lots of smooth sailing!
Now, it’s time to try higher altitudes and greater distances! You may think that the only strategy is to keep adding more hot air—but there is an easier way, use Expense Consulting!

At Expense Consulting our job is to ensure that the “hot air” you pour into your organization stays in your organization—and doesn’t leak out! Of course, we’re talking about financial leaks.

Our highly trained team of financial experts work off-site to conduct an objective inspection of your expenditures. We provide the manpower, so you and your team experience no downtime or inconvenience.

We scour dozens of spending categories such as telecommunications, waste, supplies, utilities and more. We pour over invoices and contracts in order to identify cost-savings.  We audit for billing inaccuracies and overcharges—all in order to discover and repair leaking expenses.  

Our vast experience allows us to benchmark pricing, analyze service levels and negotiate to reduce costs without adversely affecting operations or vendor relationships. 

Because we’re vendor-neutral, remain with your current vendors or make a switch—whatever makes most sense to you.

Best of all, our process won’t require much of your time and it costs nothing for us to get started! We simply share the savings we find—which means you don't have to find room in the budget. But the truth is, we’ve found savings for 100 percent of our clients and they’re now realizing an average savings in excess of 20 percent per year— most start saving within weeks! Lastly, we make sure all leaks are patched well and remain engaged even afterwards—continually auditing invoices. 
Soon your organization will be soaring to new heights of profitability, you’ll be enjoying the view—and looking better doing it!

Let Expense Consulting elevate you! 
We won’t let you down!

http://www.expenseconsulting.com

New Heights of Profitability

metadata.title: SaaS Vendors’ New Trick: Multiplying Pricing Caps by Term Length
metadata.author: UpperEdge, LLC
metadata.shortDescription:
SaaS vendors are sliding a nasty detail into SaaS renewal term price protections: taking a “3–5% cap” and multiplying it by the number of years in your next term (e.g., 3% × 3-year = 9%). That’s not a cap—that’s compounding pain. Adam shows how to spot it, why it’s spreading, and exactly how to push back. 

Key takeaways
• There needs to be a cap on the increase a SaaS vendor can apply to your pricing at renewal 
• A price increase should happen one-time at renewal 
• Price increases at renewal should not go up with more term commitment  
•Make this a front-of-funnel pricing issue (tie it to discount asks), not a late legal cleanup.
• Longer term should mean better protection (e.g., 3-year cap 3%, 5-year cap 2%), not a bigger increase.
• Vendors watch each other and manage to what Wall Street wants to see (increases to downstream revenue). Expect this tactic to spread unless you push back.

How to negotiate
1. Insist on one renewal uplift cap (define exactly what it applies to).
2. Remove conditions that hold you hostage to volume/product mix.
3. Tie discounts today to locking in clean renewal language now. 

#SaaS #CloudContracts #ITProcurement #VendorNegotiation #Renewals #PriceProtection #EnterpriseIT #SoftwareSpend #CIO #CFO #RPO #ServiceNow #Salesforce #Microsoft #UpperEdge

0:00 The clause to watch: “% × years”
0:45 Why caps got messy
1:24 What the math does to you
2:00 The right model: one-time uplift
3:13 Term vs. cap: make longer = lower
3:40 Why vendors push it (RPO)
4:21 Your playbook to push back

Don't forget to like & subscribe for more insights!
For more innovative IT sourcing and risk mitigation insights:
• Watch the full video - https://upperedge.com/knowledge-center/podcasts-and-videos/
• Contact Us -  https://upperedge.com/who-we-are/contact-us/
• Subscribe to the UpperEdge Newsletter -https://upperedge.com/knowledge-center/subscribe-to-our-newsletter/
• Follow us on LinkedIn - https://www.linkedin.com/company/upperedge-llc/
• Follow us on Twitter  -  https://twitter.com/upperedge

Set SaaS renewal price increases in MonetizeNow and carry them forward automatically to the renewal quote. This Salesforce-connected demo shows how to configure a fixed or maximum renewal uplift, disclose it on the customer quote, and apply it to existing pricing when the contract renews.

The example uses a fixed 5% uplift: a $100-per-user monthly price becomes $105 at renewal. The demo also shows the renewal opportunity in Salesforce and the guardrail that warns about further amendments when processing an early-created renewal.

See how to:
- Configure a fixed percentage or maximum percentage renewal uplift
- Show the agreed uplift on the customer-facing quote
- Create a contract and review its Salesforce renewal opportunity
- Choose end-of-term renewal or an early renewal date
- Carry the uplift into the renewal quote using an account-specific rate

segments.text: It's January.
The invoice for your design software just arrived.
40 seats, €19,200, renewed automatically.
Another year, and nobody decided.
Only 12 people actually use it.
28 seats sit there, paid for and never opened.
So you ask:
can we go down to 12?
But the contract needed notice by November 1, 60 days before the renewal.
That window closed weeks ago.
SaaS renewal management means making that call while you still can.
Here are six steps, working backward from the notice deadline.
Step one.
Build one list of every software contract.
Go through the invoices and company card charges,
check what IT knows about, and ask the team leads.
For each tool, note the team, an owner, a backup, and where the contract lives.
Watch for tools whose buyer has left the company.
Nobody owns them anymore, so give them a new owner.
It happens all the time.
The person who bought the webinar tool moves on.
Their replacement gets the login, but not the notice terms.
So the tool keeps renewing, and nobody notices.
Step two.
Find the dates and terms in each agreement.
The start and end date, how it renews, the notice period,
any deadline for reducing seats, the price rules, and the minimums.
Read the order form and the main agreement together,
because one often explains the other.
Before a contract renews, check seven things.
How it renews.
How long the next term is.
The notice period, and how notice has to be sent.
Whether the price can go up.
Any seat minimums.
Your downgrade rights.
And how you get your data out if you leave.
Prices move quietly, too.
An email about new pricing goes unread.
At renewal, single sign-on and API access turn into paid add-ons,
and the price still goes up.
And read the notice period exactly as it's written.
60 days before December 31 is November 1.
Two months before is October 31.
One day can make the difference.
Step three.
Work backward from the notice deadline.
The renewal is on December 31.
Notice is due November 1.
So the review starts in early October,
with time to decide, negotiate, and send notice.
The reminder goes to the owner and to a backup.
And if replacing the tool means moving data, start even earlier.
Here's why the date matters so much.
Roughly 70% of SaaS contracts renew automatically.
If you do nothing, you keep paying.
So watch the right date.
A reminder one week before the renewal arrives 53 days after the notice deadline.
By then it's too late.
And monthly billing doesn't mean a monthly commitment, either.
Step four.
Check real usage with the tool's admin or with IT.
40 licenses, 12 active users.
Then ask the team what the numbers miss:
new hires, contractors, people who only use it now and then.
Here, 18 seats would do.
Step five.
Decide:
renew, renegotiate, downgrade, or cancel.
Here, you downgrade.
Then give notice the way the contract says.
A friendly chat with the account manager may not count.
Written notice to the right address does, and keep proof that it arrived.
Missed the deadline?
Ask the vendor for a reduction.
Deleting accounts doesn't end the commitment.
Step six.
File the outcome.
The signed amendment goes into the contract record:
18 seats, the next renewal date, the next review date, and the owner.
Then the loop starts again for next year.
If you're leaving the tool, plan the data export and access removal with IT.
You're done when the next deadline is covered.

With fynk, every software contract lives in one place.

so you see at a glance what you have, who owns it, and what it costs.

the end date, the renewal terms, and the notice period.
You just check them against the wording, and you're set.
Then fynk keeps an eye on the dates for you.

metadata.title: Seat Pricing or Token Pricing: What Zendesk and HubSpot Chose
metadata.author: The Innovation Attorney
metadata.shortDescription:
Salesforce, Zendesk, and HubSpot moved AI pricing toward usage based and outcome based models during 2025 and 2026 because seat based subscriptions could not track token costs or delivered value in a venture funded AI product.

A venture funded AI product should move to usage based or hybrid pricing once its inference cost per customer varies by more than roughly three to one across the user base. Salesforce priced Agentforce at $2.00 per conversation in October 2024, added $0.10 per action Flex Credits in May 2025, and still sells $125 per user per month seats, because no single model fits every buyer. This video explains why the shift is happening, what it costs companies that move carelessly, and how a founder or investor should evaluate the choice in 2026.

What you will learn:
How frontier token prices fell close to three hundred times since March 2023
Why Anthropic cut its own 2025 gross margin forecast to about 40 percent
What Cursor and Replit got wrong when they moved to usage based billing in 2025
Why HubSpot cut its Breeze Customer Agent price to $0.50 per resolved conversation
How investors now price usage based revenue into valuation multiples

I am The Innovation Attorney, with roughly thirty years of Silicon Valley technology and venture law practice counseling companies through commercial contract negotiation and pricing strategy. I write and publish analysis connecting engineering reality to commercial and investment decisions for technology companies.

My next piece examines how billing infrastructure vendors are building the metering systems this shift depends on, and what founders should demand from them before signing a contract.

Schedule a call with me www.calendly.com/theinnovationattorney

This video is for informational purposes only and is not legal advice.
