segments.text: Usage-based pricing for venture funded
AI products in 2026 executive summary
Salesforce, Zendesk, and HubSpot shifted
AI pricing toward usage-based and
outcome-based models during 2025 and
because seat-based subscriptions could
not track token costs or delivered
value. A venture-funded AI product
should move to usage-based or hybrid
pricing when its inference cost per
customer varies by more than roughly 3
to 1 across the user base. The threshold
several pricing operators used to flag
margin risk under flat seat pricing.
Salesforce priced Agentforce at $2.00
per conversation at its October 2024
launch, then layered in $0.10
per Action Flex credits in May 2025,
and still sells seats starting at $125
per user per month under its agentic
enterprise license agreement because no
single model fits every buyer. The right
answer depends on gross margin at the
90th percentile user, deal size, and how
predictably the company can forecast
consumption, not on which model draws
the most attention.
The underlying driver is a token cost
collapse that moved faster than most
pricing committees tracked it. Input
token prices for frontier-grade language
models fell from $30 per million tokens
for GPT-4 in March 2023
to roughly $0.10
per million tokens for comparable
capability by early 2026,
a decline close to 300 times in under 3
years. Anthropic cut its own 2025 gross
margin forecast to about 40% as
inference costs outran its revenue
growth, even as 2025 revenue reached
approximately $10 billion.
A company billing a flat $29 monthly
seat against a 90th percentile user
consuming $21
00 in tokens has already lost money on
that account before any other cost is
counted. The comparative evidence favors
a hybrid structure over either pure
model standing alone.
Vertex's second quarter 2026 contract
data placed usage-based pricing the
single most common primary model at
36.5% of software contracts, ahead of
per-user pricing at 32.1%
while LEK
Consulting's April 2025 valuation
analysis found hybrid pricing companies
carrying a six
nine X mean revenue multiple against 6.5
X for pure subscription companies. For
an investor, the practical implication
is that the pricing model a portfolio
company selects in 2026 shows up
directly in gross margin, net revenue
retention,
and the multiple the company commands at
its next financing before any product
feature does. Definition, scope, and
technical context usage based pricing
charges a customer for the metered
quantity of a resource consumed,
most commonly the input and output
tokens processed by a large language
model,
while seat-based pricing charges a fixed
fee per named user regardless of how
much of the product that user consumes.
This analysis treats outcome-based
pricing as a third category,
a charge triggered by a completed
result, such as HubSpot's dollar 0.50
fee per resolved Breeze customer agent
conversation after April 14, 2026 or
Salesforce's dollar two
00 per agent force conversation at its
October 2024 launch. The analysis covers
venture-funded, cloud-delivered AI
products sold to businesses,
meaning software companies that purchase
frontier model access through an
application programming interface rather
than companies that train and sell their
own foundation models. The analysis
excludes consumer-facing subscription
products such as a standalone chatbot
application because consumer willingness
to pay follows different psychology than
enterprise procurement,
and it excludes open source self-hosted
deployments
where the customer bears the inference
cost directly and the vendor pricing
question does not arise. In the same
form, the relevant engineering
classification is metered cloud services
pricing applied to a workload whose unit
cost is itself falling rapidly
and whose consumption per user varies
far more than consumption of a
conventional software seat. A seat on a
conventional SaaS product, a project
management tool or a word processor,
consumes a roughly fixed quantity of
server compute regardless of how
actively the named user works because
the software is deterministic and the
marginal cost of an additional click is
near zero. An AI agent seat consumes a
variable quantity of token generating
compute tied directly to how many
queries the user submits and how complex
each query is, so the cost basis
underneath the seat is no longer flat.
That difference, not any feature of the
product itself, is what forces the
pricing question addressed throughout
this report. Underlying scientific and
engineering principles, a large language
model generates output one token at a
time through autoregressive decoding
and the compute cost of that process is
driven by the number of parameters
activated per token,
the length of the input context the
model must attend to, and the hardware
generation running the calculation,
which is why token price is the correct
unit of cost measurement rather than a
flat per query or per seat charge.
Every additional output token requires a
full forward pass through the active
parameters of the model, so output
tokens cost substantially more per unit
than input tokens in nearly every
published price list. OpenAI priced
GPT-5.2 input tokens at $1.75 per
million and output tokens at $14.00
per million in the first quarter of
an 8 to 1 ratio that a flat per seat
price cannot reflect without
overcharging light users or losing money
on heavy ones. Three forces drive the
token cost decline that makes
usage-based pricing newly viable where
it was not viable two years earlier. The
first is architectural efficiency.
Mixture of Experts designs, such as the
one behind DeepSeek's V3 model released
in January 2025,
activate only a fraction of total
parameters per token, cutting compute
per token without cutting model quality
by a proportional amount. The second is
hardware. NVIDIA own estimates put
inference cost per token down roughly
ten-fold from its A100 generation to its
B200 generation. The third is
competitive pricing pressure among
frontier model providers themselves.
Visible in OpenAI's December 2024 cut of
60% on GPT-4o real-time input pricing
and 87.5% on output pricing.
A reduction driven by competition from
Google's Gemini line and Anthropic's
Claude line rather than by a change in
the underlying hardware cost. That same
week, some of these constraints are
contingent and some are closer to fixed.
The decline in cost per unit of model
quality is contingent. It depends on
continued algorithmic research,
continued hardware generations, and
continued competitive pressure among
several serious frontier labs, any of
which could slow. Closer to fixed, at
least over a multi-year horizon, is the
shape of the cost curve itself. Output
tokens will keep costing more than input
tokens because generation is inherently
more compute-intensive than
comprehension.
And heavy users will keep costing
substantially more than light users
because query complexity and token count
move together. A pricing model built on
the assumption that this variance will
disappear is building on a trend that
history gives no reason to expect.
System architecture and process flow
usage-based or hybrid pricing system
requires four subsystems that a
seat-based product does not need in the
same form.
A metering layer that counts the input
and output tokens, application
programming interface calls or completed
actions a customer generates, a rating
engine that converts that raw count into
a customer-facing charge, a credit or
wallet abstraction that decouples the
vendor's actual model cost from the
price the customer sees,
and an invoicing and dunning system able
to handle postpaid overage charges
rather than a single flat monthly draft.
Cursor built by Enso Sphere illustrates
the credit abstraction directly. Each
paid plan carries a monthly credit pool
size to roughly match its subscription
price. The company's own models draw
down that pool at a favorable internal
rate and third-party models such as
Claude or GPT draw it down at each
model's actual application programming.
Interface price, so the customer sees
one number while the company's own
margin varies underneath by which model
handled the request.
materials for this architecture is now a
specialized vendor category in its own
right. Companies such as Orb and
Metronome sell metering and rating as a
standalone service because building an
accurate, auditable, real-time usage
ledger is a materially harder
engineering problem than billing a fixed
number of seats once a month.
Salesforce's own architecture shows the
same complexity from a different angle.
It currently operates three pricing
systems at once inside Agentforce, a
per-conversation meter inherited from
its October 2024 launch, a flex credits
ledger priced at $0.10
per standard action introduced in May
and a traditional per-seat license under
its agentic enterprise license agreement
priced from $125 per user per month
starting in late 2025,
each running on different internal
plumbing and reconciled against the same
customer invoice. The architectural
tradeoff a venture-funded company faces
is between simplicity,
which seat pricing delivers natively,
and cost accuracy, which usage metering
delivers natively. A hybrid design, a
base seat fee that includes a usage
allotment with metered overage above it,
is the architecture most pricing data
from 2025 and 2026 shows companies
converging toward because it inherits
the forecasting simplicity of a seat for
the committed portion of spend while
exposing the vendor to the true cost
curve only on the margin, where the risk
of underpricing a heavy user actually
lives. Quantitative performance metrics,
the clearest quantitative split is the
net revenue retention figure recorded by
pricing model in High Alpha's 2025 and
2026 benchmark research. Hybrid pricing
companies posted 105% net revenue
retention, subscription companies 102%,
outcome-based companies 100%, and pure
consumption-based companies 99%,
even though the same research found
outcome based companies growing revenue
65% year over year and consumption based
companies growing 43 per
both ahead of the 34% growth rate posted
by subscription companies. Growth is not
retention and a company evaluating its
own pricing choice needs both figures
rather than either alone.
Adoption data confirms the shift is
underway rather than complete. Growth
Unhinged 2025 state of B2B monetization
study of more than 240 software and AI
companies
found seat based pricing falling from
21% to 15% of primary pricing models
over 12 months while hybrid pricing rose
from 27% to 41% over the same period and
three and four surveyed companies change
their pricing at least once during the
year.
Vertices second quarter 2026 contract
data drawn from live Enterprise software
agreements found per usage pricing the
single most common model at 36.5% of
contracts up from 34.0% in the first
quarter of 2026 with per user pricing
falling to 32
4% over the same quarter. A survey of
100 Enterprise Chief Information
Officers conducted by Andreessen
Horowitz cited in L E K Consulting's
April 2025 analysis found 39% preferred
usage based pricing specifically for AI
applications against 21% who still
preferred seat based pricing with 23%
preferring a hybrid. Cost data explains
why buyers are pulling pricing in this
direction.
Token prices for Frontier grade models
fell from $30 per million input tokens
for GPT-4 in March 2023 to roughly $0
10 per million tokens for comparable
capability by early 2026. A worked unit
economics example priced a single AI
agent action at $0.035
in blended token cost producing a
monthly inference cost of $4.20 for 50th
percentile user at 120 actions per month
for 90th percentile user at 600 actions
per month,
a five to one spread that a single flat
dollar 29 monthly price cannot absorb
without losing money on the heaviest
fifth of the customer base. Xylo's 2026
SaaS Management Index found the buyer
side consequence of this volatility
directly.
78% of information technology leaders
reported unexpected charges tied to AI
features or consumption pricing,
and 61% said they cut a planned project
because of unplanned software cost
increases. Key advantages and
limitations usage and token-based
pricing carries one advantage that seat
pricing structurally cannot deliver.
It ties the vendor's revenue to the
vendor's own cost curve, protecting a
company from the specific failure that
cost Anthropic roughly 10 percentage
points of projected 2025 gross margin,
where inference costs rose faster than
the company's own forecasts assumed. It
also aligns price with delivered value
once an AI agent begins doing the work a
human seat used to do. Salesforce's own
pricing documentation frames its dollar
125 per user per month agentic
enterprise license agreement seat as
including a digital workforce, precisely
because the logic of one named human
user per license breaks down when the
unit of work is performed by software.
McKinsey's 2026 Service Operations
Research found an automated resolution
costing dollar 0.62 against dollar 7.40
for resolution handled by a human agent.
A 12-fold cost gap per seat price has no
mechanism to capture on either the cost
side or the value side. The limitation
on the other side of the ledger is
forecasting risk, running in both
directions between buyer and vendor.
Xylo's 2026 data on unexpected AI
charges shows the buyer side of this
risk directly.
In Replit's September 2025 shift to what
it called effort-based pricing produced
individual customer bills that rose in
user reports gathered after its agent
three launch on September 10, 2025
by a factor the company's own support
channels described as roughly 20 times a
prior month's typical charge. The vendor
side of the same risk is revenue
unpredictability. A sales team that is
sold flat seats for years cannot
forecast next quarter's revenue from a
usage-based book with the same
confidence because usage, unlike head
count, can fall as easily as it rises if
a customer's own business contracts or a
customer learns to prompt more
efficiently. Seat-based pricing retains
one advantage usage pricing has not
replicated, procurement simplicity. A
finance department approving a vendor
contract can model a seat price with a
single multiplication named users times
price per seat. While a usage-based
contract requires the buyer to model its
own future consumption, a forecasting
exercise many procurement teams are not
equipped to run accurately, which is one
reason Vertice's own contract data still
placed per user pricing at 32
4% of enterprise software agreements
even after a year of usage pricing
gaining share. The limitation seat
pricing cannot escape is that it caps
vendor revenue at head count, a fixed
input inside a product category where
the customer's own economic benefit
scales with the number of tasks the AI
completes rather than the number of
humans who log in to supervise it.
Technical failure mode analysis, the
most visible failure mode in metered AI
pricing is bill shock.
The acute case in which a usage-based or
credit-based account consumes far more
of its allotment than the customer
anticipated inside a single billing
period. Cursor's June 2025 shift to
usage-based billing for premium model
requests produced by its own users'
public accounts, a case in which a
team's $7,000 annual subscription was
consumed in a single day. And founder
Michael Troull acknowledged in early
July 2025 that the rollout had been
handled poorly before the company added
clearer spend limits and selective
refunds. Replit's parallel incident
followed its September 10, 2025 launch
of Agent 3 under effort-based pricing in
which one documented user reported a
charge of $1,000 in a single week
against a typical monthly spend of
dollar 180 to dollar 200. And the
company itself acknowledged in July 2025
that its new checkpoint structure could
end up costing moreover a project's life
than the model it replaced. A second
failure mode is definitional ambiguity
in what triggers a charge. Salesforce's
original October 2024 agent force
pricing dollar 2.00 per conversation ran
into this problem directly.
A single customer query could trigger
many backend reasoning steps and tool
calls before resolving. So buyers found
the per conversation price difficult to
model against their own expected usage.
Part of why Salesforce added its dollar
0.10 per action flex credit structure
only seven months later.
Constellation Research analyst Liz
Miller described the resulting opacity
across the AI customer service category
generally as a black box in which
neither the buyer nor, in some cases,
the vendor can state with confidence
what a given month's bill will be before
the invoice arrives. A third failure
mode is structural rather than acute.
The principal agent misalignment
inherent in pure outcome based pricing
in which a vendor is paid only when it
records a resolution giving it a
financial incentive to classify
ambiguous interactions as resolved
whether or not the underlying customer
problem was actually solved. This
degradation failure mode compounds with
the bill shock failure mode described
above
because a customer who already distrusts
the vendor's usage counting has no
reason to extend the benefit of the
doubt on resolution counting either. The
two failure modes together help explain
why 25% of companies surveyed in growth
unhinged research expect outcome based
pricing to become their primary model by
even though only 5% used it as their
primary model in 2025.
A gap that reflects resolution counting
methods still largely self reported by
vendors rather than independently
verified in 2026 contracts. Real world
applications and deployment context
customer service is the sector where
outcome based and usage based AI pricing
is most commercially mature. Zendesk
charges between dollar 1.50
and dollar 2.00 per automated
resolution.
Intercom's Finn agent charges dollar
0.99 per outcome, and HubSpot moved its
Breeze customer agent from dollar 1.00
to dollar 0.50 per resolved conversation
effective April 14, 2026,
citing a 65% conversion rate and 39%
faster resolution times across more than
8,000 customers as the performance basis
for the new price.
Service Now deploys a parallel
consumption model it calls billing per
AI skill execution applied to Enterprise
Information Technology Service
Management rather than customer-facing
chat. Forrester's research found more
than 45% of surveyed organizations
already using AI agents in production
with another 25% piloting them, placing
this sector well past the early adopter
phase.
Software development tooling shows the
same pricing migration under different
commercial pressure. Cursor, built by
Anthropic, moved from a fixed request
allotment to usage-based billing in June
and was reported to have grown
annualized recurring revenue past dollar
100 million within 12 months of its
earlier more subsidized pricing, then
past dollar 200 million afterward.
GitHub Copilot runs a parallel structure
inside Microsoft's own distribution.
Unlimited basic code completion bundled
into a flat per seat fee starting at
dollar 10 per month for individuals with
a separate premium request allotment,
300 per month on the Pro tier, billed at
dollar 0.04 per request once that
allotment is exhausted, a hybrid design
that keeps the predictable base feature
flat while metering only the more
expensive premium model calls. Replit's
parallel deployment shows the less
settled edge of this trend. It September
2025 moved to effort-based pricing for
its Autonomous Agent 3 product, arrived
alongside a dollar 250 million funding
round that included Google's AI Futures
Fund, evidence that capital markets
continue to back the technology even as
its pricing mechanics were still being
worked out in public. Legal services
shows a narrower but telling data point
at the high end of outcome pricing.
Harvey, a legal AI company, was reported
at approximately dollar 190 million in
annual recurring revenue. Operating in a
sector where the dollar value of a
correctly drafted or reviewed document
is high enough that law firm buyers have
shown more tolerance for value-based and
outcome-linked pricing than
price-sensitive small business buyers
show in other sectors. Economic and
scalability considerations, the primary
cost driver inside a venture-funded AI
products income statement is inference
compute.
A cost category a conventional SaaS
company's income statement does not
carry incomparable size,
which is why the 80% plus gross margin
benchmark that defines software
investing for two decades is not the
right comparison for an AI-native
company. Pricing researchers surveying
AI-native company data decks in 2026
described a working floor of 60% gross
margin as the level needed to support a
credible series of financing narrative
with a target range of 50 to 70% gross
margin replacing the older benchmark
entirely
and recommended that a company set its
base price to clear 60 percent margin at
the 50th percentile user rather than at
the average since the average is
distorted upward by a small number of
very light users. The experience curve
of working in every AI company's favor
is the token cost decline itself.
A decline on the order of 10 times per
year in frontier inference cost
compounding into the nearly 300 times
reduction over three years documented
earlier in this report. That decline is
a tailwind for gross margin only if a
company's pricing captures it
deliberately.
A company that locks a flat proceed
price for 18 months while its own input
costs fall tenfold is leaving margin
uncaptured while a company that reprices
too aggressively on the same schedule
risks the bill shock failure mode
described above. Pricing researchers
recommend a repricing cadence closer to
every 90 days specifically to stay
inside this window without triggering a
cursor style trust event. The bottleneck
constraining how fast any individual
company can scale its own usage based
revenue is not customer demand, but
graphics processing unit supply and data
center capacity at its underlying model
provider,
a constraint outside the pricing
company's own control. Anthropic's own
2026 capital spending reported in the $6
billion to $9 billion range for the year
against OpenAI's reported spending above
$14 billion
illustrates the scale of capital
intensity sitting upstream of every
venture funded company that resells
access to these models rather than
training its own. The financing market
has already begun pricing this
distinction into valuation multiples,
LEK. Consulting's April 2025 analysis of
the SaaS capital index found usage based
pricing companies carrying a 7.4x mean
revenue multiple and hybrid pricing
companies a 6.9x mean multiple, both
ahead of the 6.5x mean multiple for pure
subscription companies with hybrid
pricing companies also posting 19%
trailing 12 month revenue growth against
the broader index. For a venture funded
company preparing its next financing
round, the pricing model is no longer a
product decision made once and left
alone. Investors are now pricing it
directly into the multiple. Future
development trajectory, the clearest
milestone on the horizon is IDC's
forecast that seat based pricing will be
largely obsolete by 2028,
a forecast consistent with the
trajectory already visible in Vertices
quarter over quarter contract data
showing per user pricing losing roughly
2 and 1/2 percentage points of share in
a single quarter of 2026.
Gartner's parallel forecast puts a
number on the scale of disruption at the
high end. Agentic AI could affect
approximately 20% of enterprise SaaS
spending and could see 35% of point
product SaaS tools replaced or absorbed
by agents by 2030, though the same
research found more than 40% of agentic
AI projects were expected to be canceled
by the end of 2027.
And that only about 130 of the thousands
of vendors currently claiming agentic
capability
were found to meet Gartner's own
criteria for that label. The credibility
of the 2028 seat obsolescence forecast
rests on a contingent assumption, not a
fixed one.
That metering and billing infrastructure
vendors such as Orb and Metronome keep
maturing fast enough that usage-based
billing becomes as operationally
reliable for a mid-sized software
company as a flat monthly draft is
today. That infrastructure risk is
improvable, unlike the token cost curve
itself, which is governed by compute
economics and hardware supply, not by
how fast a billing team can build
software. This analysis characterizes
the risk that usage-based pricing fails
to reach the 2028 milestone as moderate.
The economic logic favoring the shift is
close to settled, but the billing
systems, finance team processes, and
sales compensation plans built around
them are still catching up. And a
shortfall in that tooling, not a
reversal in underlying cost economics,
is the more likely cause of any delay.
The competing trajectory worth tracking
is a split market rather than a single
winner. The Andreessen Horowitz Chief
Information Officer survey finding 39%
usage preference against 23% hybrid and
21% seat preference
read alongside Vertice's hybrid share
holding near 31% for two consecutive
quarters
points toward a three-way split that has
held across multiple reporting periods
rather than a full migration to any
single model.
The venture-funded companies that win
the next financing cycle will likely be
the ones offering buyers a choice of
structure rather than the ones that bet
the whole product on one model. Open
questions The first question concerns
billing infrastructure maturity. Will
metering vendors such as Orb and
Metronome reach a level of accuracy and
auditability that eliminates the
reconciliation errors behind episodes
such as Cursor's June 2025 Bill Shock?
A question resolvable within two to
three years as vendors publish audited
usage data and as more enterprise buyers
demand it in contract terms. And one
that matters because the 2028 seat
obsolescence forecast assumes this
infrastructure keeps pace with pricing
ambition. The second question concerns
resolution verification in outcome-based
pricing.
Will an independent or third-party
standard emerge for what counts as a
resolved customer interaction, resolving
the principal agent problem identified
in this report, or will vendors continue
defining their own resolution metrics?
This question matters because growth
unhinged research found adoption
intentions for outcome pricing running
well ahead of current trust levels, and
the gap will not close through marketing
alone. The third question concerns the
durability of the token cost decline
itself.
Will the roughly tenfold annual decline
in frontier inference cost continue at
its recent pace, or will power supply
and data center construction
constraints, already visible in reported
capital spending above dollar 14 billion
annually at OpenAI and dollar 6 billion
to dollar 9 billion at Anthropic, slow
the curve within the next five to 10
years? The answer determines whether
usage-based pricing keeps gaining
structural advantage or whether cost
volatility becomes a shared industry
problem rather than a competitive lever.
The fourth question concerns enterprise
procurement adaptation. Will corporate
finance and procurement functions build
the forecasting capability to approve
usage-based contracts with the same
confidence they apply to seat-based
contracts within the next two to three
years, or will large enterprises
continue favoring seat pricing
specifically for budgeting
predictability even where usage pricing
would lower their total cost? The fifth
question concerns capital markets
durability. Will the revenue multiple
premium documented by
consulting for usage-based and hybrid
pricing companies hold if a broader
financing downturn forces investors to
prioritize predictability over growth?
A macro-dependent question that will not
resolve on any fixed timetable, but that
materially affects which pricing model a
founder should choose when raising a
series B or series C in 2026. Beyond

videos.full_text: Usage-based pricing for venture funded AI products in 2026 executive summary Salesforce, Zendesk, and HubSpot shifted AI pricing toward usage-based and outcome-based models during 2025 and 2026 because seat-based subscriptions could not track token costs or delivered value. A venture-funded AI product should move to usage-based or hybrid pricing when its inference cost per customer varies by more than roughly 3 to 1 across the user base. The threshold several pricing operators used to flag margin risk under flat seat pricing. Salesforce priced Agentforce at $2.00 per conversation at its October 2024 launch, then layered in $0.10 per Action Flex credits in May 2025, and still sells seats starting at $125 per user per month under its agentic enterprise license agreement because no single model fits every buyer. The right answer depends on gross margin at the 90th percentile user, deal size, and how predictably the company can forecast consumption, not on which model draws the most attention. The underlying driver is a token cost collapse that moved faster than most pricing committees tracked it. Input token prices for frontier-grade language models fell from $30 per million tokens for GPT-4 in March 2023 to roughly $0.10 per million tokens for comparable capability by early 2026, a decline close to 300 times in under 3 years. Anthropic cut its own 2025 gross margin forecast to about 40% as inference costs outran its revenue growth, even as 2025 revenue reached approximately $10 billion. A company billing a flat $29 monthly seat against a 90th percentile user consuming $21 00 in tokens has already lost money on that account before any other cost is counted. The comparative evidence favors a hybrid structure over either pure model standing alone. Vertex's second quarter 2026 contract data placed usage-based pricing the single most common primary model at 36.5% of software contracts, ahead of per-user pricing at 32.1% while LEK Consulting's April 2025 valuation analysis found hybrid pricing companies carrying a six nine X mean revenue multiple against 6.5 X for pure subscription companies. For an investor, the practical implication is that the pricing model a portfolio company selects in 2026 shows up directly in gross margin, net revenue retention, and the multiple the company commands at its next financing before any product feature does. Definition, scope, and technical context usage based pricing charges a customer for the metered quantity of a resource consumed, most commonly the input and output tokens processed by a large language model, while seat-based pricing charges a fixed fee per named user regardless of how much of the product that user consumes. This analysis treats outcome-based pricing as a third category, a charge triggered by a completed result, such as HubSpot's dollar 0.50 fee per resolved Breeze customer agent conversation after April 14, 2026 or Salesforce's dollar two 00 per agent force conversation at its October 2024 launch. The analysis covers venture-funded, cloud-delivered AI products sold to businesses, meaning software companies that purchase frontier model access through an application programming interface rather than companies that train and sell their own foundation models. The analysis excludes consumer-facing subscription products such as a standalone chatbot application because consumer willingness to pay follows different psychology than enterprise procurement, and it excludes open source self-hosted deployments where the customer bears the inference cost directly and the vendor pricing question does not arise. In the same form, the relevant engineering classification is metered cloud services pricing applied to a workload whose unit cost is itself falling rapidly and whose consumption per user varies far more than consumption of a conventional software seat. A seat on a conventional SaaS product, a project management tool or a word processor, consumes a roughly fixed quantity of server compute regardless of how actively the named user works because the software is deterministic and the marginal cost of an additional click is near zero. An AI agent seat consumes a variable quantity of token generating compute tied directly to how many queries the user submits and how complex each query is, so the cost basis underneath the seat is no longer flat. That difference, not any feature of the product itself, is what forces the pricing question addressed throughout this report. Underlying scientific and engineering principles, a large language model generates output one token at a time through autoregressive decoding and the compute cost of that process is driven by the number of parameters activated per token, the length of the input context the model must attend to, and the hardware generation running the calculation, which is why token price is the correct unit of cost measurement rather than a flat per query or per seat charge. Every additional output token requires a full forward pass through the active parameters of the model, so output tokens cost substantially more per unit than input tokens in nearly every published price list. OpenAI priced GPT-5.2 input tokens at $1.75 per million and output tokens at $14.00 per million in the first quarter of 2026, an 8 to 1 ratio that a flat per seat price cannot reflect without overcharging light users or losing money on heavy ones. Three forces drive the token cost decline that makes usage-based pricing newly viable where it was not viable two years earlier. The first is architectural efficiency. Mixture of Experts designs, such as the one behind DeepSeek's V3 model released in January 2025, activate only a fraction of total parameters per token, cutting compute per token without cutting model quality by a proportional amount. The second is hardware. NVIDIA own estimates put inference cost per token down roughly ten-fold from its A100 generation to its B200 generation. The third is competitive pricing pressure among frontier model providers themselves. Visible in OpenAI's December 2024 cut of 60% on GPT-4o real-time input pricing and 87.5% on output pricing. A reduction driven by competition from Google's Gemini line and Anthropic's Claude line rather than by a change in the underlying hardware cost. That same week, some of these constraints are contingent and some are closer to fixed. The decline in cost per unit of model quality is contingent. It depends on continued algorithmic research, continued hardware generations, and continued competitive pressure among several serious frontier labs, any of which could slow. Closer to fixed, at least over a multi-year horizon, is the shape of the cost curve itself. Output tokens will keep costing more than input tokens because generation is inherently more compute-intensive than comprehension. And heavy users will keep costing substantially more than light users because query complexity and token count move together. A pricing model built on the assumption that this variance will disappear is building on a trend that history gives no reason to expect. System architecture and process flow usage-based or hybrid pricing system requires four subsystems that a seat-based product does not need in the same form. A metering layer that counts the input and output tokens, application programming interface calls or completed actions a customer generates, a rating engine that converts that raw count into a customer-facing charge, a credit or wallet abstraction that decouples the vendor's actual model cost from the price the customer sees, and an invoicing and dunning system able to handle postpaid overage charges rather than a single flat monthly draft. Cursor built by Enso Sphere illustrates the credit abstraction directly. Each paid plan carries a monthly credit pool size to roughly match its subscription price. The company's own models draw down that pool at a favorable internal rate and third-party models such as Claude or GPT draw it down at each model's actual application programming. Interface price, so the customer sees one number while the company's own margin varies underneath by which model handled the request. materials for this architecture is now a specialized vendor category in its own right. Companies such as Orb and Metronome sell metering and rating as a standalone service because building an accurate, auditable, real-time usage ledger is a materially harder engineering problem than billing a fixed number of seats once a month. Salesforce's own architecture shows the same complexity from a different angle. It currently operates three pricing systems at once inside Agentforce, a per-conversation meter inherited from its October 2024 launch, a flex credits ledger priced at $0.10 per standard action introduced in May 2025, and a traditional per-seat license under its agentic enterprise license agreement priced from $125 per user per month starting in late 2025, each running on different internal plumbing and reconciled against the same customer invoice. The architectural tradeoff a venture-funded company faces is between simplicity, which seat pricing delivers natively, and cost accuracy, which usage metering delivers natively. A hybrid design, a base seat fee that includes a usage allotment with metered overage above it, is the architecture most pricing data from 2025 and 2026 shows companies converging toward because it inherits the forecasting simplicity of a seat for the committed portion of spend while exposing the vendor to the true cost curve only on the margin, where the risk of underpricing a heavy user actually lives. Quantitative performance metrics, the clearest quantitative split is the net revenue retention figure recorded by pricing model in High Alpha's 2025 and 2026 benchmark research. Hybrid pricing companies posted 105% net revenue retention, subscription companies 102%, outcome-based companies 100%, and pure consumption-based companies 99%, even though the same research found outcome based companies growing revenue 65% year over year and consumption based companies growing 43 per both ahead of the 34% growth rate posted by subscription companies. Growth is not retention and a company evaluating its own pricing choice needs both figures rather than either alone. Adoption data confirms the shift is underway rather than complete. Growth Unhinged 2025 state of B2B monetization study of more than 240 software and AI companies found seat based pricing falling from 21% to 15% of primary pricing models over 12 months while hybrid pricing rose from 27% to 41% over the same period and three and four surveyed companies change their pricing at least once during the year. Vertices second quarter 2026 contract data drawn from live Enterprise software agreements found per usage pricing the single most common model at 36.5% of contracts up from 34.0% in the first quarter of 2026 with per user pricing falling to 32 4% over the same quarter. A survey of 100 Enterprise Chief Information Officers conducted by Andreessen Horowitz cited in L E K Consulting's April 2025 analysis found 39% preferred usage based pricing specifically for AI applications against 21% who still preferred seat based pricing with 23% preferring a hybrid. Cost data explains why buyers are pulling pricing in this direction. Token prices for Frontier grade models fell from $30 per million input tokens for GPT-4 in March 2023 to roughly $0 10 per million tokens for comparable capability by early 2026. A worked unit economics example priced a single AI agent action at $0.035 in blended token cost producing a monthly inference cost of $4.20 for 50th percentile user at 120 actions per month but $21.00 for 90th percentile user at 600 actions per month, a five to one spread that a single flat dollar 29 monthly price cannot absorb without losing money on the heaviest fifth of the customer base. Xylo's 2026 SaaS Management Index found the buyer side consequence of this volatility directly. 78% of information technology leaders reported unexpected charges tied to AI features or consumption pricing, and 61% said they cut a planned project because of unplanned software cost increases. Key advantages and limitations usage and token-based pricing carries one advantage that seat pricing structurally cannot deliver. It ties the vendor's revenue to the vendor's own cost curve, protecting a company from the specific failure that cost Anthropic roughly 10 percentage points of projected 2025 gross margin, where inference costs rose faster than the company's own forecasts assumed. It also aligns price with delivered value once an AI agent begins doing the work a human seat used to do. Salesforce's own pricing documentation frames its dollar 125 per user per month agentic enterprise license agreement seat as including a digital workforce, precisely because the logic of one named human user per license breaks down when the unit of work is performed by software. McKinsey's 2026 Service Operations Research found an automated resolution costing dollar 0.62 against dollar 7.40 for resolution handled by a human agent. A 12-fold cost gap per seat price has no mechanism to capture on either the cost side or the value side. The limitation on the other side of the ledger is forecasting risk, running in both directions between buyer and vendor. Xylo's 2026 data on unexpected AI charges shows the buyer side of this risk directly. In Replit's September 2025 shift to what it called effort-based pricing produced individual customer bills that rose in user reports gathered after its agent three launch on September 10, 2025 by a factor the company's own support channels described as roughly 20 times a prior month's typical charge. The vendor side of the same risk is revenue unpredictability. A sales team that is sold flat seats for years cannot forecast next quarter's revenue from a usage-based book with the same confidence because usage, unlike head count, can fall as easily as it rises if a customer's own business contracts or a customer learns to prompt more efficiently. Seat-based pricing retains one advantage usage pricing has not replicated, procurement simplicity. A finance department approving a vendor contract can model a seat price with a single multiplication named users times price per seat. While a usage-based contract requires the buyer to model its own future consumption, a forecasting exercise many procurement teams are not equipped to run accurately, which is one reason Vertice's own contract data still placed per user pricing at 32 4% of enterprise software agreements even after a year of usage pricing gaining share. The limitation seat pricing cannot escape is that it caps vendor revenue at head count, a fixed input inside a product category where the customer's own economic benefit scales with the number of tasks the AI completes rather than the number of humans who log in to supervise it. Technical failure mode analysis, the most visible failure mode in metered AI pricing is bill shock. The acute case in which a usage-based or credit-based account consumes far more of its allotment than the customer anticipated inside a single billing period. Cursor's June 2025 shift to usage-based billing for premium model requests produced by its own users' public accounts, a case in which a team's $7,000 annual subscription was consumed in a single day. And founder Michael Troull acknowledged in early July 2025 that the rollout had been handled poorly before the company added clearer spend limits and selective refunds. Replit's parallel incident followed its September 10, 2025 launch of Agent 3 under effort-based pricing in which one documented user reported a charge of $1,000 in a single week against a typical monthly spend of dollar 180 to dollar 200. And the company itself acknowledged in July 2025 that its new checkpoint structure could end up costing moreover a project's life than the model it replaced. A second failure mode is definitional ambiguity in what triggers a charge. Salesforce's original October 2024 agent force pricing dollar 2.00 per conversation ran into this problem directly. A single customer query could trigger many backend reasoning steps and tool calls before resolving. So buyers found the per conversation price difficult to model against their own expected usage. Part of why Salesforce added its dollar 0.10 per action flex credit structure only seven months later. Constellation Research analyst Liz Miller described the resulting opacity across the AI customer service category generally as a black box in which neither the buyer nor, in some cases, the vendor can state with confidence what a given month's bill will be before the invoice arrives. A third failure mode is structural rather than acute. The principal agent misalignment inherent in pure outcome based pricing in which a vendor is paid only when it records a resolution giving it a financial incentive to classify ambiguous interactions as resolved whether or not the underlying customer problem was actually solved. This degradation failure mode compounds with the bill shock failure mode described above because a customer who already distrusts the vendor's usage counting has no reason to extend the benefit of the doubt on resolution counting either. The two failure modes together help explain why 25% of companies surveyed in growth unhinged research expect outcome based pricing to become their primary model by 2028 even though only 5% used it as their primary model in 2025. A gap that reflects resolution counting methods still largely self reported by vendors rather than independently verified in 2026 contracts. Real world applications and deployment context customer service is the sector where outcome based and usage based AI pricing is most commercially mature. Zendesk charges between dollar 1.50 and dollar 2.00 per automated resolution. Intercom's Finn agent charges dollar 0.99 per outcome, and HubSpot moved its Breeze customer agent from dollar 1.00 to dollar 0.50 per resolved conversation effective April 14, 2026, citing a 65% conversion rate and 39% faster resolution times across more than 8,000 customers as the performance basis for the new price. Service Now deploys a parallel consumption model it calls billing per AI skill execution applied to Enterprise Information Technology Service Management rather than customer-facing chat. Forrester's research found more than 45% of surveyed organizations already using AI agents in production with another 25% piloting them, placing this sector well past the early adopter phase. Software development tooling shows the same pricing migration under different commercial pressure. Cursor, built by Anthropic, moved from a fixed request allotment to usage-based billing in June 2025 and was reported to have grown annualized recurring revenue past dollar 100 million within 12 months of its earlier more subsidized pricing, then past dollar 200 million afterward. GitHub Copilot runs a parallel structure inside Microsoft's own distribution. Unlimited basic code completion bundled into a flat per seat fee starting at dollar 10 per month for individuals with a separate premium request allotment, 300 per month on the Pro tier, billed at dollar 0.04 per request once that allotment is exhausted, a hybrid design that keeps the predictable base feature flat while metering only the more expensive premium model calls. Replit's parallel deployment shows the less settled edge of this trend. It September 2025 moved to effort-based pricing for its Autonomous Agent 3 product, arrived alongside a dollar 250 million funding round that included Google's AI Futures Fund, evidence that capital markets continue to back the technology even as its pricing mechanics were still being worked out in public. Legal services shows a narrower but telling data point at the high end of outcome pricing. Harvey, a legal AI company, was reported at approximately dollar 190 million in annual recurring revenue. Operating in a sector where the dollar value of a correctly drafted or reviewed document is high enough that law firm buyers have shown more tolerance for value-based and outcome-linked pricing than price-sensitive small business buyers show in other sectors. Economic and scalability considerations, the primary cost driver inside a venture-funded AI products income statement is inference compute. A cost category a conventional SaaS company's income statement does not carry incomparable size, which is why the 80% plus gross margin benchmark that defines software investing for two decades is not the right comparison for an AI-native company. Pricing researchers surveying AI-native company data decks in 2026 described a working floor of 60% gross margin as the level needed to support a credible series of financing narrative with a target range of 50 to 70% gross margin replacing the older benchmark entirely and recommended that a company set its base price to clear 60 percent margin at the 50th percentile user rather than at the average since the average is distorted upward by a small number of very light users. The experience curve of working in every AI company's favor is the token cost decline itself. A decline on the order of 10 times per year in frontier inference cost compounding into the nearly 300 times reduction over three years documented earlier in this report. That decline is a tailwind for gross margin only if a company's pricing captures it deliberately. A company that locks a flat proceed price for 18 months while its own input costs fall tenfold is leaving margin uncaptured while a company that reprices too aggressively on the same schedule risks the bill shock failure mode described above. Pricing researchers recommend a repricing cadence closer to every 90 days specifically to stay inside this window without triggering a cursor style trust event. The bottleneck constraining how fast any individual company can scale its own usage based revenue is not customer demand, but graphics processing unit supply and data center capacity at its underlying model provider, a constraint outside the pricing company's own control. Anthropic's own 2026 capital spending reported in the $6 billion to $9 billion range for the year against OpenAI's reported spending above $14 billion illustrates the scale of capital intensity sitting upstream of every venture funded company that resells access to these models rather than training its own. The financing market has already begun pricing this distinction into valuation multiples, LEK. Consulting's April 2025 analysis of the SaaS capital index found usage based pricing companies carrying a 7.4x mean revenue multiple and hybrid pricing companies a 6.9x mean multiple, both ahead of the 6.5x mean multiple for pure subscription companies with hybrid pricing companies also posting 19% trailing 12 month revenue growth against the broader index. For a venture funded company preparing its next financing round, the pricing model is no longer a product decision made once and left alone. Investors are now pricing it directly into the multiple. Future development trajectory, the clearest milestone on the horizon is IDC's forecast that seat based pricing will be largely obsolete by 2028, a forecast consistent with the trajectory already visible in Vertices quarter over quarter contract data showing per user pricing losing roughly 2 and 1/2 percentage points of share in a single quarter of 2026. Gartner's parallel forecast puts a number on the scale of disruption at the high end. Agentic AI could affect approximately 20% of enterprise SaaS spending and could see 35% of point product SaaS tools replaced or absorbed by agents by 2030, though the same research found more than 40% of agentic AI projects were expected to be canceled by the end of 2027. And that only about 130 of the thousands of vendors currently claiming agentic capability were found to meet Gartner's own criteria for that label. The credibility of the 2028 seat obsolescence forecast rests on a contingent assumption, not a fixed one. That metering and billing infrastructure vendors such as Orb and Metronome keep maturing fast enough that usage-based billing becomes as operationally reliable for a mid-sized software company as a flat monthly draft is today. That infrastructure risk is improvable, unlike the token cost curve itself, which is governed by compute economics and hardware supply, not by how fast a billing team can build software. This analysis characterizes the risk that usage-based pricing fails to reach the 2028 milestone as moderate. The economic logic favoring the shift is close to settled, but the billing systems, finance team processes, and sales compensation plans built around them are still catching up. And a shortfall in that tooling, not a reversal in underlying cost economics, is the more likely cause of any delay. The competing trajectory worth tracking is a split market rather than a single winner. The Andreessen Horowitz Chief Information Officer survey finding 39% usage preference against 23% hybrid and 21% seat preference read alongside Vertice's hybrid share holding near 31% for two consecutive quarters points toward a three-way split that has held across multiple reporting periods rather than a full migration to any single model. The venture-funded companies that win the next financing cycle will likely be the ones offering buyers a choice of structure rather than the ones that bet the whole product on one model. Open questions The first question concerns billing infrastructure maturity. Will metering vendors such as Orb and Metronome reach a level of accuracy and auditability that eliminates the reconciliation errors behind episodes such as Cursor's June 2025 Bill Shock? A question resolvable within two to three years as vendors publish audited usage data and as more enterprise buyers demand it in contract terms. And one that matters because the 2028 seat obsolescence forecast assumes this infrastructure keeps pace with pricing ambition. The second question concerns resolution verification in outcome-based pricing. Will an independent or third-party standard emerge for what counts as a resolved customer interaction, resolving the principal agent problem identified in this report, or will vendors continue defining their own resolution metrics? This question matters because growth unhinged research found adoption intentions for outcome pricing running well ahead of current trust levels, and the gap will not close through marketing alone. The third question concerns the durability of the token cost decline itself. Will the roughly tenfold annual decline in frontier inference cost continue at its recent pace, or will power supply and data center construction constraints, already visible in reported capital spending above dollar 14 billion annually at OpenAI and dollar 6 billion to dollar 9 billion at Anthropic, slow the curve within the next five to 10 years? The answer determines whether usage-based pricing keeps gaining structural advantage or whether cost volatility becomes a shared industry problem rather than a competitive lever. The fourth question concerns enterprise procurement adaptation. Will corporate finance and procurement functions build the forecasting capability to approve usage-based contracts with the same confidence they apply to seat-based contracts within the next two to three years, or will large enterprises continue favoring seat pricing specifically for budgeting predictability even where usage pricing would lower their total cost? The fifth question concerns capital markets durability. Will the revenue multiple premium documented by consulting for usage-based and hybrid pricing companies hold if a broader financing downturn forces investors to prioritize predictability over growth? A macro-dependent question that will not resolve on any fixed timetable, but that materially affects which pricing model a founder should choose when raising a series B or series C in 2026. The biggest takeaway from this is understanding your total compensation before you negotiate with Salesforce. It's very important because then you're going to know exactly how much your pay package is worth and you know everything that you should be able to negotiate. So don't skip that. The second step is going to be what I call doing your due diligence and asking strategic questions. This is where you review the Salesforce offer and come back with a list of questions there for your recruiter. This is not only going to help you clarify any questions you might have about the offer, but it also is going to allow you to strategically ask questions that are going to actually build leverage in the negotiation. So don't skip this, okay? you're going to count all items where it might not be as competitive as your current company or what some of their competitors offer. And if you need ideas on this and why it's so big, feel free to go ahead and grab um our list of questions on our templates page. That way, you know what to ask because I don't want you to skip this step. [music] Even if you think you understand the offer and you know everything they're including, it's very important for your negotiation leverage because it shows you're doing your research. It shows you're doing your due diligence before you send a counter offer. That way, one, your counter offer is not going to come out of left field. They're going to take it as more legitimate, as well as you might secure any freebies that are on the tables that Salesforce might use as trade-offs later on if you don't get them out of the way early. So, keep that in mind. And the third step is to do your Salesforce compensation research. Okay? You want to find the base salary and the total compensation ranges for the specific role, the location, and the level at Salesforce. You can use various online resources to find this data, but make sure you're using multiple sources in averaging the results. What we're trying to do here is try to identify the compensation ranges so we can see where your initial offer sits on that range and how much more room there is for improvement. So, you can take a database approach [music] because Salesforce, like a bunch of other tech companies, try to hire their employees at the low to mid end of the pay bands. But, I'm always going to suggest that you push towards the top end of the pay range because you should be paid as anyone else doing that role. So, that's where you want to target. But you want to make sure it's obviously real realistic, okay? Because remember this is publicly reported data and it [music] might not always be accurate. So what you want to do is make sure your average results and if [music] you need help, feel free to go ahead and use our compensation research comparison tool on our templates page or check out our course that's actually going to show you exactly how to do this compensation [music] research. so you can prepare for your Salesforce counter offer. They explore how partners can simplify and manage integrations, automate actions based on platform events, and what’s coming next with MCP and AI-powered agents. A great strategy means nothing if it never turns into results.

In this episode of Academy Live, Scott Berns, SVP of Revenue & GTM Americas at Pax8, breaks down the fundamentals of building a business plan that actually drives outcomes.

🔑 Key Topics Covered
 ✅ Why many MSPs struggle to translate strategy into real results
 ✅ How prioritization helps businesses focus on what truly moves the needle
 ✅ Understanding market dynamics and aligning them with your plan
 ✅ Creating actionable plans your teams can execute against
 ✅ Using leading indicators to track progress before results appear
 ✅ Why measurement and feedback loops drive continuous improvement
 ✅ How MSPs can shift from reactive operations to intentional growth
 ✅ Practical ways to connect strategy, execution, and business outcomes

So on the core principles of of go to market, let's let's talk about making sure that we have that focus before scale. So more often than not, you're not going to scale by doing more things. metadata.shortDescription:
Pax8 is a portal that allows Managed Service Providers (MSPs) and xSPs to self-serve and bill, manage and analyse their business ecosystem.

The Pax8 team of wingmen offers bespoke support and enablement for MSPs. It’s all designed to help MSPs sell better and deliver better service!

In this video, Richard Tubb speaks to Phylip Morgan, Chief Channel Officer, and Tom Welton, Partner Solutions Engineer, at Pax8.

Richard gets a tour of the Pax8 platform and learns more about the benefits for MSPs.

Tom explains how to customise the Pax8 dashboard, how Pax8 integrates with a range of RMM and PSA tools and the different views that are available to different departments in an organisation.

#MSP #cloudservices #cloudcomputing

metadata.title: From £2 Add-On to a Service Clients Understand: Lessons From Pax8
metadata.author: usecure
metadata.shortDescription:
Josh Greenberg spent two and a half years on Pax8's go-to-market team helping MSPs take security to their clients, and has just joined usecure as EMEA Channel & Alliances Manager. Filmed at Pax8 Beyond in Copenhagen, he talks through why human risk usually comes last in the stack, how MSPs package security so clients see the value, tool sprawl, and what uHealth adds.

"Oddly enough, and I think it's quite a common knowledge, human risk is normally the last element that MSPs look at today."

Brought to you by usecure, the Human Risk Intelligence platform. https://www.usecure.io/

Chapters
0:00 Intro
0:33 The Pax8 years
0:49 Packaging security
1:19 The human side
2:15 Securing the human
3:20 The rest of the stack
3:42 Surprises by region
4:44 Taking it to market
6:34 The upsell conversation
7:19 Tool sprawl
9:51 The road map
10:33 What uHealth does
11:38 Stop doing in 2027
12:37 Wrap-up

About Josh
Josh Greenberg is EMEA Channel & Alliances Manager at usecure, which he joined six weeks before Pax8 Beyond. Before that he spent a good part of his career at Pax8, on the go-to-market team, working with MSPs on how to position and sell their cybersecurity offering.

#Pax8Beyond #MSP #usecure

metadata.title: 90%+ Customer Adoption? The Cybersecurity Sales Strategy MSPs Should Know | Blackpoint at Pax8 EMEA
metadata.author: Magic Chats
metadata.shortDescription:
What if you could start selling 24/7 managed cybersecurity services without building your own Security Operations Center (SOC)?

At Pax8 Beyond EMEA 2026 in Copenhagen, I sat down with Sham Miah from Blackpoint Cyber to explore how traditional IT resellers can transform their businesses into Managed Service Providers (MSPs) by taking greater responsibility for their customers' cybersecurity.

Cybersecurity is one of the most promising entry points into managed services. But building a security practice from scratch requires skilled people, proven processes, sophisticated technology, and the ability to respond to threats around the clock.

What if you could leverage a partner that already has these capabilities?

In our conversation, we explore:

- From reseller to MSP: Why cybersecurity is an attractive starting point for building recurring revenue and deeper customer relationships.
- SOC and MDR as a service: How Blackpoint Cyber helps partners deliver 24/7 threat monitoring and response without building everything themselves.
- The opt-out strategy: A fascinating approach to selling managed cybersecurity services, where customers explicitly acknowledge the risks of declining protection. Sham discusses adoption rates exceeding 90%.
- Proving the value: How a 180-day historical security scan can help uncover existing threats and create compelling customer conversations.
- AI and cybersecurity: Why AI can accelerate threat detection but human expertise and judgment remain essential.
- Beyond selling security tools: How MSPs can shift toward ongoing responsibility, proactive protection, and measurable business value.

One of my favorite insights from Sham is the opt-out campaign.

Rather than simply asking customers whether they want another cybersecurity product, MSPs explain the risks of operating without proactive protection — and ask customers to formally acknowledge those risks if they decline the service.

It's an interesting way to change the conversation from selling technology to managing business risk.

And that's exactly the transformation I'm exploring through Magic Chats and Outconomy.

Customers don't really want antivirus licenses, firewalls, or security dashboards. They want their businesses protected, their operations uninterrupted, and someone they can trust to take responsibility.

For resellers looking to enter the managed services market, cybersecurity could be one of the most practical places to start.

#MagicChats #BlackpointCyber #Pax8Beyond #MSP #MDR #SOC #Cybersecurity #ManagedServices #RecurringRevenue #BusinessOutcomes #Outconomy

metadata.shortDescription:
AI is changing how businesses operate and Managed Service Providers have a choice: lead the transformation or watch someone else do it.

In this episode of Academy Live, we're joined by David Schafran, VP of Partner Enablement at Pax8, to unpack the newly available Managed Intelligence Provider (MIP) Program and explain how MSPs can begin their journey into managed intelligence services. 

🔑 Key Topics Covered
✅ What the MIP Program is and who it's designed for
✅ How AI maturity assessments help identify your organization's starting point
✅ Understanding the Broker vs. Builder approach to managed intelligence
✅ Why managed intelligence is an evolution of great consulting and not a replacement for MSP services
✅ The six MIP plays: Discover, Sell, Buy, Build, Implement, and Manage
✅ How MSPs can monetize AI and automation opportunities
✅ The role of QBRs and business conversations in uncovering intelligence opportunities
✅ How the Agent Store, enablement resources, and user communities support growth

Whether you're a technical leader, business owner, salesperson, or strategist, this episode will help you understand how to begin incorporating managed intelligence into your business and where to find the resources to get started.

metadata.title: Pax8's Eric Torres Discusses Enhanced Nerdio Partnership & MSP Marketplace Solutions: NerdioCon 2025
metadata.author: VMblog
metadata.shortDescription:
In this exclusive interview from NerdioCon 2025 in Palm Springs, California, VMblog speaks with Eric Torres, VP of Channel and Community Engagement at Pax8. Torres provides insights into how Pax8 serves as a comprehensive cloud marketplace for Managed Service Providers (MSPs), offering a one-stop solution for SaaS licensing needs across 140+ MSP-friendly vendors.

The interview highlights Pax8's strengthened partnership with Nerdio, which now includes dedicated Nerdio ambassadors, 13 specialized and certified Nerdio engineers, and co-developed live Nerdio support to provide faster resolution times for partners using both platforms.

Torres explains the unique value Pax8 brings to MSPs through:
* Streamlined billing and invoicing processes
* Integration with existing MSP tools
* Comprehensive support for all marketplace solutions
* The Pax8 Academy offering tech, sales, marketing, and business training
* Peer groups led by experienced MSP owners

Torres also shares recent company announcements, including their upcoming "Beyond Pax8" partner conference in Denver this June, which is expected to host 3,000 MSPs, and the appointment of Craig Foster as their new CFO.

MSPs interested in learning more about Pax8's offerings can visit pax8.com to explore their marketplace vendors, academy resources, peer groups, and upcoming events.

#NerdioCon2025 #Pax8 #MSP #CloudMarketplace #ManagedServiceProviders #SaaSSolutions

metadata.title: What is Telecom Expense Management (TEM)?
metadata.author: brightfin
metadata.shortDescription:
What is Telecom Expense Management?

Organizations have a tough challenge managing all the IT invoices and expenses generated from their fixed/telecom, mobile, and cloud assets. Examples of these expenses are dedicated lines, switches, smartphones, tablets, project management software, and more. Telecom Expense Management (TEM) began with fixed assets and as organizations have deployed more mobile devices and cloud-based services, the meaning of TEM has grown as well.

TEM platforms automate all of your IT-related invoices. By gaining visibility of IT spend, business leaders can answer the tough questions like:

- What assets do we own and where are they?
- Which invoices have we paid?
- Are we paying the right amount?
- Could we be spending less?
- How much should we budget for next year?

These questions are incredibly hard to answer when you have invoices coming in from different places and in different formats. But while traditional TEM may solve for individual categories of IT spending, this data is often still siloed in different platforms. So IT and Finance leaders still rely on manual spreadsheets or BI tools to get a holistic view of IT spending.

This is where brightfin's unified telecom expense reporting is so powerful.

brightfin goes beyond traditional TEM to include IT financial management and industry-leading services. This approach to Telecom Expense Management ensures that IT is aligned with the overall strategic goals of the business by providing cost saving opportunities and full visibility into what is being spent, why, and for whom.

Learn more at: https://www.brightfin.com/telecom-expense-management/

Are you confused by Microsoft Partner Center and what it actually means for your business? In this video, we break down everything you need to know about this essential hub, from the FY26 benefit tiers to the upcoming AI features that will change how you work. 🚀

Microsoft Partner Center is often misunderstood as a portal just for giant resellers, but it is actually the command center for any business building on, reselling, or consulting around Microsoft products. Whether you are a small consulting shop or a large managed service provider, this platform is where you manage your benefits, track incentives, and handle customer relationships. 💻

We dive deep into the new FY26 benefit structure, exploring the differences between the Launch, Core, and Expanded tiers. You will learn how to unlock Microsoft 365 Copilot licenses, manage your Azure credits, and utilize internal-use security tools like Defender for Business and Intune. We also cover the technical side, including how to avoid the common viral user setup problem and why having a break glass account is a non-negotiable security step. 🔒

Stay ahead of the curve as we discuss the future of the platform, including the new AI Assistant for support and the mandatory MFA requirements for all API calls coming in 2026. Understanding these changes now will ensure your organization stays compliant and maximizes the value of your Microsoft partnership.

metadata.title: Unlocking Private Equity Value with OMNIA Partners’ Spend Path and The Power of Group Purchasing
metadata.author: OMNIA Partners
metadata.shortDescription:
In today’s evolving private equity (PE) landscape, longer holding periods and economic uncertainty are putting more pressure on firms to improve operational efficiency across their portfolio companies. In this conversation, Ara Arslanian, Senior Vice President of Private Equity at OMNIA Partners, discusses the challenges of data fragmentation and the growing need for strategic, streamlined procurement in PE. 

Discover how OMNIA Partners, the GPO of choice for PE, delivers value beyond savings with Spend Path — a proprietary solution that can help PE firms turn spend data into actionable insights.  

What you’ll learn in this video: 

Why procurement plays a critical role in PE operational strategy 

The increasing complexity of spend management across portfolio companies 

How Spend Path streamlines data integration and provides real-time spend insights 

The speed and simplicity of implementing Spend Path (2–3 weeks to start seeing results) 

How OMNIA Partners layers buying power with data integrity to unlock new value 

Whether you're navigating integration challenges, looking to optimize spend, or evaluating supplier risk across your portfolio, OMNIA Partners can help your organization achieve meaningful efficiencies, improve EBITDA, and stay ahead of the curve. 

Connect with us: 

Website: https://www.omniapartners.com  

LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/omnia-partners  

Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/OMNIAPartners

metadata.title: B2B SaaS Sales Quota Benchmarks 2026: SDR Meetings, AE Quota, OTE, Ratios
metadata.author: GrowthSpree - AI Native B2B Marketing Agency
metadata.shortDescription:
SDR and AE quotas are set by gut feel in 47% of B2B SaaS companies. It shows in ramp times, churn rates, and pipeline misses. Set quotas too low and you burn budget on under-utilized reps. Set them too high and you churn 41% of new hires inside 12 months. The right SDR meeting target depends on ACV, the right AE quota depends on motion, and the right SDR:AE ratio depends on both. This is the complete 2026 benchmark report.

In this video: median and top-quartile SDR meetings, SQL conversion, AE quota, OTE, win rate, and SDR:AE ratios by ACV segment and sales motion. Plus the 6 quota-setting mistakes that lead to rep churn and the framework to set quotas that hold.

The headline: median AE quota is $720K, OTE $192K. Top quartile AE hits $1.3M quota with $280K OTE. Median SDR books 12 meetings/month, top quartile hits 22.

Sources: Bridge Group SDR Metrics 2026, OpenView SaaS Benchmarks 2026, Salesforce State of Sales 2026, internal GrowthSpree data across 60+ B2B SaaS sales orgs.

RESOURCES MENTIONED

Full quota playbook: https://www.growthspreeofficial.com/
Free 30-min sales productivity audit: https://meetings.hubspot.com/ishan-m

TIMESTAMPS
00:00 Why 47% set quota by gut
01:00 The quota-setting framework
02:00 SDR productivity by ACV
02:45 SDR meetings + SQL conversion
03:30 Quota-setting mistakes to avoid

KEY BENCHMARKS (2026)

SDR productivity by ACV (median monthly meetings / SQLs): Sub-$10K 24/18, $10K-$50K 18/13, $50K-$250K 14/9, $250K+ 10/6

AE quota by ACV (median annual ARR): Sub-$10K $480K, $10K-$50K $720K, $50K-$250K $1.1M, $250K+ $1.6M

AE OTE by ACV (median): Sub-$10K $135K, $10K-$50K $192K, $50K-$250K $245K, $250K+ $310K

Quota attainment median: 54% / Top quartile: 78%
AE ramp time median: 5.8 months / Top quartile: 3.4 months
AE annual churn median: 28% / Top quartile: 14%

SDR:AE ratio by motion: PLG 0.5:1, Sales-led 1.5:1, Hybrid 1.2:1, ABM-led 1.8:1
Win rate by motion (median): PLG 34%, Sales-led 19%, Hybrid 24%, ABM-led 31%
Pipeline coverage at quarter start (median): 3.2x
GrowthSpree avg pipeline lift in 90 days: 2.8x

KEY INSIGHTS

Quota must back into pipeline math. Quota = (target ACV x deals needed) ÷ rep capacity. Most teams set quota first and reverse-engineer pipeline.

ACV determines SDR meeting target. Sub-$10K SDRs hit 24 meetings/month because deals are transactional. $250K+ SDRs hit 10 because each meeting needs deeper research.

AE quota scales with ACV but not linearly. Sub-$10K AE quota $480K, $250K+ $1.6M. 3.3x quota jump for 25x ACV jump. AEs close fewer, larger deals.

OTE ratio to quota stays at 4:1 across segments. Above $1M quota, OTE leverages slightly.

Quota attainment median is 54%, top quartile 78%. Below 50% means quotas wrong or product-market fit off, not that reps need pressure.

SDR:AE ratio is determined by motion. PLG 0.5:1 because product creates pipeline. ABM-led 1.8:1 because committee outreach is labor-intensive.

PLG has highest win rate (34%) and lowest SDR:AE ratio. Product does qualification work SDRs do in other motions.

ABM-led has highest SDR:AE ratio (1.8:1) and 31% win rate. Multi-touch on multi-stakeholder accounts. Tight targeting wins.

AE ramp time median is 5.8 months. Top quartile 3.4. Gap is onboarding rigor, role clarity, SDR pipeline quality during ramp.

AE annual churn at 28% kills ramp investment payback. Top quartile keeps at 14% by setting attainable quotas, providing pipeline, paying competitively.

The 6 quota-setting mistakes: (1) copying competitor quotas, (2) annualizing year-1 reps' best quarter, (3) ignoring ramp time, (4) over-weighting bookings vs ARR, (5) flat quotas across territories, (6) no clawback for early churn.

Senior operators set quotas with 70-75% attainment as target. Junior teams set 100% target and watch reps churn.
