metadata.title: Your Life as Every Level of a SaaS Sales Rep — From SDR to VP
metadata.author: Money Machine
metadata.shortDescription:
You're 24 years old. You make $45,000 base. The red bar on your screen says you're at 42% to quota, the quarter ends in fourteen days, and your roommate makes $95,000 writing code from home in sweatpants. You put the headset back on and hit dial. Someone says "not interested" and hangs up before you finish your name.

This is the full career ladder of a SaaS sales rep, told as one continuous life — from the 20-year-old with a marketing degree and $40,000 in student loans, to the bullpen where thirty 23-year-olds make 80 dials a day, to the AE running demos and losing a $40,000 deal over an indemnification clause, to Enterprise Sales selling $500,000 contracts to Fortune 500 CIOs, to the Sales Manager listening to recorded calls in Gong and firing someone for the first time, to the VP of Sales who is responsible for $20 million in ARR and has never built a single thing.

Along the way it breaks down what the job actually is: the SDR funnel from 80 dials to 2 meetings, MEDDPICC and why the Economic Buyer is usually on vacation in Cabo, the Champion with no political capital, sandbagging, Monday forecast calls, the $300-a-head steakhouse dinners called "relationship building," and the hollow feeling of a $60,000 commission check that should mean everything and doesn't.

And it ends on the part nobody tells you — that the best salespeople aren't liars or slick-haired closers. They're professional disqualifiers. The red bar was never really about the money.

If you've ever worked in sales, been on the other end of that sales call, or wondered what's actually happening behind the software you use every day, this one is for you.

This video is for educational purposes. It is a dramatized, composite account and not career or financial advice.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

SOURCES

Bridge Group — Sales Development Benchmark Report, annual data on SDR activity metrics, dials, connect rates, and meeting quotas

RepVue and Glassdoor — public compensation data for SDR, AE, Enterprise AE, Sales Manager, and VP of Sales roles

Salesforce — State of Sales, annual report on quota attainment, sales cycle length, and rep-to-manager ratios

Gong — published research on recorded sales calls, talk ratios, and discovery question analysis

MEDDPICC — sales qualification framework originally developed at PTC by Jack Napoli, widely documented in The Qualified Sales Leader by John McMahon

Sales Management literature and industry interviews on sandbagging, forecast accuracy, and compensation plan design

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Note: The character, company, and specific figures — $45,000 base, $85,000 OTE, 42% to quota, $600,000 AE quota, $140,000 Enterprise base, the lost $40,000 deal, and the $2 million close — are composite and illustrative, drawn from publicly reported compensation ranges and industry benchmarks rather than any single person's record. Individual numbers vary widely by company, segment, and market. Specific reports and data points can be linked here if you want viewers to verify the ranges.

want to buy the software and trick them

sales factory. You are given a list of
250 names and phone numbers every
morning. You are given a script. You are
given a software called a dialer, which
auto dials the next number the second

You make 80 dials a day. You leave 40
voicemails. You get 10 conversations.
You book two meetings.
The first week you are terrified of the
phone. Your voice shakes. You read the
script like a hostage reading a ransom
note. You hear the word no 60 times a
day. It used to sting. By month two, the
word no means nothing. It is just a
sound. It is the static of your new
life.

"I completely understand. I just need 30

sweating.
Your only goal is to pass the baton to
an AE, an account executive, the
closers.
At 25, you get promoted. You become the
AE.
You get a base salary bump to $65,000
and a higher commission rate. You are no
longer on the phone for 8 hours a day.
You are running demos on Zoom.
This is where the actual psychological
warfare begins.
You are given a quota, usually a number
around $600,000
a year. You are responsible for bringing
in that much revenue.
The company has a framework called
MEDDPICC.
It is an acronym. Metrics, economic
buyer, decision criteria, decision
process, paper process, identify pain,
champion, competition. You learn that
selling software is not about convincing
someone your product is good. It is
about navigating a maze of corporate
bureaucracy.
You learn that the person you are
talking to on Zoom might love your
product, but if they aren't the economic
buyer, they cannot sign the check. You
learn to ask, "Who else needs to be
involved in this decision?" You learn
that the answer is almost always a
45-year-old vice president who doesn't
care about your product, only cares

You learn about the champion. This is
the person who is going to fight for
your software internally when you aren't
in the room. You learn that if your
champion doesn't have political capital
in the company, you will lose the deal.
You spend 90% of your time chasing. The
follow-up email, the just checking in
phone call, the looming dread of the end
of the quarter when the prospect
suddenly goes dark.
You lose your first big deal, a $40,000
contract. Everything was perfect. The
demo was flawless. The champion loved

team rejected the terms because of an
indemnification clause. The deal dies.
The revenue disappears. Your commission
disappears.
You go into the stairwell. You sit on
the concrete steps. You don't cry. You
just stare at the wall and feel a
strange hollow anger.
Then you go back to your desk and open a
new browser tab.
At 28, you move up to enterprise sales.
You are selling $500,000
software contracts to Fortune 500
companies. Your base salary is now
You are living in a different world.
The deals take 9 months to close. You
have to speak to C-suite executives,
chief information officers, chief
financial officers. You have to
understand their architecture, their
compliance requirements, their data
security protocols.
You learn that at this level, your
product doesn't even have to be the
best. It just has to be the safest. No
one gets fired for buying IBM. No one
gets fired for buying Microsoft.
You get really, really good at managing
people's fear. You learn how to make a
purchase feel like a low-risk decision.
You learn to write business cases that
justify the expenditure to a board of
directors.
You are 28 years old and you are flying
first class to Chicago to take a group
of middle-aged executives to a
steakhouse that costs $300 ahead. The
company pays for it. It's called
relationship building. It's really
called bribing them with Wagyu beef so
they sign on the dotted line.
You don't close a deal that year. It
takes you 11 months to close your first
one. But when you do, the commission
check is $60,000.
You look at the number in your bank
account and you feel nothing. It's just
numbers on a screen.
At 31, you stop selling. You become a
sales manager.
You have eight eyes reporting to you.
You have a team quota of $6 million.
Your job is no longer to talk to
customers. Your job is to talk to your
reps.
You spend your days in a tool called
Gong listening to recorded Zoom calls.
You critique their discovery questions.
You point out the exact minute they lost
the deal.
You learn that managing sales reps is
like managing professional athletes with
anxiety disorders. Half of your team is
depressed because they are behind quota.
The other half is arrogant because they
are ahead of quota and think they are
invincible.
You have a forecast call every Monday.
You sit with your boss, the VP of sales,
and you look at the pipeline. You have
to guess what is going to close. You
have to guess what the number is going
to be.
You learn a term called sandbagging.
It's when a rep has a deal that is
already closed, but they hide it holding
it in their back pocket to use for a
future month when their pipeline is dry.
You have to fire someone for the first
time, a rep named Jason. He's 26. He
works hard, but he just doesn't have the
mental resilience for the rejection. He
sits in your office. He knows before you
say the words. He starts crying.
You hand him a box. You walk him to the
elevator. You go back to your desk and
start interviewing his replacement the
next day.
The machine never stops.
At 35, you're the VP of sales.
You report directly to the chief revenue
officer. You sit in the board meetings.
You are responsible for $20 million in
annual recurring revenue.
You don't know any of the customers
anymore. You don't know their pain
points. You don't know their tech
stacks. You just know the math. You know
the lifetime value of a customer. You
know the cost of acquisition. You know
the churn rate.
You are no longer a person who sells
software. You are a person who manages
the revenue engine. You build the
compensation plans that make your reps
aggressive. You set the quotas that make
them terrified. You design the
territories that make them fight each
other.
You are 35 years old and you have never
built a thing in your life. You have
never written a line of code. You have
never designed an interface. You have
never shipped a product.
You just extracted money from one
corporation and moved it to another. You
are a professional middleman.
You're standing at the office window on
a Thursday afternoon. It's raining.
You look down at the street below. You
think about the 24-year-old version of
yourself. The kid with the headset
getting hung up on 60 times a day. The
kid who thought no was just static.
Here's the part nobody tells you about
this industry. It's not about being a
liar. It's not about being a
slick-haired, shark-toothed Wall Street
stereotype.
The best sales people are professional
disqualifiers.
Your job is not to force someone to buy.
Your job is to figure out as quickly as
humanly possible if this person is going
to be a good customer. If they aren't,
you have to be strong enough to walk
away. You have to save your time, your
company's time, and their time.
The reason people hate sales people is
because most sales people are bad at
disqualifying. They chase bad deals.
They beg for money. They act out of
desperation.
You didn't survive in this industry
because you were a good liar. You
survived because you were an expert at
diagnosing problems. You asked the hard
questions. You looked at a business and
found the exact place where the blood
was leaking out.
The red bar on your screen was never
about the money. It was about the truth.
You look at your phone. Your top guy
just sent you a message. He closed a $2
million deal. The quarter is saved.
You stare at the message, you don't feel
joy, you don't feel excitement. You feel
the same thing you felt at 24 when you
finally got someone to say yes after 16
no's.
Relief.
You go back to your desk, you open the
CRM, the numbers are green.
If this made you think differently about
the person on the other end of that
sales call, or the pressure behind the
software you use every day, hit like and
subscribe.
And I want to know something specific.
Have you ever worked in sales? Have you
ever had a job where your entire income
was tied to a single number on a screen?
Tell me in the comments. I'll be
reading.

metadata.title: Unlocking Sales Success: Ben Murray and QuotaPath on Building Scalable Compensation Plans
metadata.author: The SaaS CFO
metadata.shortDescription:
Join Ben Murray in this enlightening episode of his no-fluff webinar series, focused on educating the SaaS community. In this session, Ben, a fractional CFO and SaaS metrics expert, is joined by Ryan Milligan and Graham Collins from Quotapath to delve into the complexities of designing effective sales compensation plans for SaaS companies.

The webinar addresses a range of critical topics including the transition from founder-led sales to a sales-led motion, the importance of aligning sales comp plans with corporate objectives, and the essential components of a scalable sales compensation plan. Ryan and Graham bring their extensive experience to the table, having conducted over 700 compensation plan consultations.

They discuss the key elements of a successful sales comp plan, such as setting on-target earnings (OTE), determining the correct pay mix between base salary and variable commission, and establishing appropriate quotas and commission structures. The conversation also covers the impact of Annual Contract Value (ACV) on quota setting, the use of financial models for quota determination, and the strategies for adjusting quota frequency based on sales cycles and average sales prices (ASP).

One of the highlights includes a deep dive into different commission models like single-rate commissions, accelerators, and decelerators. Ryan and Graham also explore the challenges and best practices for implementing multi-year contracts, managing customer profitability, and including services in sales comp plans.

Throughout the session, they emphasize the importance of creating compensation plans that motivate sales teams while aligning with broader business goals. This highly interactive webinar encourages audience participation, with live Q&A segments where Ben, Ryan, and Graham address concerns and provide tailored solutions. Questions range from the effectiveness of decelerators in sales compensation, methods to incentivize non-discounting behaviors among sales reps, and strategies for handling different deal sources.

The session concludes with practical tips and additional resources for those looking to further refine their sales compensation plans. Whether you're a SaaS founder, executive, or part of a sales leadership team, this webinar provides actionable insights and expert guidance on building and optimizing your sales compensation plans to drive sustainable business growth.

To learn more about Ben check out the links below:

Join Ben’s SaaS community here: https://www.thesaasacademy.com/offers/ivNjwYDx/checkout

Follow Ben on LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/benrmurray

metadata.title: 🔥 20 SaaS Sales Hacks That’ll Make You Close Deals Like a Boss 💰🚀
metadata.author: Oz SaaS Master
metadata.shortDescription:
Want to 10x your SaaS sales? 🚀 I wasted years figuring this out—save yourself the pain. Here are 20 cheat codes I wish I knew 13 years ago.

👇 Steal These Pro Moves:
✅ Stop Selling Benefits—Buyers pay to kill pain, not chase rainbows.
✅ Speed Wins—Respond fast or lose forever. ⚡
✅ Demos That Convert—Only show what solves their problem (skip the fluff!).
✅ Multi-Thread Like a Spy—Swarm deals by connecting with every stakeholder.
✅ Price Talk Last—If they’re negotiating too early, you messed up.

💡 Golden Rule: Make the buyer the hero—not your product.

🚨 Drop a comment: Which hack are you trying TODAY? Let’s talk shop! 👇

#SaaSSales #SalesHacks #CloseMoreDeals #NoMoreStruggle #ozsaasmaster 

🔥 P.S. Tag a sales rep who needs this. Watch their close rate soar. 📈
P.P.S. Want cold email scripts that work? Watch next

your hand. If you know your buyer so

metadata.title: Pricing for B2B SaaS
metadata.author: Willingness to Pay
metadata.shortDescription:
Pricing for B2B SaaS

In this video, I break down the four essential pricing strategies every B2B SaaS company needs to understand before choosing a pricing model. We explore the difference between pricing strategy and pricing model, and why your decision to go premium or low-cost fundamentally shapes your business growth, customer acquisition, and long-term competitiveness.

I also walk through real-world examples like Atlassian and Rackspace to show how these strategies play out in practice. Whether you're considering a land-and-expand approach, a premium positioning strategy, or trying to compete on price, this video will help you understand the trade-offs and make smarter pricing decisions for your SaaS business.

The Pricing Roadmap Book: https://www.willingnesstopay.com/the-pricing-roadmap

➢ Website: https://www.willingnesstopay.com/ 
➢ Linkedin: https://www.linkedin.com/in/ulriklehrskovschmidt

Thank you for your support! I love to hear from you, so please continue to comment, like, and favorite. If there is a topic or issue you want me to cover? Go ahead and leave a comment and I'll have it up for you soon!
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Contact:
➢ Mail: ulrik@willingnesstopay.com 
#SaaS #Saaspricing #saassales 
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Like, all that is in the pricing model and that's great. But, before you get to that part, you need to determine if you're going to be an expensive or a low-price offering. And that basically means that we have two primary pricing strategies. And then, when we add the element of time going from now into the future, we get two more. So, let me walk you through that and show you how I think about pricing strategy. So, initially, you have the choice of whether you want to go high-price, that is premium, or low-price. Let's just call it low-price. Sometimes I also call it shrinking the market. And I'll explain why. So, here is how each of these work. So, low-price first. So, if you have a market right now, here, and you have the same price as everyone else, you might be able to get this sort of tiny slice of the market up here. So, you might be able to sort of get a few percentage of this marketplace because you're just trying to get the same customers as everyone else and you're priced the same and so forth. So, if you are here, then you might want to say, "Hey, if I cut my price in half or to a tenth of the competitors, then essentially what I'm doing is I'm saying, this market that might before be a billion-dollar market, I'm now going to slice it in half. What's going to happen is that it's no longer a billion-dollar market. It is now half a billion-dollar market. But because I'm there first with my low pricing, I might be able to capture 30% of this now smaller market. So, this is why I sometimes call the strategy of low pricing shrinking the market. So, it is a shrinking the market strategy where saying, "This thing that you're used to paying 100 bucks for, now it's 10 bucks or it's 50 bucks." And in that, you're suddenly getting a lot of the customers' attention to you instead of to the competitors. So, a few examples of shrinking the market. So, when Atlassian launched Jira in the early 2000s, they were competing against sort of large, like, what it was called big iron uh competitors, like, HP um and other sort of quality assurance uh providers. And they were entering the market with prices for Jira. I think one of the iconic early prices was 10 users for $10 a month. So, this was a fraction of the cost of the previous uh market players in the quality assurance space. And suddenly they were able to capture a big part of the market by going so low. Also, they actually acquired more users that didn't before had access to [music] to these tools. So, but effectively, they shrunk the market. They made it a cheaper product compared to what we had before. So, the first strategy is to have a low price and hence shrink the market but gain a larger part of that market. So, you capture a larger part by lowering the overall price. So, high volume, low-price strategy number one. Strategy number two is a premium strategy. So, let's do a bit of math here. So, let's say that your baseline is that you have a price of 10. >> [music] >> And then you see here, so there's a price of 10. And then you see you have a customer acquisition cost of, let's say, two. >> [music] >> And then you see, say you have a delivery cost of another two. And let's say you have service costs of one. So, it costs you two to acquire a customer. It costs you two to onboard that customer, get them up and running, all these things. So, this is just sort of one-time costs. And then every year, in order to have the service running and everything else, you have a price of sort of one. So, you sort of add all this up and then you get five left over. So, that's great. So, you have five of profit to cover your general expenses, new development, all these. So, if all of your competitors are doing the same, then essentially, it's just a matter of time and how good your product is to the others, but it isn't really sort of a pricing strategy. So, what you might want to do is you want to want to create this other scenario where you say, "Hey, we're actually going to go premium here. So, we're going to double the price." So, what's going to happen is you now need to sort of figure out how you want to spend all this money because the pricing that you have is also the budget you have >> [music] >> to then use on all these other things. So, you could say, "Hey, with a price of 20, you might actually say, let's actually triple the acquisition cost. We might triple the delivery cost, the onboarding. Maybe the service is the same. So, we're adding this up, we still get a seven of profit left over." So, with a premium scenario where we just charge twice everyone else, we can actually spend three times as much acquiring the customer. We can onboard them three times as well. So, we can spend three times as much time, like, creating bespoke integrations, doing configuration work, doing training of their people, just making sure that they adopt the product, etc., etc. So, actually generating value for the client. Probably the service cost, the fixed costs in the business are the same. And we actually can still end up with more profit. So, by having a premium strategy, what you're doing is that you're saying, "Hey, market, I want more money from you because I have a good way to turn that money into value." Because of course, these seven, you now have an extra two or an extra seven, depending on how you look at it, to also invest into future product development. So, having a high price can turn into this virtuous cycle where you charge more money, then you can spend more money to acquire customers. So, you actually can have an even higher sort of revenue growth. But you can also have money left over to actually have more product development. And thus, the whole momentum of the business actually is stronger than if you just stayed at the sort of same price than everyone [music] else. So, overall, I think that you have these sort of two directions to go. You have the premium high-price where you outspend everybody else. And then you have the low-price shrinking the market just trying to acquire way more customers than anyone else. So, the idea is that low-price usually means extremely high volume of customers. But also, you need to actually be able to maintain this low price over time or competitors will eat it. So, these are the first two scenarios. Then, you can say [music] that the premium strategy can just keep on going in time. The low-price strategy can just keep on going in time. If you have a low-price strategy that keeps on going in time, it means that you need to be able to deliver your service or your product cheaper than anyone else over time. So, if you undercut the market by half the price, and then you acquire a lot of customers. If your competitors also undercut you by half the price, suddenly you're just ending up with less profit. So, for example, Rackspace did this back in 2013 for cloud computing costs and said, "Hey, we're now going to slash, I think it was 33% of their price to acquire a lot of customers." What happened? AWS said, "That's great. We want to play that game, too." And they just also slashed their price. And suddenly Rackspace was just left with less profit. And they did not have the same scale as Amazon. So, ultimately, they were squeezed out of the price game. >> [music] >> And they were relegated to a much more fringe or smaller position of the market than they had intended to. So, their low-price scenario did not stick because they couldn't keep their costs low for a long time. >> [music] >> So, if you have a low-price entry scenario, you need to be able to keep the low price by having a low cost base compared to everyone else forever. So, it is a very difficult pricing strategy to actually execute. Very, very few companies can have a low-price strategy for long [music] because it requires you to have a better technology and better delivery mechanism than anyone else in the market. Premium, this can happen here. If you keep this for long, you just need to be able to keep delivering more value than anyone else, caring more about your customers in order to actually keep that high price point. What often happens is that you will find that you have an ICP, you have a certain customer profile that you want to focus more and more on. So, if you get squeezed as a premium provider in a marketplace and competitors come in and try to offer the same value as you, you either just keep performing better than they are. You just keep being the iPhone. You just keep, like, delivering something that the market wants to pay a premium for. Or, you find a smaller part of the market that you can keep doing it in, which is more easily defended. So, these are the two long-term versions of the strategy. Then you have two sort of crossover strategies. You have a low-price that goes to a high-price. This is what we would call a land and expand. So, the land and expand strategy essentially means that you go in with an offering for a low-price. >> [music] >> You acquire a lot of customers. Now you have those customers. And now you make them worth more by offering them something that really is sold at full price or premium. So, this can be anything where say, "Hey, for example, Atlassian with Jira say, we're just going to offer you something that's super cheap. And we are getting a lot of customers in. And then we're going to sell you, like, GitHub and like, the whole other sort of portfolio of products we have. And we're going to have a profitable position in the market, but not because of that low-price entry product, but because of everything else that we invented and had to sell you later that was not necessarily as cheap. So, all the other products aren't competing [music] on a low price offering. They're competing much more on a value-based offering, but the is a ecosystem that they build up where they get customers at a low price and they expand them to a high price is really what the strategy is. So, if you have a road map or you have a vision of what you want to sell, you can have a land and expand strategy where you start low, acquire the customer base or the user base, might even be free, and then you [music] upsell them to something that is full price later on. The reverse of this is what we might call skimming. So, this is the strategy where you go in often in a new category and say, "Hey, we think that we can do something really great here." And you charge a premium price for it. And then, instead of trying to defend that price when new entrants actually enter and try to take away your profits, what you do is you just start to lower the price. So, you just start high and then you just go low low low low low in order to fend off competition. So, you can do this also to really monetize those few customers in the market that are willing to pay a premium to be there early to buy the product early. And then, as you go along and competitors enter, you can then start to lower the price to get access to more and more of that marketplace. So, this usually means that you start high and then end medium or low or even as the low price competitor in this market over time. So, >> [music] >> essentially, you have these four strategies. Let's call them one, two, premium, low price, three, land and expand, and four, skimming. So, remember, your pricing strategy should support the business strategy. This has a lot to do with how your product looks today and how your product's going to look in the future. Depending on that, make a choice. And whatever you do, don't try to just be in the middle. Good luck.

What Good SaaS Pricing Looks Like: Bechmarks, Signals and Metrics

How do you know if your pricing is actually good? In this video, I explain why customer reactions—not opinions—are the best signal. When customers nod along as you present your value proposition, packaging, features, and pricing logic, you know you’re on the right track. At that point, price becomes just one friction point—not four.

I also walk through a five-slide pricing validation framework you can use in real conversations with customers. This structure helps you isolate where pricing breaks down—whether it’s your value proposition, packaging, feature set, metric, or price point itself. If you want a simple, practical way to test pricing without running a massive pricing project, this is the easiest approach.

metadata.title: The Founder's Guide to SaaS Pricing in the AI Era: Seat-Based, Usage-Based, or Hybrid? | Roee Hartuv
metadata.author: Champion Leadership
metadata.shortDescription:
AI didn’t just change the product. It changed the cost structure underneath it.

Classical SaaS could run at 85% to 95% gross margins because serving the next customer cost almost nothing. With AI, every interaction carries real compute cost, and a small group of heavy users can quietly turn profitable growth into daily losses.

This conversation explores how founders should rethink pricing and packaging, why hybrid models may offer the right balance between predictability and usage, and what it takes to price around jobs to be done instead of feature lists.

You’ll also hear why outcome-based pricing is harder than it sounds, how often pricing should be reviewed, and how an AI-generated pricing table nearly created a $1,000-a-year tier for a company selling to mid-market customers at $12,000 a year.

If AI is part of your product, your pricing can’t stay static.

42:35 Shifting from scarcity mindset

The Revenue Forecasting Crisis: How are we going to forecast our revenue? We don't know.  [00:13:36 → 00:13:40]
AI Pricing: And then go to your customers and actually ask them, what is the value that this new feature AI agent created for you? [00:18:41 → 00:18:48]

Why Enterprise Customers Shouldn’t Vibe Code: "enterprise customers should not vibe code. It's too dangerous for their organization." [00:32:59 → 00:33:04]
Claude’s Pricing Strategy Was “Spot On”: She came with a pricing strategy that Claude created. It was spot on. [00:34:32 → 00:34:35]

SaaS Leadership Lessons:
1. **Assign clear pricing ownership.**  
Pricing needs one accountable owner and regular reviews as the product and market change. [39:00]
2. **Measure AI unit economics by user.**  
Heavy users can quietly erase margins, so track cost and profitability at the individual-user level. [26:04]
3. **Consider hybrid pricing.**  
Combine a recurring base fee with usage-based charges to balance predictability and serving costs. [12:57]
4. **Test before adopting outcome-based pricing.**  
Customer outcomes vary, so validate the value with a small group before rebuilding your model. [18:06]
5. **Package around jobs to be done.**  
Feature-based tiers invite discounting. Packages tied to customer goals support stronger value conversations. [21:51]
6. **Review pricing whenever the business changes.**  
Revisit it after product launches and during long sales cycles. Track usage, churn, win-loss data, and margins. [28:10]

metadata.title: SaaS Pricing Strategy: Why Most New Startups Moved Beyond Per-Seat
metadata.author: Andrew Garberson
metadata.shortDescription:
SaaS pricing strategy for new startups: across 160 modern software companies, 56% of those founded after 2020 moved away from pure per-seat billing. The first price a startup picks is almost always wrong, but the dollar figure isn't what breaks the business. It's the unit of measurement.

Picking what you count matters more than the number on your pricing page. This video covers what new startups count instead of seats, and how to choose your unit.

Read the full breakdown on First to Market:
https://www.firsttomarket.co/p/startups-price-too-low-or-sell-the?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=pricing_seats

Get a new data-backed breakdown every week:
https://www.firsttomarket.co/?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=pricing_seats

segments.text: The first price that a startup picks is
almost always wrong. But that doesn't
mean it's an error, it just hasn't been
shaped by market feedback yet. Okay, so
if we're pretty sure that we're going to
have to adapt our pricing, how do we
make sure that one, it's possible to do,
and two, that we're set up for success
when we do that? So I coded the pricing
models of 160 startups in my category
database. And then I combed through 20
of the CRM leaders for specific details
and lessons for us all to take away.
The number that we put next to the
dollar sign almost never turned out to
be the problem. What kept showing up was
the unit. So not how much we charge, but
how we decided to count what we charge.
You know, we can always change the
number of what we charge. We can raise
it, we can lower it or discount it, we
can grandfather people in or put it
behind an annual monthly toggle. Most of
the companies in my database have done
some sort or all of that without
customers blowing up Reddit.
So changing what you count is a
different situation. Every enterprise
deal resets. Every account margin
shifts. Every customer is forced to
refactor and re-evaluate your
relationship with them. For the last 20
years, if you sold software, you were
probably selling it based on seats. That
was the default and we didn't have to
think about it very much. But it's not
that simple anymore. Of the companies
that I audited who have been founded
since 2020, 56% of them have some sort
of price mechanism on usage or outcomes
instead of only seats. In CRM, for
example, Light field gives away
unlimited seats on most of its plans and
uses credits instead. And Adio keeps
super affordable seat based pricing, but
added two separate credit pools on top
of it. So it's seats and credits, not or
credits. Day AI even prices based on the
type of work that your CRM is going to
do for you. First question to ask is
what does our customer already count?
The strongest units are numbers that our
buyers were already tracking before we
existed. It's a number that is already
in one of their dashboards somewhere.
So, let's start with Fin, the AI help
desk. That company charges per
resolution, no longer per agent or per
seat the way that its predecessor
Intercom did. Gorgeous is another help
desk company that prices based on
monthly ticket volume that the support
team already has to work through. An
Ashby an applicant tracking system
prices on company head count rather than
the number of recruiter seats because
head count is a business metric that
matters to everyone in the company. So,
I talked to Fin Glover who runs
Schematic. Uh it's a usage-based billing
platform and he described this step to
me as a translation. You figure out the
value that your customer already
intuitively perceives and then you find
the unit that captures it. You're not
inventing a metric here, it's more about
locating the one that matters to them.
And the common misstep is picking the
unit that's just easiest for you to
measure. Measuring seats are super easy,
but easy to measure and meaningful to
your customer, those are two very
different things. Question two is does
that number go up when our customer
wins? This is the one that decides
whether your pricing fights with your
customer or, you know, grabs onto their
coattails and rides along with them.
Ashby could see that when their best
customers grew head counted their
company, that was the customer
succeeding and Ashby's revenue would
also go up with them. Lightfield uses
credits against selling activities like
meetings booked and prospects contacted.
So, when the bill goes up, it's because
the sales team is actually working more,
not just because the company hires more
sales people to sit at desks. The goal
here is that the revenue that we're
making is a byproduct of customer
results. We get paid because they are
getting more value from our product or
service. But, more usage does not
automatically mean that they're getting
more value. It only really counts if
value outpaces the usage costs that
you're paying.
There even examples of usage costs
scaling faster than usage revenue. And
so, at that point we're just creating
worse margins for ourselves as our
customers do more of the thing that we
want them to do.
Question three is, can we say the price
out loud without having to sit down and
explain it? So, Finn Glover at Schematic
also told me that most of us are much
better at pitching our product than we
are at pitching our pricing. If our
pricing models require long-winded
justifications and explanations,
it's something that's going to be super
difficult for the champions at our
prospects' companies to explain to their
bosses, and their bosses to explain to
procurement, and so on. So, nutshell
prices by hours saved per month. Finn,
the AI help desk charges by resolutions.
You can say both of those in a short
sentence, and
they're easy to understand.
Now, compare that to the idea of an AI
credit. A lot of the companies that I
audit are, you know, they'll bundle 50
workflow credits a year into the
entry-level tier. But, it's almost never
obvious whether 50 is generous or is it
stingy. What does 50 credits actually do
for me as the buyer and my goals?
So, some companies will even go as far
as publishing like a table on their help
docs to show what each credit is worth
or how many actions that you can get for
it. Okay, that's transparent, but if the
buyer needs reference documentation to
even roughly estimate how much they're
going to pay each month,
the model is way too complex and too
difficult for people to understand.
And the misstep here, when we hit
resistance in the buying process, the
instinct is to that we're just too
expensive, but sometimes the blocker
isn't price. It's that prospects just
can't follow or understand the unit and
they can't translate that unit into a
positive return on investment. Question
four, will you be able to tell whether
or not the relationship is working? So,
the CEO of Flexprice and open-source
usage-based billing company pointed out
to me that there are two really good
ways to check this. First check is gross
margin on our top 10% of accounts, not
just the blended average across all
accounts. The blended number can
actually hide the tail until it's too
late. So, even Kyle Poyar has flagged
this uh same pattern with token
consumption among the heaviest AI users.
Our biggest accounts can be our least
profitable ones and raising our prices
across the board doesn't fix the top
tier when it's structurally underwater.
The second one is to split expansion
revenue into two different numbers.
There's growth because customers use
more and there's growth because we
charged customers more. The first one
suggests that our pricing is actually
working and the second one just suggests
that our growth is coming from
renegotiation or restructured
agreements.
So, take all of this as permission to be
wrong about the first price that you
introduced to market as long as you're
right about the mechanism that supports
it. So, pick a unit that the buyer
already counts. Make sure that it climbs
as they win and make sure that you can,
you know, say it to them in one sentence
and have anyone at their company
understand it. And lastly, start by
measuring it today so that you know
whether it's going to work as your
company scales.
Even if we have to change prices year in
and year out as the inputs change and
the costs vary. Having the right unit
will help us figure out the rest as we
go. The full article is in the
description. It is totally free.
Subscribe and you will get a new
framework like this every week or find
them all at firsttomarket.co.

metadata.title: Why Enterprise Buyers Hate AI Pricing Models - The AI vs. SaaS Pricing War
metadata.author: Ultimate CFO
metadata.shortDescription:
For decades, B2B software ran on a simple formula: pay per seat, use the tool. But AI has clearly broken that model. In this video, we break down why SaaS pricing feels like a predictable gym membership, while AI pricing increasingly feels like a casino—where costs are volatile, and the risk has quietly shifted from the vendor to the buyer.

As a CFO and strategy consultant, I’ve spent the last 10 years working in pricing strategy. Today, we’re looking at why the classic "per-seat" subscription is dying in the AI era, and why the alternatives are causing headaches for both founders and Fortune 500 procurement teams.

In this video, we cover:
• The Efficiency Paradox: What happens when the software does the work and you’re pricing per seat?
• The Unit Economics Trap: Why AI’s variable costs make the old SaaS margin math impossible.
• The Risk Transfer: Why a buyer is terrified of unpredictable invoices (and the data proving costs overrun by 30-50%).
• Enterprise Pushback: How buyers are fighting back and forcing a return to fixed fees.
• The Hybrid Future: Why models like Salesforce’s AgentForce are pivoting.
• Shelfware 2.0: The danger of buying AI "capability" without the organizational redesign to match.

If you're a founder building an AI tool, a CFO approving software budgets, or just trying to understand where the industry is headed, this analysis is for you.

#AIPricing #SaaS #PricingStrategy #B2BSaaS #StartupFinance #EnterpriseSales #CFO

segments.text: We all know per seat pricing in SaaS B2B software. Well, this has been the traditional pricing model
for decades in software sales. In today's video, I'll be talking about why this model
is not working well for AI powered software companies and how the pricing paradigm has
started to shift. Hey there, my name is Roland Umlauft. Welcome back to my channel. I have been
working with startups and innovation projects for almost two decades as CFO and strategy
consultant and I've been doing advisory on pricing strategy specifically for a good 10 years now
with software basically being a tool for humans value scales in a linear fashion with the number
of people using it. So why is pricing starting to shift away from this classical perceived
subscription model? There are two main reasons for this. One something I'd call the efficiency
paradox and two really pure and simple unit economics math. Let's start by talking about the
efficiency generative artificial intelligence and autonomous agentic workflows. they are
fundamentally breaking the correlation between the value that is being delivered and the amount
of users. When software is starting to perform the work itself rather than merely supporting
the human performing the work the unit of value is going to shift from the user to the task or
to the outcome. So, if AI products deliver the productivity that companies are promising and,
that's yet to be proven at this stage, enterprises should eventually also need fewer people and
therefore will buy fewer licenses and that's creating an efficiency paradox that doesn't
work so well with a per user license as a pricing model in itself as you would start selling less
licenses the more efficient your software becomes. Second, let's talk about the unit economics issue.
In traditional SaaS, the marginal cost of a user was near zero. So you had this really high gross
margins from your flat-fee per-user model and you had security in your gross margin. The problem is
that AI features, they're consuming significant variable computing costs and those explode with
usage. This is why we've observed a huge drop in seat-based pricing as a primary strategy and
we're seeing models with a usage-based component emerge over the last 12-24 months or so. However,
this shift is creating a massive problem for buyers and it is essentially an a shift of
financial risk from the software company to the client. In the old, SaaS world, the primary risk
that a software buyer was facing was something, we would call shelfware. So, that means basically
you're paying for licenses that are hardly being used. Well, this is wasteful. Your total cost
was always capped by the contract and it was fully predictable. In the AI era usage aligned
pricing - it eliminates shelfrisk. So, this is great. It makes your purchase more efficient,
but simultaneously it makes budgets extremely unpredictable. Because your AI consumption
can be volatile. It can be driven by seasonal spikes, rogue automated workflows, some crazy
super users. Your costs can spiral and research shows that actual AI consumption costs frequently
are exceeding the initial estimates provided by the software vendor by up to 30 or even 50%. So,
how are enterprise buyers specifically perceiving this? Honestly, not so great. CFOs and procurement
teams, they're used to headcount-based software budgets and no uncertainty, right? So, shifting
those budgets from labor to variable software is a nightmare and a major stumbling block in
your negotiation with a multinational uh buyer. a standard subscription invoice. It's super easy
to process and allocate across cost centers. Variable invoices that fluctuate by 40% month
over month is something most of these enterprise buyers, they are just not equipped for that. So
what happens? Enterprise buyers are pushing back massively. They're demanding predictability even
at the expense of those theoretical efficiency gains from usage-based pricing. As a result,
some industry leaders actually have adapted their consumption-based pricing models towards
seat-based or fixed-fee hybrid subscription models. These are significantly different from
the traditional seat-based models we've seen in the SaaS era. AI hybrid models will always
carry a second parameter like credit caps, AI units, tokens or so-called, fair use thresholds
that are designed to protect the software company's gross margin against any kind of
spiraling computing cost. As a famous example, Salesforce's AI product, Agent Force, it was
initially priced purely as a consumption-based model. Well, the company now offers buyers a
choice between consumption-based pricing, flex credits, and per user pricing. But also that
assumption that we had behind most of this early AI pricing strategy work of largescale workforce
reductions that has not come true at least for now. So some industry reports actually have shown
that you know more than half of companies that reduce their workforce due to AI later
regretted that decision. Simultaneously about 60% of industry leaders they expect AI investment to
actually increase their headcount rather than reduce it compared to with just under 20% of
companies expecting it to decrease. Well, with hybrid subscription models enterprise buyers are
essentially paying for capability not necessarily for outcomes. that budget predictability that
we're creating with these models it does obviously come with large shelfware risk and
let's be honest AI value in an organization it's not going to emerge automatically with a software
purchase it's going to require a significant process redesign something very similar to the
digital transformation efforts we've seen in the early 2000s. Without that work, AI software is
going to become the most expensive shelfware that enterprises have ever purchased. Over time, we can
expect pricing models to become more fragmented. If anything, products like co-pilots are likely to
remain seat-based. Others like process automation is more likely to shift towards more calibrated
usage or outcome based pricing. If you found this useful, please hit that like button. Also,
please let me know your experience and roadblocks with B2B AI pricing in the comments. Subscribe
to my channel for more AI pricing and startup finance topics. I'll see you in the next video.

metadata.title: Per Seat Pricing Is Ending? 3 SaaS Pricing Models Replacing It (Atlassian Rovo, Dec 3)
metadata.author: Soft Learn Hub
metadata.shortDescription:
On 3 December 2026, Atlassian starts billing Rovo AI usage on top of Jira and Confluence seats, and extra usage is on by default. Is this the end of per-seat pricing? Not quite. Here are the three pricing models you'll be billed on in 2027, plus four moves to protect your software budget.

In this video:
0:00 Atlassian's 3 December change
0:27 The twist: seats aren't dying
0:38 Why seat pricing worked, and why AI agents break it
1:10 Model 1: seats + credits (Atlassian, monday.com, Microsoft Copilot)
1:34 Model 2: outcomes (HubSpot, Intercom)
1:47 Model 3: the enterprise flat fee (Salesforce AELA)
2:04 Your software bill stops being fixed
2:15 4 moves before your next renewal
2:53 Recap

Sources:
- Atlassian usage-based pricing page and Rovo usage limits (billing from 3 Dec 2026, extra usage on by default, $0.01 per credit, alerts at 80% and 100%)
- Stripe SaaS pricing survey of 200 leaders (19 Oct 2026)
- monday.com: AI credit bundle required for new accounts from 6 May 2026
- Microsoft 365 Copilot pricing ($30 per user per month; agents billed in Copilot Credits)
- HubSpot Customer Agent: $0.50 per resolved conversation (since April 2026)
- Forrester on the Salesforce AELA (17 Dec 2025)
———

metadata.title: 8 SaaS pricing models explained in under 3 minutes
metadata.author: Binary Stream Software
metadata.shortDescription:
With the growing adoption of SaaS pricing models, figuring out how to price and bill for software has become an intricate process requiring data and insight into your customers’ mindsets. Traditional pricing models such as cost-based pricing (i.e. figuring out your costs and adding a profit margin) have fallen by the wayside. Many SaaS companies are implementing subscription services that focus on adding value and increasing recurring revenues through a mixture of different billing models.

Deciding on the right SaaS pricing model takes time. You need to make sure products and services are profitable and set billing up to make it easier to predict revenue and scale with your customers as they grow. In this video, we will explore each pricing model in action.

00:00 -  #1 Pay-as-you-go pricing
00:18 - #2 Per-user pricing
00:31 - #3 Tiered pricing
00:42 - #4 Flat-rate pricing
00:58 - #5 Feature-based pricing
01:14 - #6 Bundling
01:27 - #7 Freemium
01:40 - #8 Hybrid pricing
1:52 - Which should you choose?

#SaaS #PricingModels #Subscriptions
keywords: how to create a pricing model

segments.text: Let's take a quick look at the eight most popular SaaS
pricing models.
Pay as you go pricing allows customers
to pay only for what they use.
Phone companies are common users of this model
and they'll break billing down by the number of texts
or minutes used. Per User pricing allows
customers to pay for each user that uses the software,
and this encourages customers to evaluate which users actually
need access to that service. Tiered Pricing
allows for flexibility while giving customers
the opportunity to level up as they start to see the benefits.
This method combines well with other models.
Flat-rate pricing is a one- size-fits-all strategy that
cuts down the possibility of confusion for your customers.
Companies charge all customers the same amount regardless
of usage, users, or features needed.
Feature-based pricing is best for software
with a lot of impressive features.
Users will pay based on the number of features
they want to access.
And of course, the highest tier usually
offers considerably more features than the lower ones.
Bundling appeals to more of the market
with strategic packages that are built for specific targets
different customers want different things,
and this pricing strategy acknowledges that.
Freemium pricing allows customers to try services
for free and many will then upgrade to the paid version
once they've been convinced of the value.
Free versions are often ad supported. Hybrid pricing is
a combination of any of the other pricing models
and gives companies the flexibility to better price
their services based on customer and market research.
Once you've considered all the pricing models,
it's time to decide what works best for your company.
You need to choose not only the right strategy,
but the right tools to help implement it.
Generally you'll need to use a more powerful product that
can handle more complicated pricing and billing models.
Find out more by downloading our Ultimate Guide
to Subscription Management.

Value added resellers are an important part of the ICT ecosystem and without them, a lot of great products and services would never make it to the enterprise.  But what are value added resellers, or VARs, and why do they exist?

 Listen to this 10-minute podcast as Ben Fox, one of TC2’s Managing Directors, and Joe Schmidt describe what VARs do, explain some of the nuances of their pricing, and offer up some tips to help you get the most value from your value added reseller.

 If you would like to learn more about our experience in this space, please visit our  Hardware & Licensing and Success Stories webpages.

you in all of the countries in which you operate in fact quite the reverse and when purchasing hardware companies typically want to transact with their reseller on an in-country basis meaning the var needs to have an in-country entity and be appropriately licensed to sell the required products in that country otherwise the customer may end up needing to deal with various importation logistics serving as the importer of record and fulfilling responsibilities and costs associated with that and avoiding that is exactly why you're engaging with the var in the first place so that they do those things so it's important to comprehensively vet which countries the var can sell to you on a local basis and then the other coverage question is which oems the bar is authorized to sell and that may also vary by country so you can see how this rapidly gets quite complex so we found a good way to approach all this is to develop a matrix of the oems and the countries in which you need to buy hardware and effectively have potential vars respond to that matrix and fill it out with a specific coverage that they can provide you know i'll bet a lot of enterprises think that these var arrangements are pretty straightforward but as you just highlighted var services can actually quickly get quite complicated yes definitely and that's especially true when you're dealing with purchases all over the world i actually think var services you know often seem rather mundane but actually purchases of i.t products and services to resellers is typically a very significant part of companies i.t budgets and so resale is actually quite important and optimizing the cost of your var services can have a quite significant positive impact on your company's bottom line so the other thing i would say is that even once you've negotiated robust arrangements for our services we find that it's still important to solicit quotes from multiple vars for individual transactions and funnily enough we actually see sometimes that the variation in logistics and shipping charges and even taxes between vars can actually be greater than the variation in the markup fee so it's good to get quotes so you can compare those fees over and above your understanding of who's got the cheapest market and also a good tip for listing quotes when you're doing that is to insist that the vars break out any different items they aggregate under the term taxes so the differences between quotes can be better understood and so that nothing is hidden under taxes for instance we see sometimes things like importation and customs fees not taxes being represented or referred to as taxes in quotes i know that we're running out of time joe but i did want to make a final point for the customers arrangements and contracts with vars they don't replace or reduce the importance of having relationships with those key oems that you purchase products from through those bars you can absolutely negotiate certain aspects of transactions of oem purchases with the reseller but you absolutely still need to engage directly with the oem to negotiate the pricing and the terms that the oem will extend to you through metadata.author: Tech Field Day Plus
metadata.shortDescription: Value-added resellers (VARs) are often characterized as useless, adding a needless cost for something that should be sold direct to customers. In this On-Premise IT Roundtable, the panel discusses where the value actually gets added and what benefits VARs can still provide. It was an interesting discussion with a lot of different perspectives.

metadata.title: How to Stop Renewing SaaS Licenses at Last Year's Count
metadata.author: CloudEagle
metadata.shortDescription:
How many unused SaaS seats did you just renew?

In this episode of Insight in Minutes, we cover where SaaS license spend leaks, how to match license types to real usage, and what a license management tool should handle on rules you set.

Departments buy on headcount, not usage. When someone leaves, the seat frees up but never makes it back to the pool, so you buy what you already own. Then the renewal arrives and gets signed at last year's number.

Chapters:
 0:00 Where SaaS license spend quietly leaks
 1:03 What license management actually covers
 1:47 Why unused seats are a budget problem
 2:32 Matching license types to real usage
 3:18 Shadow IT, missed renewals, and idle seats
 4:01 Centralizing inventory and reviewing before renewal
 4:51 What a license management tool should automate
 5:27 Where to start this week

Read the full blog: https://www.cloudeagle.ai/blogs/saas-license-management?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=insight-in-minutes&utm_content=ep73-blog

Learn more about License Management: https://www.cloudeagle.ai/saas-management/license-management?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=insight-in-minutes&utm_content=ep73-lp

#licensemanagement  #saasmanagement #licenseharvesting #itam #saasspend #cloudeagle

segments.text: Hey everyone, welcome to episode 73 of
Insights in Minutes. Picture this, you
realize your company's paying for
dozens, sometimes hundreds of SaaS
licenses nobody's touched in months.
That's real money slipping away every
single day.
>> And even scarier, without a handle on
it, you could be doubling up on
subscriptions, missing shadow IT, or
even risking compliance. I'm so glad
we're diving into SaaS license
management today.
>> Absolutely.
I'm your host, and joining me is our
SaaS optimization expert. Together,
we'll walk you through the nuts and
bolts of managing these licenses before
they manage you.
>> We'll clarify what SaaS license

features for license management tools,
and wrap up with clear steps you can
take to stop wasting SaaS dollars. Let's
get started. So, to kick things off,
what do we really mean when we talk
about SaaS license management? It seems
simple, but there's more than meets the
eye.
>> Totally. At its core, it's about
tracking, allocating, and renewing
software licenses throughout their life
cycle. This means knowing exactly which
team member has what, who's using it,
and how much it's costing you.
>> That tracking piece is so essential.
I've seen companies lose track licenses
go unused, or worse, people lose access
to tools they need.
>> And the real magic happens when
organizations adjust license assignments
as people change roles or leave. Not
only do you avoid paying for unused
seats, but it keeps access secure and
up-to-date.
>> That brings us right to the big
question. Why should companies even care
about this? Isn't a small bit of extra
software spend just the cost of doing
business?
>> Well, it adds up shockingly fast. Cost
savings are huge when you identify
unused or duplicate licenses. You can
reclaim them instead of buying more. One
audit might save a company tens of
thousands.
>> And then there's shadow IT where teams
sign up for tools without telling IT.
That's risky and expensive, right?
>> Exactly.
Central oversight prevents SaaS sprawl,
unexpected spending, and lets IT
allocate the right tools to the right
people. All while keeping budgets in
check.
>> I keep hearing about all these different
SaaS license types: flat rate, tiered,
freemium.
Can you break down what each of these
actually means for a business?
>> Sure. Flat rate means you pay a fixed
price, no matter how much you use.
Tiered plans give you options based on
features or usage limits. Freemium lets
you try basic features for free and
upgrade for more.
>> So, if a team's usage fluctuates a lot,
maybe usage-based makes more sense. It
seems like matching the license model to
your actual needs is key.
>> Absolutely.
And don't forget per user or per feature
models. Those give flexibility if your
head count or feature needs change. The
trick is knowing your usage patterns so
you don't overpay.
>> Sounds good in theory, but the real
world's messy.
What are the biggest headaches companies
run into when trying to manage all this?
>> Limited visibility is probably the top
one often. Teams don't know who's using
what. Then there's shadow IT where
employees sign up for tools under the
radar, creating both cost and security
headaches.
>> And I imagine contract renewals can
sneak up, too, right? Suddenly you're
auto-renewed on a pricey plan you barely
use.
>> Exactly. Missed renewals, unused
licenses, and complicated vendor
contracts are all common. Without a
system, it's almost impossible to keep
everything aligned and cost-effective.
>> Let's get tactical. How do the best
teams keep things under control? I'm
sure listeners want strategies they can
put into play.
>> First off, centralizing your license
inventory is a game-changer. Keep it
updated as people join, change roles, or
leave. Then, review actual usage before
every renewal, reclaim, or reassign
licenses instead of buying more.
>> Automation must help, too.
Are there tools that can track renewals,
alert you to unused licenses, or even
handle revoking access automatically?
>> Definitely. Good SaaS license management
software does just that. Also,
standardizing your procurement and
approval process stops duplicate
purchases and keeps everything compliant
and cost-effective.
>> If someone's shopping for a license
management tool, what should they look
for beyond the basics?

metadata.title: True-Up Flexibility in Microsoft EA – How to Avoid Paying for Unused Licenses
metadata.author: Redress Compliance
metadata.shortDescription:
True-Up Flexibility in Microsoft EA – How to Avoid Paying for Unused Licenses

📉 One of the biggest traps in a Microsoft Enterprise Agreement (EA) is the inability to reduce license counts mid-term. You can add licenses anytime, but scaling down? That’s much harder — and can lead to millions in wasted spend over three years.

In this video, we show CIOs, CFOs, IT procurement leaders, and SAM professionals how to negotiate true-down rights, create flexible licensing structures, and avoid paying for shelfware.

📌 What you’ll learn:

Why Microsoft’s standard EA model locks you into unused licenses

How to negotiate annual true-down rights and license elasticity

Creative models like “elastic pools” and shortened terms for volatile users

How to use CSP plans strategically to pressure Microsoft for better EA terms

How to trade new product adoption for license reduction flexibility

Why flexibility must be documented in the contract — not left to verbal promises

💼 Bottom line: If your business may shrink, restructure, or shift during your EA term, license flexibility is essential. Lock in true-down rights early — and manage usage closely to reduce cost and risk.

🔗 Need help negotiating true-down rights in your Microsoft EA?
Visit redresscompliance.com — Independent advisors trusted by global enterprises to optimize Microsoft contracts and reduce licensing waste.

🔍 Tags / Keywords:
Microsoft true-up vs true-down, Microsoft EA flexibility, Microsoft unused licenses, Microsoft EA shelfware, Microsoft license reduction strategy, Microsoft CSP vs EA, Microsoft elastic license pool, Microsoft EA term negotiation, EA right-sizing strategy, Redress Compliance, Microsoft SAM optimization, license true-down clause, CIO software cost control, Microsoft EA negotiation tips

So contact us at YouAttest - we will address your SaaS license “Rightsizing” and you identity audit concerns -  https://youattest.com/contact/

Get Rightsized!

metadata.title: Partner Viewpoint: How Microsoft + Pax8 are skilling up the channel
metadata.author: Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program
metadata.shortDescription:
Born-in-the-cloud distributor, Pax8, makes it easier for MSPs to buy, sell, and manage Microsoft solutions to help serve SMB customers. 

To listen to the podcast, visit: https://msft.it/6009jsTwX

#MSPartner #MicrosoftPartner #MPIVodcast

segments.text: (upbeat music)
- Welcome to the Microsoft Partner Innovation Vodcast.
I'm your host, Jennifer Zarate.
Recently, I sat down with Heather Gordon,
worldwide SMB lead at Microsoft,
about what's top of mind
for our small and medium size businesses
and what they are looking for
from partners to help them to be successful.
Today, we are going to talk with one of those partners,
Pax8, to get their perspective
on how they help customers leverage digital technologies
to meet their business goals.
And with that, let me welcome back Heather Gordon
and introduce Nikki Meyer,
corporate vice president of Vendor Alliances,
who is joining us from Pax8.
Thank you both for joining me today.
- Hey Jennifer, it's so great to be back with you today.
- Yeah, great to be with both of you today.
Thanks for inviting me.
- Nikki, why don't you kick us off
and give us an overview of Pax8,
along with some of the solutions that you're working
alongside with Microsoft on.
- We make it super easy for managed service providers
to buy, sell or manage Microsoft solutions
for their customers.
All of this is done through the Pax8 Marketplace.
And what that does is it provides billing, quoting,
provisioning of all cloud products
and it allows them to do a single monthly billing
to the customer.
Apart from this we work super closely with all
of our partners to develop and build solutions
and program to meet the challenges that SMB customers face.
The other thing is,
as we see the market evolving,
Pax8 is starting to develop an advanced product roadmap
and it's gonna truly modernize the industry.
And the focus that we will have with this modernization,
is driving customer acquisition for the channel ecosystem.
- Yeah Nikki, that's awesome.
So as an organization that's really,
really focused on SMB,
you focus on your customer's success.
Tell us about how that improves your delivery model
for your customers.
- Sure Heather, when we talk about customers,
the customer in this sense, to Pax8,
is the managed service provider,
but we focus on providing solutions, services,
sales guidance and enablement with the SMB customer,
always in mind.
As I mentioned earlier,
Pax8's priority is the SMB segment.
So with this, many of our MSP's are
also 100% focused on the segment.
Understanding the customer needs and challenges is key
for driving success within the MSP's.
It's also imperative that we are
able to provide the right coaching and guidance,
in terms of the service offerings that the MSP needs
to develop to meet those customer demands.
So based on that there are kind of three core components
that we have actually built our partner experience on.
The first one is ensuring that we are connecting all
of the MSP's in our ecosystem to a really strong community
of subject matter experts with industry thought leadership.
The best way to learn is
through this peer guidance and interaction.
The second one is ensuring that we have a strong portfolio
of professional services.
And then the third component of that,
really is actually built on the second point
that I had just made.
And it's making sure that we are
able to help the MSP's to skill up their own staff,
to be able to develop and provide those skills
to the end customer.
The reason why this is so important is because,
A, we do wanna skill up the channel to be
able to monetize their own services.
But on the second point,
we really don't wanna limit the MSP
on what they can deliver based on the restraints
of resources that they have within their organization.
- What are some of the key trends
that you're seeing in the marketplace
and how do your Microsoft solutions help address these?
- We're definitely still seeing a really,
really strong trend of SMB customers thinking,
how do I protect myself from the threats that are out there
and how am I also protecting the company PI,
in terms of this now being across multiple devices.
So still a core,
or I'd say a heightened priority on security
within the channel.
But I think another really interesting point that we've seen
is that we're seeing more and more that SMB customers,
they really are not interested
in running their own IT departments,
supporting themselves as an organization.
And they are looking for organizations to provide simple,
affordable and cost effective solutions
that can be implemented and supported on their behalf.
And so it becomes more important for the MSP,
to not always just focus on what is the value proposition
for the solution and how do I sell this particular solution
but tailoring to the SMB customer in terms of,
we know what solution is that you want.
Here's how I'm going to help you deploy,
migrate and support that solution ongoing.
The other things that are super important
to the SMB customer is that ongoing management.
It is around that cost optimization.
So Heather, one of the things you asked is,
how are our solutions supporting that need
from the end customer?
Again, built on a lot of the work that we have
within our professional services.
We do a ton of work around optimizing the migration,
making sure that we're able to deliver that total cost
of ownership to the end customer and really making sure
that we are guiding the MSP's
on the best optimization path forward.
Again, these services are either delivered on behalf
of the MSP or through the skilling that we do
to be able to teach the MSP to deliver for themselves.
- One of the other things that we learned
through the pandemic though was,
companies who were able to take advantage of technologies
to actually help them shift quickly,
to change operating paradigms.
They were in a much,
much better position to stay afloat and thrive
through the pandemic.
However, when we look at the future,
there are certainly some challenges ahead of us.
And these are around ensuring
that customers have the skills to leverage the technologies
that are out there.
And there's quite a scary statistic
that the World Economic Forum tells us in their,
"Future of Jobs" report that about 85 million jobs
could be displaced in the next three years
by the shift to automation.
But the flip side of that is,
there's about 97 million new jobs that are going to emerge.
And we know that SMB's,
through this are going to have to upscale,
as well as re-skill many,
many of their employees.
So Nikki tell me how's Pax8 thinking about this.
- Another very big component of ensuring
that our partners are successful,
is ensuring that they have the technical know-how
and the business skills to be able to grow
and develop their business.
To meet this demand Pax8 developed the Academy,
which is a cloud solution education program
that's been built on learning courses that takes you
through a guided journey to develop those technical skills
within the MSP's organization.
You know, just as a side note,
over the last year we have had over 300 MSP's
that have actually graduated one of the training courses
that we do through Pax8.
We've also developed peer connection groups,
to share industry based practices.
And this is done through our partner, Advisory Council.
We deliver one-on-one coaching.
If you think about it,
particularly within very unique business needs around,
you know, gotta market.
So it's not just around the technical skilling requirements
that are there.
And then we also have more self-serve options,
where we have got an extensive library
of self-guided online resources for the MSP's,
- For MSP's who are listening in,
what should they do if they would like to connect
with Pax8 to consider your services?
- Super simple, go on to pax8.com.
You can go through the signup form,
but those of you that wanna first find out a little bit more
about Pax8, a little bit more detail around the services
and solutions that we do offer to market.
I would encourage you to go
and have a look in our event section
for when we run our next mission briefing.
This is a comprehensive three or four hour event
that we do to prospective new partners,
to really encapsulate and highlight everything
that we provide to MSP's,
which will give you more detail
on the next steps to take with Pax8.
- Excellent, well thank you both so much
for taking the time to speak with me today.
- Yeah, thanks for hosting us, Jennifer.
And Nikki, so great to have you with us today.
- It's been great thank you both so much.
- Absolutely, and that's a wrap on another episode
of the MPI Vodcast.
I'm Jennifer Zarate.
(upbeat music)

The first one is ensuring that we are connecting all of the MSP's in our ecosystem to a really strong community of subject matter experts with industry thought leadership. The best way to learn is through this peer guidance and interaction. The second one is ensuring that we have a strong portfolio of professional services. And then the third component of that, really is actually built on the second point that I had just made. And it's making sure that we are able to help the MSP's to skill up their own staff, to be able to develop and provide those skills to the end customer. The reason why this is so important is because, A, we do wanna skill up the channel to be able to monetize their own services. But on the second point, we really don't wanna limit the MSP on what they can deliver based on the restraints of resources that they have within their organization. - What are some of the key trends that you're seeing in the marketplace and how do your Microsoft solutions help address these? - We're definitely still seeing a really, really strong trend of SMB customers thinking, how do I protect myself from the threats that are out there and how am I also protecting the company PI, in terms of this now being across multiple devices. So still a core, or I'd say a heightened priority on security within the channel. But I think another really interesting point that we've seen is that we're seeing more and more that SMB customers, they really are not interested in running their own IT departments, supporting themselves as an organization. And they are looking for organizations to provide simple, affordable and cost effective solutions that can be implemented and supported on their behalf. And so it becomes more important for the MSP, to not always just focus on what is the value proposition for the solution and how do I sell this particular solution but tailoring to the SMB customer in terms of, we know what solution is that you want. Here's how I'm going to help you deploy, migrate and support that solution ongoing. The other things that are super important to the SMB customer is that ongoing management. It is around that cost optimization. So Heather, one of the things you asked is, how are our solutions supporting that need from the end customer? Again, built on a lot of the work that we have within our professional services. We do a ton of work around optimizing the migration, making sure that we're able to deliver that total cost of ownership to the end customer and really making sure that we are guiding the MSP's on the best optimization path forward. Again, these services are either delivered on behalf of the MSP or through the skilling that we do to be able to teach the MSP to deliver for themselves. - One of the other things that we learned through the pandemic though was, companies who were able to take advantage of technologies to actually help them shift quickly, to change operating paradigms. They were in a much, much better position to stay afloat and thrive through the pandemic. However, when we look at the future, there are certainly some challenges ahead of us. And these are around ensuring that customers have the skills to leverage the technologies that are out there. And there's quite a scary statistic that the World Economic Forum tells us in their, "Future of Jobs" report that about 85 million jobs could be displaced in the next three years by the shift to automation. But the flip side of that is, there's about 97 million new jobs that are going to emerge. And we know that SMB's, through this are going to have to upscale, as well as re-skill many, many of their employees. So Nikki tell me how's Pax8 thinking about this. - Another very big component of ensuring that our partners are successful, is ensuring that they have the technical know-how and the business skills to be able to grow and develop their business. To meet this demand Pax8 developed the Academy, which is a cloud solution education program that's been built on learning courses that takes you through a guided journey to develop those technical skills within the MSP's organization. You know, just as a side note, over the last year we have had over 300 MSP's that have actually graduated one of the training courses that we do through Pax8. We've also developed peer connection groups, to share industry based practices. And this is done through our partner, Advisory Council. We deliver one-on-one coaching. If you think about it, particularly within very unique business needs around, you know, gotta market. So it's not just around the technical skilling requirements that are there. And then we also have more self-serve options, where we have got an extensive library of self-guided online resources for the MSP's, - For MSP's who are listening in, what should they do if they would like to connect with Pax8 to consider your services? - Super simple, go on to pax8.com. You can go through the signup form, but those of you that wanna first find out a little bit more about Pax8, a little bit more detail around the services and solutions that we do offer to market. I would encourage you to go and have a look in our event section for when we run our next mission briefing. This is a comprehensive three or four hour event that we do to prospective new partners, to really encapsulate and highlight everything that we provide to MSP's, which will give you more detail on the next steps to take with Pax8. - Excellent, well thank you both so much for taking the time to speak with me today. - Yeah, thanks for hosting us, Jennifer. And Nikki, so great to have you with us today. - It's been great thank you both so much. - Absolutely, and that's a wrap on another episode of the MPI Vodcast. I'm Jennifer Zarate. (upbeat music)

This is purely a billing frequency change—pricing, contract terms, and subscriptions remain unchanged.

 • Sunday, Feb 1: Final monthly invoice for January orders.

 • Monday, Feb 9: Next weekly invoice (Feb 2–8 orders).
No action required, but we recommend notifying your internal finance/approval teams to prepare.  

Questions? Contact your SoftwareOne representative.

segments.text: Hello and welcome to this tutorial on
how to downsize a subscription.
Generally, an organization will choose
to downsize a subscription when there
are fewer people who require access to a
particular license. This could be due to
a devestature or organizational change
or due to a product or subscription
change.
Downsizing is simply a change order to
reduce the quantity of licenses of a
particular item that is assigned to your
organization. In general, you are only
eligible to downsize your subscriptions
around 30 days prior to the renewal
period. This means that for the
subscriptions that renew monthly, you
can downsize at any time and the changes
will be applied at the next billing
cycle. Annual or multi-year
subscriptions can only be downsized in
the period leading up to the renewal
date that the vendor has set. Remember
to check the vendor terms for grace
period rules and timelines. Since
autorenewal parameters are set by the
vendor, actual renewal times can vary
depending on the time zone you operate
in. For this reason, we recommend that
you complete all downsize orders 2 days
prior to your anniversary date to avoid
your subscriptions from being renewed at
the incorrect quantities. Now, let's see
how to do this in the client portal.
From the homepage, navigate to the menu,
select marketplace, and then agreements.
Choose the agreement that you'll be
making changes to and click buy more.
Change the quantity on the subscription
you want to downsize to the desired
number of licenses. A delta will appear
showing the total reduction. Then click
next. If desired, enter an order ID,
then click next. Review and place your
order. Thank you for watching this short
tutorial. Don't forget to like and
subscribe.

🟣 Zoom Phone: A cloud-based phone solution designed for businesses already using Zoom's ecosystem. It offers seamless video, voice, messaging, and conference calling.
🟣 RingCentral: A comprehensive VoIP communication platform with advanced call management, AI-powered analytics, and robust integrations for larger enterprises.

🟣 Ease of Use: Zoom Phone is simpler and ideal for small to mid-sized teams, especially if Zoom is already in use.

Choose Zoom Phone if you're a small or mid-sized business looking for a user-friendly communication solution.
Choose RingCentral if you need a scalable platform with advanced communication features and detailed analytics.
